#87. Apple HomeView smart home hub review: Siri gets a swanky upcoming house

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1794 w)
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci

Apple HomeView smart home hub review: Siri gets a swanky upcoming house

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1794 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • Apple’s $299 smart display has been sitting on my kitchen counter for about a week.
  • Sources indicate that the HomeView comes in two versions, and both cost $299 in the US.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›.

Apple’s $299 smart display has been sitting on my kitchen counter for about a week. It looks like a hybrid between an old-school iMac and a giant Apple Watch, but it’s a dedicated home for the recently revamped Siri. It’s an easy addition for anyone already committed to Apple gear. If your smart home runs on cameras, locks, or sensors that don’t work with Apple Home, though, you’ll want an upgrade initiative before you buy one.

Sources indicate that the HomeView comes in two versions, and both cost $299 in the US. I tested the tabletop model, which mounts a 7-inch square touchscreen on a domed aluminum speaker base and includes a 30W power adapter and USB-C cable in the box. You can have it in any color you want, as long as it’s silver, starlight, rose pink, or space gray. The Apple HomeView (Wall Mounted) drops the base and its extra speaker hardware, as well as the starlight/rose pink color options, and the panel costs more to put on a wall than its sticker price suggests. It requires a Schneider Home mount sold separately, and those start at $59.95. The cheapest USB-C mount also needs a power adapter of at least 20W, which you’ll have to supply yourself.

Sources indicate that the HomeView looks the way you’d expect an Apple product to look. Once you take off the protective coverings, the 2.1-pound, 6.82-inch tall device is pretty right out of the box. And it looks great between a breadbox and a butcher’s block, especially compared to an older smart screen that I’ve had there for years, which looks ancient next to it. A stainless steel hinge connects the screen to the base, so you can tilt the display toward wherever you’re standing. The screen stays firmly in place after you position it, even if you tap aggressively like I tend to. It doesn’t wobble or shake as you navigate on-screen menus.

Setting up the HomeView feels like setting up an iPhone or any other recent Apple device. It requires an iPhone running iOS 27.2 or later (or an iPad on iPadOS 27.2), so if your phone isn’t there yet, like mine wasn’t, you’ve got to stop and run the revision first. The HomeView played a soft, heavenly drone the whole time it waited, which is a much nicer way to sit through a software update than staring at a progress bar. Also, when you first boot things up, you might think you can immediately start asking for the kind of stuff you ask Siri on your iPhone, but you may have to go through a round or two of launching apps on the HomeView to give them permission to access your account even if your iPhone is with you.

Sources indicate that the HomeView’s Liquid Retina LED backlit screen has looked great in every lighting condition I’ve put it in. Apple rates the 1088-by-1088-pixel (220 ppi) display’s brightness between 0.3 and 500 nits, and that bottom end is what makes it work on a nightstand. In a dark kitchen, it reads as a soft glow instead of a floodlight.

According to recent reports, the multitouch True Tone touchscreen responds promptly, and it kept registering taps even when my fingers were slightly wet (even though the device doesn’t have a specific water-resistance rating). That’s a real advantage for a screen that spends its life in a kitchen.

It has been revealed that the fresh, more conversational Siri AI on the HomeView is a big jump from the old Siri. The HomeView’s four-mic design ensures Siri can hear you from throughout the room and, when a paired Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone is nearby, it can pull from personal data. If you ask about an upcoming concert, it can also check the calendar on your Apple account and tell whether you’re actually free to go.

That personal access runs through the HomeView’s 12MP Center Stage camera. It can recognize up to six Home app-registered household members by face, and it only demonstrates someone’s personal information when it recognizes that person and their paired iPhone or iPad is on the same Wi-Fi network—with support for Wi-Fi 6E (802.11ax) with MIMO—and was recently unlocked. The HomeView’s A18 chip uses what Apple calls Secure Exclaves to process the camera and microphone feeds in a separate compartment, and Apple states neither the operating system nor Apple itself can access it. Those safeguards are reassuring on paper, though they aren’t something I could independently verify while testing a smart display in my kitchen.

That reliance on a nearby iPhone or iPad is also the source of the HomeView’s most frustrating quirk. With my phone on me, Siri sometimes can’t decide which device should answer. The first few times I tried to set a simple timer, it turned into a dance between the HomeView and my phone before one of them finally took the request. It takes a little getting used to.

Sources indicate that your iPhone also supplies a significant share of the HomeView’s apps. There’s no App Store on the device. It ships with 15 built-in apps, including Safari, FaceTime, Music, and Home, and it pulls a handful of other Apple apps, like TV and News, from your phone. So, if you don’t mind some severe letterboxing, you can watch TV and movies on there. Supported third-party audio and video apps show up from a paired iPhone, too, through a system that works a lot like CarPlay. If a service you rely on doesn’t support it, there’s no way to install it on the HomeView directly.

The HomeView’s main job is running your smart home, and that’s where my experience was most mixed. It controls accessories you’ve added to Apple Home, which includes supported HomeKit and Matter devices. My Ring cameras don’t integrate with Apple Home natively, so they never appeared in the HomeView’s Home Camera face, which can otherwise show up to nine live feeds at once. It worked easily with my smart lighting and other natively compatible devices.

Sources indicate that check whether your current cameras, locks, sensors, and thermostat show up in Apple Home before you plan to run the whole house from this screen. If they don’t, budget for HomeKit or Matter replacements that do (and Apple has a whole suite of fresh options developed alongside LG and Schneider Electric).

The actual smart hub interface that displays on screen is handy for keeping tabs on what’s going on in your home. It’s important to note that this thing looks like a thermostat when it’s on the wall, but it isn’t one. Maybe a future model with a built-in thermostat could free up some wall space.

The HomeView turned out to be a great cooking assistant. Once you open a recipe page on the web, either on your iPhone or in Safari on the HomeView, a Start Cooking button reformats it so you can follow the steps in real time while you work. Recipe pages vary wildly in how they’re formatted and coded, and I expected that mess to trip it up. It has worked without a problem every time I’ve used it so far.

According to recent reports, I made a fairly simple recipe for peanut butter noodles, and the instructions and timers were helpful and easy to use. More complicated recipes are more of a challenge, especially since you can’t really perform more than one step at a time, so don’t expect it to turn you into Gordon Ramsay overnight.

As for the audio, the tabletop HomeView sounds full for its size. Its base holds a down-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators, almost like a subwoofer in miniature (but without the extension), and the display adds two custom full-range down-firing drivers of its own. I’d been using an older Google smart display before this, and the jump in sound quality is obvious.

In separate tests, PopSci editor Tony Ware spent a couple of nights with his own HomeView and some of his favorite songs and came away with positive impressions. Compared to a HomePod mini, the beat hits more convincingly. While there’s not much room for excursion in the base, output manages to be surprisingly potent without sacrificing clarity. It won’t beat some recent whole-home audio-focused connected speakers (or Apple’s own full-sized 2nd-gen. HomePod, for that matter), but it’s plenty room-filling for such a compact, multipurpose enclosure. Whether you’re chopping carrots or choppin’ it up with friends, the HomeView is more than enough speaker for a smaller space.

Industry observers note that what was more impressive was the airy, open presence of Dolby Atmos tracks from Apple Music, given the use of reflections and computational audio rather than an actual array of directional drivers. With accelerometers and Apple silicon adjusting the acoustic system’s EQ and output based on the screen’s tilt, the result is more incisive than immersive … how it will always be when you can’t surround yourself with speakers. Still, it projects clearly without sounding overly bright or edgy, which is good for podcasts to playlists.

There are occasional kinks, however. If you’re into spatial audio, the best way to ensure you’re getting the correct version of a track is to ask the HomeView to pull Apple Music directly from the cloud; sometimes the Dolby Atmos badge won’t pop up when you send a track from your phone over AirPlay, so you can’t be certain it’s not just stereo. Alternatively, you can hand off whatever is playing on your phone by bringing it close enough to the HomeView to get an AirDrop ripple animation and the album art to show up. Also, you might find yourself instinctively running your finger along the edge of the display looking for volume buttons, but there are no physical controls, which isn’t surprising from an aesthetic standpoint but still feels like a shortcoming.

The Apple HomeView makes the most sense on a nightstand, on the wall next to your thermostat, or in the kitchen. Its Photos face turns it into a digital picture frame, which keeps it from looking like a giant Apple Watch stuck to your wall or sitting on your table (though the clock faces are cute and colorful).

If your home already runs on an iPhone and Apple Home accessories, HomeView slots right in and puts it all on one screen you’ll actually want to look at. If you’ve built your smart home around gear that doesn’t work with Apple Home, however, plan to replace it before you make the jump.

#85. Breaking: Young sea turtles make an unexpected home in the Gulf of Oman

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci

Breaking: Young sea turtles make an unexpected home in the Gulf of Oman

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (564 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For one group of young sea turtles, a protected wetland in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) proved a perfect oasis.
  • Sources indicate that in 2003, the basin was excavated as an extension of the Khor Kalba mangrove trees.
  • It has been revealed that “Our results show just how critical coastal wetlands can be to young green turtles,” Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For one group of young sea turtles, a protected wetland in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) proved a perfect oasis. A team tracking nine juvenile green turtles (Chelonia mydas) found they were spending over 80 percent of their time in the Al Qurm Wa Lehhfaiiah Protected Area, a human-made lagoon on the UAE’s Gulf of Oman coast. Large numbers of turtles are also found in this basin built beyond the salt-tolerant trees and shrubs along the coast. A study published today in the journal Aquatic Conservation details the findings.

Sources indicate that in 2003, the basin was excavated as an extension of the Khor Kalba mangrove trees. The resulting Al Qurm Wa Lehhfaiiah Protected Area has been recognized as a wetland of international importance under the Ramsar Convention and as a Key Biodiversity Area since 2013.

It has been revealed that “Our results show just how critical coastal wetlands can be to young green turtles,” Dr. Owen Exeter, a study co-author and marine conservation ecologist from the University of Exeter, said in a statement. “The fact these turtles are using the artificial basin appears to be a happy accident, and an example of how wildlife can find a way in a world increasingly shaped by humans. However, without the natural mangroves connecting to this system, it’s unlikely that this would have occurred.

It has been revealed that according to the team, the floor of the basin is covered with algae, which likely means the turtles have enough food. A few sharks are making their way to this habitat.

The turtles are now also showing “strong reliance” in the man-made basin, with five times higher odds of being found there than in surrounding habitats.

It has been revealed that while this spot can be a refuge, the natural mangrove channels also play a critical role in connecting the juvenile turtles (those with a shell less than 23 inches across) to the sea. These channels allow them to move with the tides and show the importance of protecting the entire ecosystem, not just parts of it.

It has been revealed that “The government of Sharjah right now protects most of this area from building development, fishing and boating—preserving the last mangrove ecosystem on UAE’s east coast,” Exeter said. “Coastal wetlands are tropical nature hotspots, providing essential nursery and foraging habitats for species including sea turtles. Wetlands are among the most threatened ecosystems globally, so we urgently need to understand how key species use both modified and protected wetlands.”.

In a recent development, while these findings are positive for the turtles living in the protected area, their life cycle depends on nesting beaches. Many of these beaches have already been lost to coastal development, and fishing, vessel traffic, and pollution affect the other nearby areas.

One of the turtles swam over 430 miles south to central Oman, highlighting the need for conservation management of these mobile species once they are old enough to leave critical wetland sites.

“Overall, our findings show that coastal wetlands, including engineered ones, can provide valuable habitat for juvenile turtles, provided they are designed for ecological connectivity and subsequent human pressures and threats are minimised,” concluded study co-author Brendan Whittington-Jones from the Sharjah Environment and Protected Areas Authority (EPAA) who led the study.

#81. UK climate minister Katie White: COP31 must respond to ‘really scary’ science

UK climate minister Katie White: COP31 must respond to ‘really scary’ science

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4362 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Carbonbrief

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The upcoming COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey need to respond to the latest science on global warming, which is “really scary”, says UK climate minister Katie White.
  • In an interview with Carbon Brief setting out the UK’s priorities for the summit, White also responds to suggestions that the government is walking back its climate policies.
  • White says the “shocking” impact of extreme heat and wildfires this summer makes it clear that climate change “isn’t something far off; it’s something we’re living through”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The upcoming COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey need to respond to the latest science on global warming, which is “really scary”, says UK climate minister Katie White.

In an interview with Carbon Brief setting out the UK’s priorities for the summit, White also responds to suggestions that the government is walking back its climate policies.

White says the “shocking” impact of extreme heat and wildfires this summer makes it clear that climate change “isn’t something far off; it’s something we’re living through”.

She adds that the UK will be working to “hold up the science”, including the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) reports that should be the “basis of discussions”.

The COP31 presidency push on electrification is “going to be key”, notes White, who points to other priorities for the UK that include tackling methane emissions and reducing deforestation.

White says the recent approval of the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea is “fully in line” with carbon budgets and that the UK continues to support the “transition away from fossil fuels”.

She adds that the Hormuz crisis has helped drive the “biggest uptake…we’ve ever seen” in the UK for solar, electric vehicles and heat pumps.

Finally, White defends the new approach set out in the budget by chancellor John Healey, including a greater focus on affordability, as a “natural evolution” of UK government policy.

According to recent reports, carbon Brief: Katie White, thank you very much for joining Carbon Brief today. Next week we’re going to be heading to COP31 climate talks in Antalya in Turkey.

It has been revealed that we’ve seen this year the UN warning that a temporary overshoot of 1.5C degrees is now inevitable. We’ve had 50,000 excess heat deaths across Europe this summer. We’ve had extreme weather events hitting Nepal, deadly floods there. Heading into the talks, what would you say the UK’s priorities are?

In a recent development, katie White: Thanks, Simon. Look, just to say, it’s great to be here. I’m a big fan of Carbon Brief and the work you’ve been doing. I think it’s incredibly important that there are people who are focused on the facts and have really excellent commentary. So just to say thank you, and it’s good to be here to discuss with you.

Look, this year has been a very significant year in terms of climate, particularly sat here in the UK. I think we have really felt the impacts of climate change for the first time. For you and me, who’ve been working on this for a long time [and] we talk about it. But even so – I don’t know how you felt – but I was even shocked by the implications of what that was for everyday life, for people actually sleeping at night. You know, in terms of parliament, I had colleagues who had to go pick up their children because their schools weren’t available, and you know, tragedies in terms of older people struggling in the heat.

Not to mention the wildfires that we had across the country. I went to visit one in Romford and I think just standing – literally in the ashes – and seeing people’s homes really close by. My colleague in Stourbridge, obviously, they had burnt-out houses – you know, devastating. And you think about it – and I talked with her about – the actual real-life implications of that.

Obviously, people think about it, but then the after-effects, and you know the challenges with insurance and the challenge with all these sky boxes, and all of the things that come –  those smaller things, as well as the tragedies around your photos, and all of that being lost.

According to recent reports, so I think it’s really opened, sadly, another door for us in terms of the climate-change journey. This isn’t something far off; it’s something we’re living through. I know that’s been the case for many countries for a long time, but it really felt like a shift here in the UK.

You’re right, the science, once again, is really scary. The overshoot report is incredibly concerning. Scientifically, obviously, they look for a longer period. But I think the main message – for me as a politician – is this is really worrying. And every year we have another call to action. How do we translate that call into actual delivery? And that’s the bit we need to make sure of, because you know, I think we have to be listening to the science, and the science is fundamental and key. And we might talk about the IPCC [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change] and all the elements of that. But also, for me, how do we translate that?

Industry observers note that it’s not, as you all know, it’s not the big global stocktake COP [this year in Antalya]. So it’s not going to be that big event, where we have it every five years. But we still need to be making significant progress. So we really focus a lot on the science, on the “action agenda” and on those political decisions – that “cover decision” that the Australian presidency [of negotiations] has remarked that they’re going to pursue.

In a recent development, so in terms of the action agenda, which obviously the Turkish [presidency] has led on and [has] been really forthright about leading on this, I think electrification is going to be key. It’s something that shot up the agenda.

In a recent development, I think most of your audience will know what electrification is, but for anyone outside of the climate bubble [it is] around electrifying our homes, electrifying our transportation. And in the UK, we’ve done a good job of decarbonising our electricity system, but we need to be pulling down on that and increasing demand to make sure that we take full advantage of the clean electricity that we have, which would be good for bills, but also around reducing our emissions as well. So something around electrification, we’re expecting a lot of talk of that. [It is] something the Turks have been talking about a lot.

In a recent development, methane is another area which we’ve been working on, but I expect there will be some progress in terms of methane. Forests, you’ll know that we’ve pledged an investment to the [Tropical Forest Forever] TFFF, so we will be hoping for some momentum around that forests agenda.

So, I think, those are some of the really practical areas of action, as well as making sure we’re moving forward, holding up the UNFCCC [UN Framework Convention on Climate Change], holding up the science, so we can keep moving forward and making progress on any of those areas within the cover decision that the Australians will obviously steer us through.

Recent findings suggest that CB: Great, thank you. You mentioned electrification. Obviously, that’s a target unveiled by the Turkish presidency earlier this year. They remarked they want to see the adoption of a global target for 35% of final energy to come from electricity by 2035.

According to recent reports, KW: Good questions. Look, so we’ll wait and see how we manage the next couple of weeks in terms of [that]. I think we have definitely, domestically, been looking at electrification and how we take advantage of the clean electricity that we have more effectively. Because of the Middle East crisis, broadly, we’ve seen interest in EVs, in solar panels and heat pumps, just shoot up this year, as people have got increasingly concerned about energy prices. And for those who are in a position, you know, a lot of them have taken advantage.

Sources indicate that so we are seeing shifts in the market, and we’re looking at what role we can play to encourage and accelerate that. Whether it’s supporting the rollout of charging points for electric vehicles. You’ll probably know this, Simon, but there are more public charging points in the UK now than petrol pumps, which I think is an incredible fact – and most people don’t know. That’s not including those within driveways, of which nearly 70% of the UK has access to a driveway, so all of those people who might have their own home charging, there is more public.

According to recent reports, we are making this infrastructure more easy, more accessible, so that people can make that shift. But we are [already] seeing the shift, you know, we’ve got two million EVs on the road. Super excitingly for the motor geeks, the second-hand [EV] car market is really starting to – excuse the pun – “motor”. Actually, that does mean a major shift in terms of accessibility.

According to recent reports, so we’re seeing this happen within the UK. We’ll look at whether that’s a helpful target for us, but in terms of the focus, the ambition on electrification in the UK will remain. And I’m really pleased to see it as part of the negotiations this year or the action agenda.

Industry observers note that it was interesting to see the Europeans do their own electrification – I don’t know whether they called it a proposal or a roadmap, everybody gets caught up on these words – but they also brought forward [an “action plan”]. So obviously, we’re looking at where we can, you know, be a little bit more aligned with them.

Sources indicate that CB: You mentioned roadmaps. Now, obviously, last year at the COP, the massive debate, slightly outside of the formal negotiations, was around the idea of a roadmap away from fossil fuels and the UK was one of more than 100 countries that were really pushing for that to again be brought into the formal outcome of the summit in Brazil. Is that something that the UK is going to be pushing again this year?

In a recent development, KW: For sure. So look, we very much support the agenda around the transition away from fossil fuels. You know, in terms of, how do we support countries, how do we work together in terms of moving away from that? You’ll know that Rachel Kyte, our special representative, was in Santa Marta in April of this year to talk through [this topic] and we hosted a follow-up event at Wilton Park around the London Climate Action Week. So you know, very keen to support and work that through.

It’s obviously a hard agenda, but it’s something that I think we should have been discussing for a while in terms of the COP processes. So it was great that we managed to do that. I think it was as a result of lots of different people talking about it, different campaigns, different, you know, how do we work together around this, in terms of managing the resources we have most effectively, and transitioning away. [That’s] for climate reasons, for health reasons and, in large part, economic reasons as well.

CB: Great. You mentioned the IPCC timeline. This is obviously something that’s been rolling on for quite a while. There’s been a group of countries making a concerted effort to delay the publication of the next IPCC assessment report, so that it won’t align with the next global stocktake under the Paris Agreement.

It has been revealed that the UK, as far as I understand, is pushing for that timeline to be accelerated, or to at least align with the stocktake. I just want to confirm that that’s the UK’s position and then ask, what is your understanding of the arguments being made for not doing that, for not aligning those timelines?

KW: So look, we obviously would like to have as much of the science ready for the global stocktake. That would be the ideal outcome in terms of what we are looking for, and we have noted that we will continue to say that we would also like an outcome.

So, in a sense, we would like to make sure that we have a decision and we are moving this forward, and we don’t get caught up in having longer negotiations, which stall us making any progress at all.

In a recent development, I wasn’t at the [IPCC] meeting this autumn, but in terms of [what] I understand, [IPCC chair Prof] Jim Skea did a good job of trying to navigate that and making sure that this is inclusive. We want to listen to concerns around inclusivity, but we also want to make progress, because of the reasons that we talked about right up front: there is some really scary science going forward. The IPCC is peer-reviewed, it’s the best in the world, and we want to make sure that that is the basis of discussions.

In a recent development, so the more we can align that together, the better. But we’re also practical. We want to work with everybody. We want to listen to everybody. But we are keen to move that forward and hold up the IPCC in the way it has been. It’s become the most respected, established platform for all that the negotiations are based on.

In a recent development, CB: Great, thank you. I want to turn to the UK now, if I can. So, under the Paris Agreement, the UK has pledged to cut its greenhouse gas emissions to 68% below 1990 levels by 2030. In June, the Climate Change Committee, in its assessment, said something like 17% of the cuts required to meet that target just didn’t have looks in place.

According to recent reports, the government’s own carbon budget delivery plan said that current policies were falling short of what would be needed. And then, obviously, since then we’ve had a number of cuts. We’ve had cuts to heat pump subsidies, cuts to hydrogen and carbon-capture and storage. We’re expecting to see further watering down of the zero-emission vehicles mandate for electric vehicles. We just had approval of newly introduced drilling at Jackdaw. When you’re at the COP in Antalya, how will you be reassuring UK partners that the UK remains committed to its climate pledge?

KW: So look, it’s absolutely right that you pick out any of the challenges – and say where the challenges are to our evidence. That’s really helpful, as part of our process of doing that. We put forward a carbon budget growth and delivery plan last year that we had to redo, because obviously there had been a legal challenge. We did that. It was a very comprehensive process. You know, a huge amount of work to make sure that we were on track to deliver that. So that is the case. The Climate Change Committee was obviously coming back on what was happening now, and we will report to parliament [in response to the committee] in the normal way. I will leave that report to talk for itself when it comes out to parliament.

Recent findings suggest that we also – the great thing about the Climate Change Act and the carbon budgets is that it does allow flexibility over time. In a recent development, so let’s take the Middle East crisis. Obviously, that’s been a significant disruption to our energy and climate system. Arguably, one of the biggest disruptions we’ve ever had. Now, that has led to a few things happening.

One is to say that electrification – you know, people are moving towards the biggest uptake in solar, heat pumps and EVs that we’ve ever seen. So we’re seeing that trajectory go up. That’s great, and that is on the positive side. At the same time, it has meant geopolitically, people are looking at their energy security and where you do have access to fossil fuels, people are considering those options.

According to recent reports, we made the Jackdaw decision fully in line [with our carbon budgets]. We looked at the emissions – and emissions would actually be a tiny bit lower because of transportation from Norway. So it is absolutely within those boundaries.

But of course, I’m constantly keeping an eye on how that budget is moving. In the same way that over the road [in Whitehall] at HMT [the Treasury], they’re keeping an eye on their financial budget, as they should do, I will keep an eye on the carbon budget, as will the secretary of state [Miatta Fahnbulleh]. So we will be keeping a look.

But I think let’s also be clear that the UK has got a good story to tell. I of course want it to be better, and that’s part of my job, to make sure that we have the next chapter evolving and we can keep telling our story.

Recent findings suggest that but right now, we have a pretty good story to tell. You know, we’ve got over [a] 50% reduction in emissions, whilst having 80% [economic] growth since 1990. So we have got a good story to tell. We are making those transitions and we will continue to say that. But also, we’ll continue to listen and learn because nobody has got the perfect plan for this. No one country has got all the answers or the solutions.

So I think, being clear where we’ve had success, being honest where it’s not worked, and having a bit of humility to learn from others along the way, is how we’re going to approach the COP.

Industry observers note that CB: Great, thank you. I want to ask about climate finance. The UK is one of the only major donors to have made a fresh climate-finance pledge, offering £6bn, I believe, over three years. In a recent development, so, look, we have the £11.6bn [and] we delivered absolutely every bit of it. Recent findings suggest that so, look, of course, I will be talking about what we have done and what we continue to do, and how we’ve listened to countries and laid that [strategy] out, so there is some element that they can help plan ahead. But also, looking at what those alternative sources, for instance, around the structuring of the TFFF, to make sure we’re looking at other options, because we do need to meet the need. The need is growing, and the finance pot needs to do the same.

Industry observers note that CB: Thank you. One final question, if I may. Last week we obviously had the first budget from the fresh chancellor, John Healey. There’s been a lot of conversation and media coverage since that budget about what he described as a new path for energy policy in the UK. KW: So, look, the first thing I’d say is it was great to hear the chancellor say on the floor of the house [of parliament] about net-zero, his commitment to net-zero by 2050 and our steadfast approach to delivering that. I think it’s really helpful. You know, the chancellor’s voice counts for a lot. We’ve heard the prime minister say it twice. He’s written articles on it as well, so it’s great to see that commitment from the top. There has been a lot of politicisation around net-zero, so I think the direction of travel is absolutely clear.

Sources indicate that [The] secretary of state has said that her number one aim is around affordability. We know that we are in a cost of living crisis. At the same time, the Climate Change Committee has said the best thing we could do [to lower emissions] is bring down electricity prices, and so I think there is a really great alignment between those three things [cost, climate and security].

The clean-power mission has been incredibly effective in terms of getting a lot of clean power built. We now need to make sure we’re utilising that clean power across the board, and we need to, and we want to do it in the most cost-effective way possible.

Sources indicate that as you can probably hear from my accent, I’m from Yorkshire. We’re a little bit tight [careful with money] and I want to make sure that we are using that energy most effectively. And the system at the moment is not set up to do that. There are some pretty ineffective elements of it, that we want to make sure that we’re using far more effectively.

So I think that is the shift we’re looking at. We’re now in the next chapter of, how do we make sure that energy – and specifically electricity – is as affordable as possible for consumers, for our constituents up and down the country, but also for small businesses. You know, the last government did build some of these offshore wind turbines. They just didn’t connect them all, so we need to make sure that we’ve got all of these things connected, and then we’re utilising it really effectively, and we’re supporting consumers and businesses to draw down on that.

So I think it’s a really exciting opportunity for us. But I think it’s just a natural evolution of the next step, to make sure that the UK citizens are getting the best value from the infrastructure that we already have.

In a recent development, CB: Brilliant, very, very quickly, before you have to go, the UK is going to be leading the umbrella group of countries at the COP. So coming back to the COP, I’m just curious how the UK is going to deal with being in that spotlight [and] make use of that position?

Industry observers note that KW: Look, we are sending a great team of ministers to the COP. CB: Brilliant! Thanks very much, Katie, and great to have you.

#80. Smartwatch blood pressure monitoring was okay. AI is making it better.

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1023 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci

Smartwatch blood pressure monitoring was okay. AI is making it better.

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1023 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that when the United States Food and Drug Administration cleared the Apple Watch’s Hypertension Notification Feature last year, some saw it as a turning point in the fight against one of the leading causes of cardiac disease.
  • While that sounds great, the reality of smartwatch hypertension tools is more nuanced.
  • According to recent reports, that context is worth keeping in mind when considering newly introduced research from scientists at Google and a clinical partner from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School recently published in the journal Nature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that when the United States Food and Drug Administration cleared the Apple Watch’s Hypertension Notification Feature last year, some saw it as a turning point in the fight against one of the leading causes of cardiac disease. Rather than booking a doctor’s appointment and strapping a bulging cuff around one’s arm, users could instead receive passive hypertension alerts from the watch’s optical sensors to track blood flow patterns. Watch wearers who were previously unaware that they had signs of this ever-common “silent killer” would receive an alert advising them to seek out a clinician. Early intervention could mean a better chance at beginning life-saving interventions.

While that sounds great, the reality of smartwatch hypertension tools is more nuanced. Apple’s own validation data highlighted that their feature would miss around 59 percent of people with undiagnosed high blood pressure. Newer United States population level research from the University of Utah and the University of Pennsylvania went a step further, and warned that the absence of an alert could give wearers a false sense of security, potentially making them less likely to go get a proper cuff screening. The feature, in other words, isn’t necessarily harmful, but it also isn’t a medical silver bullet.

According to recent reports, that context is worth keeping in mind when considering newly introduced research from scientists at Google and a clinical partner from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School recently published in the journal Nature. The team claims they created a new AI system that pairs with a consumer smartwatch to passively detect signs of high blood pressure, “with accuracy levels comparable to traditional cuffed blood pressure devices.”.

It has been revealed that the new system draws on two sensors already found in many consumer smartwatches: an optical pulse sensor (which tracks changes in blood volume at the wrist) and an accelerometer. An AI algorithm then analyzes several days of  readings, factors in the wearer’s height, and then calculates the probability that they have hypertension.

Recent findings suggest that google’s system builds on Apple’s approach by adding in the watch’s accelerometer to the mix, which can pick up the faint wrist vibrations of each heartbeat. The results look promising. In initial screenings, the combined system caught more cases of high blood pressure than a standard office cuff reading, though it still missed about a third of cases. And while the researchers involved still advise against using the tool as a substitute for seeing a doctor, it’s potentially another step forward in attempts to use common wearable tech to catch underlying signs of disease earlier.

“By gently prompting at-risk individuals to step into a clinic for formal assessment, this technology holds the potential to significantly close the global awareness gap and catch hypertension before it causes permanent cardiovascular damage,” Google researchers note in a blog post.

Heart disease remains the leading cause of death in the U.S. , claiming more than  900,000 lives in 2023 alone. Chronic high blood pressure (referred to as hypertension medically) is one of the key early risk factors. Around half of all Americans likely have it, but an estimated four in ten people don’t know they have it, partly because it often does not present with any clear symptoms. And while hypertension is treatable when caught early, many simply don’t see a doctor often enough to be screened regularly. That combination of an invisible condition and spotty screening makes the issue an attractive target for always-on smartwatch sensors.

According to recent reports, the sensors on commercial smartwatches can pick up useful data, but those signals still need to be interpreted by an AI model. In this case, Google states it trained its system on nearly 500,000 hours of sensor data collected from 2,109 people. The optical sensor captures the shapes of each pulse wave at the wrist, while the accelerometer shows signs of the subtle physical vibrations that occur at the wrist when blood is ejected from the heart into the aorta. Both of those signal data are cut into 5-second PPG and ACC waveforms. The AI converts those signal snippets into numerical summaries, which Google refers to as an “embedding.”.

According to recent reports, over time, the AI model was able to pore over those different numerical values and determine which types of pulses are likely associated with hypertension. By analyzing data collected from one wearer to the next, the AI sees numerical patterns that distinguish one person’s signals from another. But simply relying on a measurement from one point in time risks introducing what the researcher calls “environmental noise” that can skew results. To account for all that noise, they aggregated the sensors’ data over multiple days of use to establish a wearer’s persistent state. That data then gets fed into a logistic regression classifier, which comes out with a score corresponding to a person’s likelihood of having hypertension.

Industry observers note that the team tested their system on 196 participants over seven days of real-world monitoring, checking their results against 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring, which they refer to as the “gold standard” in the field. The AI smartwatch system ultimately detected hypertension with a sensitivity of 65.8 percent. That means 65.8 percent of people who were proven to have hypertension were accurately identified by their AI system. That’s far from perfect, but it was still higher than the 55.3 percent caught by initial office cuff readings in the study.

“Taken together, the results show that our system can detect hypertension with accuracy levels comparable to traditional cuffed BP devices in the existing clinical framework,” Google notes.

Like Apple before it, Google and the other medical researchers involved in this story were quick to stress that these findings, noteworthy as they may sound, shouldn’t lead people to think of this system as a complete replacement for clinical blood pressure monitoring .Going to see actual human doctors isn’t going away anytime soon, but this system, if widely accessible, could help nudge more people towards getting checked out.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following this year’s UN COP17 biodiversity conference, Carbon Brief’s journalists hosted a livestream to explain what happened at the summit.

Carbon Brief’s Orla Dwyer and Aruna Chandrasekhar have been on the ground in Yerevan, Armenia, over the past two weeks, covering the negotiations.

They were joined on the livestream by associate editors Dr Giuliana Viglione and Daisy Dunne, who were following the talks from Washington DC and London, respectively.

Carbon Brief has also published its 10,000-word explainer of COP17, which lays out the key outcomes in detail.

Orla and Aruna kicked off the livestream by explaining the biggest issues at the event, including biodiversity finance and the first “global review” of progress towards reversing nature loss.

The four journalists then took live questions from the audience in an “ask me anything” format, covering complications such as “nature-harming subsidies”, marine biodiversity and the status of the Cali fund, which is meant to raise private-sector finance.

A recording of the webinar (below) is now available to watch on YouTube.

#75. Tech Report: Yanhe Technology rolls out three perovskite solar module technologies into orbit

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Pv-magazine

Tech Report: Yanhe Technology rolls out three perovskite solar module technologies into orbit

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that yanhe Technology launched three independently developed space photovoltaic modules into a 535 km sun-synchronous orbit aboard Galactic Energy’s Ceres-2 Y3 rocket from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center on Nov.
  • Two tandem modules – a perovskite-crystalline silicon device and a perovskite-CIGS device – are installed on the North University of China-1 satellite.
  • It has been revealed that A flexible single-junction perovskite module is installed on the Yunyao-1 28 satellite.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that yanhe Technology launched three independently developed space photovoltaic modules into a 535 km sun-synchronous orbit aboard Galactic Energy’s Ceres-2 Y3 rocket from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center on Nov. 7. The tech giant described the mission as China’s first simultaneous in-orbit validation of three perovskite-based PV technologies.

Two tandem modules – a perovskite-crystalline silicon device and a perovskite-CIGS device – are installed on the North University of China-1 satellite. The spacecraft operates in a dawn-dusk orbit, where near-continuous sunlight places demanding requirements on power density and long-term stability.

It has been revealed that A flexible single-junction perovskite module is installed on the Yunyao-1 28 satellite. The device will undergo imaging during thermal cycling and performance monitoring to assess degradation caused by particle radiation and atomic oxygen exposure.

Yanhe has not disclosed the conversion efficiencies, rated power outputs, active areas, or weights of the three modules. The company had not responded to a request for additional technical specifications at the time of publication. Yanhe’s official announcement and independent industry reports confirmed the launch, satellite platforms, and orbital altitude.

In a recent development, the mission builds on an earlier in-orbit testing campaign rolled out in September, when Yanhe deployed a flexible perovskite module aboard the Tianyi-52 satellite for long-term performance monitoring. The company described that deployment as China’s first component-level in-orbit test of flexible perovskite PV technology.

In October, Yanhe also established a joint laboratory with the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology to conduct research on perovskite solar cells, space photovoltaics, orbital energy systems, and flexible devices.

In a recent development, yanhe Chief Technology Officer Peng Zongyang noted the perovskite-silicon and perovskite-CIGS tandem architectures target different segments of the space PV market. He said the latest mission aims to evaluate the efficiency and stability of both technologies under actual orbital conditions.

The tech giant is assessing the fully thin-film perovskite-CIGS tandem architecture for potential advantages in flexibility and radiation resistance over silicon-based tandem devices.

Perovskite solar cells have attracted interest for space applications because of their potential for high specific power and lower material costs compared with the III-V gallium arsenide solar cells commonly used in satellite power systems.

Yanhe is targeting the growing low Earth orbit satellite constellation market, where lighter PV modules could help reduce launch costs.

However, the ability of perovskite solar modules to maintain performance under prolonged radiation exposure and repeated thermal cycling remains a key technical challenge.

The latest mission is expected to generate comparative in-orbit performance data for the three architectures. Yanhe has not specified the duration of the monitoring campaign or the amount of telemetry data expected from the satellites.

#72. Q&A: What is in the global ‘roadmap’ for transitioning away from fossil fuels?

📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1358 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Carbonbrief

Q&A: What is in the global ‘roadmap’ for transitioning away from fossil fuels?

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1358 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Carbonbrief

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Transitioning away from fossil fuels is “urgent, inevitable and, yet, possible”, according to a first-of-its-kind global “roadmap” produced by Brazil.
  • The host of last year’s climate summit, COP30, has set out a voluntary proposal for how countries can move away from coal, oil and gas.
  • The roadmap claims there is no “one-size-fits-all” approach to transitioning away from fossil fuels and asks countries to “diagnose” their own “readiness” to start the process.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Transitioning away from fossil fuels is “urgent, inevitable and, yet, possible”, according to a first-of-its-kind global “roadmap” produced by Brazil.

The host of last year’s climate summit, COP30, has set out a voluntary proposal for how countries can move away from coal, oil and gas.

The roadmap claims there is no “one-size-fits-all” approach to transitioning away from fossil fuels and asks countries to “diagnose” their own “readiness” to start the process.

After mapping out their specific circumstances, countries should then pursue “tailored levers” to take action, according to the roadmap.

These efforts should culminate by 2033, it notes – 10 years on from when the COP28 climate summit in Dubai called on all countries to contribute to a global transition away from fossil fuels.

Below, Carbon Brief examines what the roadmap says and how it could influence debates about fossil fuels at the upcoming COP31 climate summit, which begins next week in Turkey.

Calls for a global “roadmap” away from fossil fuels dominated debates at COP30, which was held in the Amazonian city of Belém.

A group of 85 countries called for a reference to a newly introduced roadmap for transitioning away from fossil fuels to be part of COP30’s formal negotiated outcome.

This call came after the first “global stocktake” of action towards the world’s climate goals at COP28 in 2023 asked all countries to contribute to transitioning away from fossil fuels.

However, another group of countries opposed such an inclusion.

Recent findings suggest that it was claimed that this group included 84 countries. However, Carbon Brief’s analysis of the “informal list” revealed inconsistencies and errors, meaning the total number of countries opposing the roadmap was likely smaller.

After two weeks of fierce debate, Brazil unveiled that the fossil-fuel roadmap would not be part of COP30’s negotiated outcome – but that the presidency would work to create a roadmap outside of the UN climate process.

This roadmap is voluntary and countries are not obligated to respond to its findings.

At COP30, the presidency also announced that the roadmap would be informed by a first-of-its-kind conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels taking place in Santa Marta, Colombia.

In a recent development, these talks, co-hosted by Colombia and the Netherlands in April, saw ministers and climate envoys take part in informal discussions about the barriers they face in transitioning away from fossil fuels. (See Carbon Brief’s full coverage of the talks.).

As well as the fossil-fuel roadmap, Brazil has also produced a latest roadmap for ending deforestation. (See Carbon Brief’s in-depth breakdown of the deforestation roadmap).

The roadmap acknowledges that, after decades of delayed action on fossil fuels, the world is no longer able to meet its ambition to limit global warming to 1.5C without first “overshooting” the target.

It also notes that the global transition to clean energy is already underway – and that the policies needed for transitioning away from fossil fuels already exist and are readily deployable.

It continues, however, by saying that transitioning away from fossil fuels is “as much a development question as a climate one, especially for emerging markets and developing economies”.

It has been revealed that in this context, it sets out looks for what it calls a “Belém readiness index”. This is a “voluntary self-assessment tool” that countries can use to calculate their dependency on fossil fuels and their capacity for transitioning away.

At a press briefing announcing the roadmaps, COP30 CEO Ana Toni described this as the “diagnosis” stage of the roadmap, “instead of imagining there is a one-size-fits-all answer”.

After identifying their “readiness” for transition, countries will be sorted into four “archetypes”, says the roadmap, leading to the identification of specific policy “levers” for taking action.

The roadmap calls for action in three distinct “phases”.

The first phase should be from now until 2028, when the second global stocktake of progress towards the Paris Agreement is due to conclude at COP33.

In this phase, “efforts focus on institutions and long-term signals”, notes the roadmap.

The second phase is from 2028-2030, when the next round of UN climate pledges, known as nationally determined contributions (NDCs), are due.

This phase should focus on the “physical transformation of energy systems”, says the roadmap.

The final phase is 2031-2033 – 10 years after the call for all countries to help with “transitioning away from fossil fuels” in “this critical decade” at COP28.

This phase should focus on the scaling up of the transition, according to the roadmap.

All of these elements are summarised in the graphic below, which was presented to journalists and civil society during a press briefing.

At the press briefing, Toni added that each stage of the roadmap was designed to be “extremely pragmatic and easy for countries to take a look at it”.

The approach has broadly been welcomed by civil society and experts.

Dr Natalie Jones, a senior policy adviser at the International Institute for Sustainable Development (IISD), tells Carbon Brief that the roadmap sends an “crucial political signal that the transition away from fossil fuels remains firmly on the international agenda”. She adds:.

“It also gives governments practical guidance to proposal that transition in ways that reflect their national circumstances, strengthen energy security and protect livelihoods.”.

Avantika Goswami, a climate policy expert at the Centre for Science and Environment in New Delhi, India, tells Carbon Brief that the roadmap is a “unique and consultative method of multilateralism”. She notes:.

“[The roadmap] is one that is put forth by a developing country, via a consultative process that invited submissions from all parties and civil society.

“The analytical framework proposed captures the complexity of the fossil-fuel transition. Countries must now use it to chart out pathways in line with their historical responsibility and current capacity.”.

Sources indicate that ploy Achakulwisut, a former UN adviser on fossil fuels, wrote on LinkedIn that she was “deeply impressed” with Brazil’s approach, including its use of a “readiness index”. She added:.

“[The index] provides a method for identifying countries that face similar transition conditions and for understanding how different exposure-capacity ‘archetypes’ can generate distinct implementation needs and opportunities.

“The latter can ‘support more targeted international cooperation’, helping the international community to align finance, technology, capacity-building, and technical assistance with country-specific needs and existing capabilities.”.

Brazil’s fossil-fuel roadmap comes just a week before the next round of UN climate talks, COP31, kicks off in Antalya, Turkey.

COP31 co-presidents Turkey and Australia have set out a wide range of priorities for the summit, including a target to increase the share of global final energy consumption met by electricity from almost 24% in 2023 to 35% by 2035.

Speaking at the press briefing, COP30 president André Aranha Corrêa do Lago remarked that this electrification goal was “complementary” to the aims of the fossil-fuel roadmap.

Carbon Brief understands that some parties feel that Turkey and Australia’s focus on electrification over fossil fuels is an attempt to avoid a re-hashing of the lengthy debates at COP30.

Both Corrêa do Lago and Toni were reluctant to speculate on how the fossil-fuel roadmap might be taken up and discussed during COP31, with Toni telling journalists that they were “hoping for the best”.

When asked about how Brazil hoped the roadmap would be received by those that specifically opposed its inclusion at COP30, Corrêa do Lago declined to address other countries directly, but said:.

“Let’s remind ourselves we already have a consensus [on transitioning away from fossil fuels, agreed at COP28] and we already have the instruments.”.

Jones tells Carbon Brief that, following on from the roadmap, the “task now is to build on that signal with action”, adding:.

It has been revealed that “At COP31, more governments should announce national fossil-fuel transition roadmaps and explain how these will inform their national climate intends. The conference should also [formally] recognise the global roadmap and establish a route for its findings to inform the second global stocktake.

Industry observers note that “For vulnerable countries dependent on fossil-fuel revenues, credible looks must be matched by international finance and support to diversify their economies and sustain public services. This roadmap can help turn a shared commitment into practical progress.”.
