📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it took a few hours longer than expected, but the SS United States now rests at the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico. The nearly 1,000-foot-long ocean liner sank off the coast of Pensacola, Florida, to a depth of about 190 feet on November 11, where it is now officially the world’s largest artificial reef. In the years ahead, biologists and conservationists will monitor the vessel’s remains as numerous marine species slowly convert the ship into their own home.

Recent findings suggest that ahead of the next phase in the United States’ recycled life, divers from the RV Explorer swam to document the vessel’s location and post-scuttling condition. On November 13, the team released a brief video of their successful excursion. Interestingly, the footage shows the ship is resting upright on the ocean floor despite initially sinking on its side.

In a recent development, “It was just epic,” diver Rustin Cassway told a local Philadelphia news outlet. “It was very cleaned up. I mean, you could see people really took their time to clean it really nicely.”.

The project marks the first time ecologists will be able to monitor a shipwreck’s transformation in real-time. Researchers now proposal to conduct annual visits to the SS United States to chart not only the artificial reef’s progress, but how the ship’s materials may affect the surrounding ocean conditions.

Recent findings suggest that in its heyday, the SS United States was the world’s fastest ocean liner. Larger than the RMS Titanic, she was the most powerful, advanced, and modern passenger liner when she first took to the ocean in 1952. In addition to the 1,700 passengers, 7,935 quarts of ice cream and 500 pounds of caviar were also on board. During that maiden voyage (July 3-7, 1952), she broke the transatlantic speed record held by the RMS Queen Mary by over 10 hours. The United States made the crossing from the United Kingdom to New York in three days, 10 hours, and 40 minutes at an average speed of 40.96 mph.

She was designed by naval architect William Francis Gibbs (August 24, 1886 – September 6, 1967), and was built to be converted into a troopship if the United States Navy needed during a time of war. But she never was called into military service. Instead, the United States transported immigrants and celebrities, including future President and First Lady John and Jacqueline Kennedy, actors Grace Kelly, Gary Cooper, and Marilyn Monroe, artist Salvador Dali, and musicians Duke Ellington and Irving Berlin. Walt Disney even filmed parts of the 1962 comedy Bon Voyage aboard the ship.

An engineering marvel, some of the key design features were in the rudder, radar mast, and propellers.

The rudder was designed for good maneuverability at high speeds. The Titanic’s relatively small rudder was one factor behind the ship’s collision with an iceberg and tragic sinking in 1912.

The SS United States had the latest radar equipment, which allowed the crew to see the locations of  other ships and objects in the ocean despite the weather. It was among the first ocean liners to use radar, which was located at one of the highest points on the ship, so in addition to her radar “eyes,” a lookout could be stationed there to warn the captain of any danger in the ship’s path.

According to recent reports, considered a top-secret design, the ship had four propellers—two with four blades and two with five. According to the SS United States Conservancy, this configuration was tested and selected for its superior hydrodynamic performance. The propeller design was overseen by a pioneering Gibbs & Cox engineer named Elaine Kaplan.

Recent findings suggest that ocean liners became a less attractive option once air travel became quicker and less expensive. The SS United States ceased operations in 1969, and stayed in drydock in several cities before becoming the world’s largest artificial reef.

Backed by its shareholders TAQA, ADNOC, and Mubadala, the manufacturer plans to inject an additional $20 billion into the U.S. market over the coming decade.

Industry observers note that masdar is targeting an expansion of its U.S. renewable energy portfolio to as much as 25 GW by 2030, driven heavily by surging power demand from commercial data centers, industrial electrification, and domestic manufacturing load growth. 📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • China’s carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions fell by 3.1% in the third quarter of 2026, as the Hormuz crisis continued to hit oil demand and coal use also dropped.
  • Lauri Myllyvirta, lead analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.
  • This was the largest quarterly reduction since the 2022 Covid lockdowns and means that China’s CO2 emissions have now fallen by an estimated 0.5% in the year to date.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

China’s carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions fell by 3.1% in the third quarter of 2026, as the Hormuz crisis continued to hit oil demand and coal use also dropped.

Lauri Myllyvirta, lead analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

This was the largest quarterly reduction since the 2022 Covid lockdowns and means that China’s CO2 emissions have now fallen by an estimated 0.5% in the year to date.

The new analysis for Carbon Brief, based on official figures and commercial data, indicates that coal use fell by 3% year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026, while oil was down 4%.

The main drivers were a fall in power-sector coal consumption, a continued sharp reduction in transport oil consumption and slowing growth in the coal-to-chemical industry.

The sharp decline in China’s CO2 emissions extends a “flat or falling” trend that began in March 2024 and has now lasted more than two years, as shown in the figure below.

The outlook for China’s CO2 emissions depends on the balance between rising energy demand, clean-energy growth and the government response to a GDP slowdown.

Key drivers of the fall in CO2 in the third quarter of 2026 included a 3.3% drop in coal-power generation, after demand growth slowed and the amount of “wasted” wind and solar fell.

In a recent development, power generation from solar, wind and nuclear increased by 110 terawatt hours (TWh) year-on-year, more than twice as much as the growth in total electricity demand. This added clean-power generation equal to Germany’s total power output in the same time period.

The fall in coal-power output and CO2 emissions came despite the fact that China continues to build fresh coal-power capacity at near-record rates. This means that average running hours for coal plants are falling even faster than total generation, eroding their profits.

Meanwhile, transport oil consumption continued to fall sharply, down 9% year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026. Electric vehicles (EVs) continued to gain market share, hitting a record 67% of passenger car sales and 50% of heavy trucks in September.

The amount of electricity used by EVs grew by 53%, much faster than the number of EVs on the road, showing increased usage of the existing fleet in preference to fuelled vehicles.

Elsewhere, growth in the coal-to-chemical industry continued to slow down in the third quarter of 2026. The sector has been a key source of emissions growth, but high coal prices have weakened profitability and higher output prices hurt downstream demand.

Finally, CO2 emissions from cement and steel production continued to fall in the third quarter, as the contraction in construction volumes accelerated.

Energy consumption growth has been falling after a period of exceptionally high growth during Covid, while clean-power growth has been robust.

This makes it likely that the growth in clean-power generation will exceed total energy demand growth this year, maintaining the structural fall in fossil-fuel use.

Looking ahead, this balance also relies on progress in removing barriers to new solar and wind power being added to the grid, which result in some clean electricity being “wasted”.

The recent slowdown in energy demand growth is partly – but not fully – explained by exceptionally mild weather in the third quarter.

Another key factor is weaker GDP growth. Since reported GDP growth remains within target, however, there is reduced pressure for further stimulus policies.

The focus of the economic stimulus declared to date is “six networks”, which includes the power grid and the transportation network.

These networks are highly relevant for energy and emissions – and they are already covered by policies that emphasise “green” and zero-carbon solutions.

Robo-frog swims with liquid crystal muscles powered by light

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (458 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Popsci

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A silicone frog built by engineers at Denmark’s Aarhus University can’t swim nearly as fast as its amphibian inspiration, but it still manages to get the job done without any moving parts.
  • According to recent reports, the team’s novel system is detailed in a study recently published in the journal Advanced Materials Technologies.
  • “I could easily imagine these robots being used as toys before we see them on rescue missions,” Cecilie Ryberg, Aarhus University chemist and study co-author, mentioned in a profile.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A silicone frog built by engineers at Denmark’s Aarhus University can’t swim nearly as fast as its amphibian inspiration, but it still manages to get the job done without any moving parts. The odd invention owes its slow-but-steady aquatic maneuvering to a set of six artificial muscles specially designed to contract when exposed to near-infrared light.

According to recent reports, the team’s novel system is detailed in a study recently published in the journal Advanced Materials Technologies. Although similar setups may one day boost the capabilities of soft robots tasked with search and rescue or environmental monitoring, its creators are a bit more realistic about this frog-bot’s near-term uses.

“I could easily imagine these robots being used as toys before we see them on rescue missions,” Cecilie Ryberg, Aarhus University chemist and study co-author, mentioned in a profile. “I think people would have fun playing with a frog like this using a suitable light source.”.

Each of the robot’s muscles is built using crystal elastomers. These materials are specifically manufactured to contract while they are heating, and then revert back to their original shape once cooled. In this case, Ryberg and her collaborators also added a molecule that converts near-infrared light into heat. This allows the muscles to tighten after directly exposing them to a lamp. That mentioned, the process isn’t as simple as sticking the elastomers onto their model frog and dropping it into water.

“Getting the six muscles to work together was a major challenge,” explained Brigitte Städler, a study co-author and Aarhus University chemist. “If they don’t contract in a coordinated way, the frog won’t swim forwards. It may simply spin around.”.

Industry observers note that A lot of trial-and-error also went into concocting the elastomers themselves. In addition to contracting properly, the material needed the proper consistency to use in a 3D printer. To do this, Ryberg experimented with various molecular ingredients and molecule chain lengths to perfect the robot muscle recipe.

Industry observers note that “In a conventional 3D printer, you typically melt a solid plastic filament. Our material is more like very thick syrup or icing that you squeeze through a piping bag when decorating a cake,” mentioned Ryberg.

The final result is a light-powered soft robot that’s quite unique, but also not in any hurry. At its best pace, the frog swam a little over three inches in about two minutes. That may not get it to its destination promptly, but the proof-of-concept successfully offers a fresh way to think about robotic design, and the ways engineers can power their creations. Until then, there is always the potential for robo-frog toys.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Carbonbrief

‘Simply staggering’: Rapidly developing ‘super El Niño’ on track to peak in December

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (557 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Carbonbrief

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The ongoing “super El Niño” is likely to peak at the end of 2026 and push average global temperatures to record levels next year.
  • That is according to Carbon Brief’s latest “state of the climate” revision, which analyses El Niño forecasts from more than a dozen climate models, as well as six global temperature datasets.Dr Zeke Hausfather, Carbon Brief’s climate science contributor, described this year’s El Niño as “simply staggering” when answering questions from CB+ members during a CB Connect “ask me anything” session.
  • El Niño is a naturally occurring climate pattern in the tropical Pacific that releases heat from the ocean into the atmosphere and temporarily boosts global temperatures.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The ongoing “super El Niño” is likely to peak at the end of 2026 and push average global temperatures to record levels next year.

That is according to Carbon Brief’s latest “state of the climate” revision, which analyses El Niño forecasts from more than a dozen climate models, as well as six global temperature datasets.Dr Zeke Hausfather, Carbon Brief’s climate science contributor, described this year’s El Niño as “simply staggering” when answering questions from CB+ members during a CB Connect “ask me anything” session.

El Niño is a naturally occurring climate pattern in the tropical Pacific that releases heat from the ocean into the atmosphere and temporarily boosts global temperatures.

This year’s El Niño event – which has been underway since June – has already broken a number of records and reshaped the world’s weather, fuelling fires in Indonesia and “super typhoons” in the west Pacific.

The strength of an El Niño is tracked using the “Niño3.4 anomaly”, which is a measure of how much warmer sea surface temperatures are than average in a section of the central Pacific.

According to recent reports, analysis of more than 600 forecasts from 14 different climate models by Hausfather for Carbon Brief’s “state of the climate” enhancement indicates how models project this year’s El Niño will peak with an anomaly of around 4C. This would be more than a degree above the previous record in 2015-16.

Writing on CB Connect on 5 November, Hausfather wrote:.

Sources indicate that “This El Niño event is developing so rapidly and is reaching sea surface temperatures so warm that it’s simply staggering. We haven’t seen anything like this in the historical record and it may end up being the strongest El Niño event in the past millennium.”.

This year’s El Niño has already chalked up a number of milestones.

On 18 September, the daily anomaly in the Niño3.4 region broke the satellite-era record set in 2015 when it reached 3.11C.

Meanwhile, September as a whole recorded the highest monthly Niño3.4 region temperature anomaly – 2.84C – since sea surface temperature records began in the mid-1800s.

Hausfather wrote on CB Connect that this year’s El Niño had been “running well above any prior El Niño event since June, at times by a full degree [Celsius]”.

Carbon Brief’s “state of the climate” analysis indicates that El Niño is set to continue to intensify into December, with 10 out of 14 models expecting temperatures in the Niño3.4 region to peak in the final month of this year. The remainder anticipate a November peak.

While human emissions of greenhouse gases are responsible for almost all of long-term global warming, temperatures in specific years are strongly influenced by El Niño events.

The “state of the climate” analysis explains that this year’s El Niño event will have its largest effect on global temperatures in 2027. This is because global temperatures typically lag warming in the tropical Pacific by around three months.

Carbon Brief projects that the 2027 average global temperature will reach around 1.74C above pre-industrial levels. It calculates a 96% chance that next year will be the warmest on record.

This projection is based on the historical relationship between year-on-year temperature changes and El Niño conditions the preceding autumn. It also factors in uncertainty around how global temperatures will develop across the remainder of 2026.

#52. Designed to Be Unsinkable, the World's Fastest Ocean Liner Finally Hits the Ocean Floor. The 53,330-Ton S.S. 'United States' Is Now the World's Largest Artificial Reef

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1090 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smithsonianmag

Designed to Be Unsinkable, the World's Fastest Ocean Liner Finally Hits the Ocean Floor. The 53,330-Ton S.S. 'United States' Is Now the World's Largest Artificial Reef

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that on June 29, 1952, a state-of-the-art ocean liner, nearly 1,000 feet long, opened up to the public.
  • Almost immediately, the liner proved worthy of the intense interest.
  • On Wednesday, more than 70 years after its record-setting maiden voyage, crowds once again came out in droves to see the legendary liner depart on one last journey.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that on June 29, 1952, a state-of-the-art ocean liner, nearly 1,000 feet long, opened up to the public. Some 70,000 people flooded to its berth in New York City to catch a glimpse of the S.S. United States before it hit the Atlantic for its maiden voyage.

Almost immediately, the liner proved worthy of the intense interest. On July 3, 1952, the S.S. United States reached England in a record-breaking three days, 10 hours and 40 minutes, a speed that has yet to be surpassed to this day by any passenger liner. In its 17-year run, the ship would go on to host numerous notables, including Marilyn Monroe, Walt Disney, Salvador Dalí and even the Mona Lisa, after the painting’s one and only trip to the United States.

On Wednesday, more than 70 years after its record-setting maiden voyage, crowds once again came out in droves to see the legendary liner depart on one last journey. This time, the S.S. United States was heading to the bottom of the sea for a new life as an artificial reef and diving destination in the Gulf of Mexico.

Designed by the prolific 20th century naval architect William Francis Gibbs, the ocean liner represented the peak of post-World War II maritime technology. Over 100 feet longer than the Titanic, the United States contained no wood except the ship’s grand pianos, built with fire-resistant mahogany. “She will have more aluminum in her than Mr. Gibbs cares to say, a design feature that will contribute to the dual goal of strength and relative lightness,” George Horne reported for the New York Times in 1951. “There are other metals that are even more secret.” In fact, its construction was kept entirely out of the public eye.

Throughout the 1950s and ‘60s, the liner completed more than 800 journeys across the Atlantic, carrying more than 1 million passengers, including many celebrities and politicians.

Did you know? Presidential passengers.

In a recent development, throughout its 17-year tenure, the S.S. United States carried four presidents: Harry Truman, Dwight Eisenhower, John F. Kennedy and a young Bill Clinton, who took it to study at Oxford University as a Rhodes Scholar in 1968.

With its intricately designed interior featuring patriotic art, amenities including a movie theater and its unparalleled speed, the S.S. United States provided many passengers with lasting memories.

“The ship going at this incredible speed—it was almost dangerous sometimes for a kid my size to go out on the deck,” Warren Jones, a board member for the nonprofit S.S. United States Conservancy who sailed on the liner as a child, tells FOX Weather’s Julian Atienza and Brandy Campbell. “Those engines, you felt the vibrations and sailed past the Statue of Liberty. It was unforgettable.”.

Sources indicate that but as airline travel became more accessible, the age of luxury ocean liners soon drew to a close. In 1969, the S.S. United States was abruptly decommissioned. Even crew members were shocked by its sudden withdrawal from service. Several left personal belongings on board, assuming they would go back to work the next day, only to show up to locked gangway doors.

For the next nine years, it languished as a reserve ship for the U.S. Navy, ready to for action if the need arose. But there was no need, and in 1978, the ship was put up for sale.

In the following decades, the ship passed from port to port, from owner to owner, each with different looks for the ship: floating condominiums, hazardous waste removal in Ukraine, a revived cruise liner. But no idea garnered enough money or momentum to last. By 2024, the ship had foundered on a Philadelphia pier for decades.

In a recent development, when the pier’s landlord raised the daily dockage fee to $1,700—$620,500 per year—the S.S. United States was evicted and faced the possibility of getting scrapped. Instead, Florida’s Okaloosa County purchased the ship for $1 million, with plans to turn it into the world’s largest artificial reef. The county already has a fleet of sunken ships off its coast, but the S.S. United States is its crowning jewel.

Officials expect the liner-turned-reef will become home to a variety of marine species, including red snapper, grouper, amberjack, mackerel and tuna. The ship will also be open to divers.

“She’s being reefed and will remain intact and will become a vibrant and dynamic marine habitat,” Susan Gibbs, the conservancy’s president and granddaughter of the ship’s designer, tells the Guardian’s Richard Luscombe.

The conservancy plans to run a museum adjacent to the pier where diving expeditions will set out, featuring the ship’s iconic smokestacks, alongside other parts of the ship’s interior and a collection of artifacts and memorabilia.

A post shared by CBS News' "Sunday Morning" 🌞 (@cbssundaymorning).

Unlike the liner’s legendary maiden voyage, the trip from Philadelphia to the ocean floor was far from speedy. After a handful of false starts and a last-ditch lawsuit, it took months of preparation at a port in Alabama to ready the vessel for its voyage to the bottom of the sea, the New York Times’ Jesse Pesta reports.

It has been revealed that workers removed the ship’s wiring, ductwork, glass and anything that could potentially pose a danger to divers or marine life. They also cut strategic passages through the ship’s interior to create open pathways that would reduce stagnant water and enable divers to easily pass in and out. Finally, they removed off the ship’s two iconic, six-story smokestacks, earmarked for the future museum. The S.S. United States was finally ready for sinking.

It has been revealed that on Wednesday afternoon, the ship set out from Destin, Florida. A crew cut holes in the ship and removed more than 400 portholes. Water flooded in, but as night descended, it still hadn’t sunk.

“She was designed to be unsinkable, and that fact has definitely given our crews some challenges today,” Nick Tomecek, a spokesperson for Okaloosa County, told ABC 6.

Or, as William Francis Gibbs once bragged, “You can’t set her on fire, you can’t sink her and you can’t catch her.”.

Industry observers note that but in the end, only two of those bold claims held true. At 8:59 p.m. Central time, the S.S. United States slipped below the waves, starting a fresh chapter as a home for marine life and a destination for divers from across the world.

Gabby Shell is an editorial intern with Smithsonian magazine.

In 2022, Tokyo's Nakagin Capsule Tower was demolished, bringing an end to one of modern architecture's most recognizable experiments in adaptability. Designed by Kisho Kurokawa and completed in 1972, the building consisted of 140 prefabricated capsules attached to two concrete cores. Its architectural proposition was radical: individual capsules could be replaced as needs evolved, allowing the building to renew itself without dismantling its principal structure. Yet over five decades, the proposed replacement system was never realized. Despite various preservation efforts, deteriorating building services and difficulties in collective decision-making eventually led to its demolition.

‘The times I regret are the ones when I didn’t value myself enough to speak up’

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1223 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pv-magazine

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I believe every business benefits from diverse teams, and the evidence supports that.
  • This matters especially in our industry.
  • Recent findings suggest that the scale of what we need to deliver is huge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I believe every business benefits from diverse teams, and the evidence supports that. McKinsey’s 2023 report, Diversity Matters Even More, found that companies with the most gender-diverse executive teams were 39% more likely to outperform financially.

This matters especially in our industry. Technology, policy, the global picture and grid demands are shifting rapidly, so we need teams that can adapt. In my experience, diverse teams are exactly that. They spot problems faster and find ways through change. Yet women hold only 32% of renewable energy jobs, so we’re missing out on talent we need.

Recent findings suggest that the scale of what we need to deliver is huge. The UK government’s Solar Roadmap aims for at least 45 GW of solar capacity by 2030, and its Clean Energy Jobs Strategy expects around 400,000 additional clean energy jobs by then. We will not fill those roles by recruiting from the same, largely male, talent pool. Widening who we reach, through visible role models and by promoting the exciting careers on offer, brings in more talent. That’s what makes a sector resilient.

According to recent reports, the biggest challenge is that the benefits are not always immediate or obvious, like a rise in sales figures. They build over time: wider talent pools, better working conditions, and creative teams with broader perspectives. The bigger prize is our sector meeting its skills challenge with homegrown talent. Microsoft research found girls were almost twice as likely to be interested in science, technology, engineering and maths when they had role models. When young people see people like them in solar, they can picture themselves there. Inclusion is how we grow our sector well.

Sadly, I’m yet to see the shifts we really need. I’m researching the barriers to completing electrical apprenticeships, and there’s still very little diversity on courses or out on site. Women make up just 11% of engineering and construction apprenticeship starts and only 14% of electrical and electronic engineering degree entrants. Leadership starts with that pipeline. We need to make these great careers more visible in schools and colleges and make construction sites good places for women to work.

The wonderful thing about moving into renewables as a woman in my fifties is that, frankly, I give far fewer sh**s about what people think. By this stage of life, you know who you are and what matters. For me, that means making a difference for our planet and the beautiful people who live on it. We need to decarbonise, do it promptly and make the transition fair. I want to be part of making that happen.

I’ve been incredibly lucky. My co-directors, Scott Burrows and Steve Baker, who co-founded Eden Sustainable and Eden Sustainable Power, believed in me, championed me and gave me opportunities. I came to solar later than they did, with less experience, and they were endlessly patient with my questions. They helped fast-track me into leadership, and I’m so grateful to lead alongside them.

I’ve never had a formal mentor, but I’ve learned so much from my co-directors and friends. We’ve been each other’s sounding boards, sharing challenges and mistakes. I’ve also worked part-time for years as a palliative care specialist nurse, where we had regular psychotherapy. I was sceptical, but now I’d recommend knowing yourself better to everyone. If you don’t have a mentor, I’d encourage you to find your people and learn together.

Recent findings suggest that be passionate, be enthusiastic and be keen to learn. Dig in, put the time in and, when you don’t understand something, speak up and ask questions. Be prepared, then be even more prepared. I need to take my own advice on that one, but I know that’s when I’m at my best. Take a deep breath and bring your difference to the table. The times I regret are the ones when I didn’t value myself enough to speak up.

For me, an inclusive culture starts with leading by example. Treat people as you would want to be treated, and encourage the team to do the same. The best thing we did at Eden was talk about our values as a team and get clear about what we all wanted together. That way, everyone owns those values, lives them and holds each other accountable. We make sure everyone can tell us when things aren’t landing and help shape how we do better. Culture needs time and care, yet it’s often the first thing to go when you’re busy, or money is tight. So we need to protect it.

The most gorgeous impact has been watching flexible working take hold across our teams. Men and women alike can regularly do their share of school runs, school plays, sports days and dentist appointments. I’ve watched family life flourish as a result, and we’ve seen the benefits in our team feedback. That started with a leadership team who understood those pressures from the inside and modelled what we value.

Industry observers note that in Solar Energy UK’s skills working party, we’ve been talking about how talent and teams grow best in fertile soil. If we want young people, women and people from diverse backgrounds to build careers in solar, our sites and teams have to be places where they want to work and can thrive. We created Solar Energy UK’s Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Toolkit to give smaller, busy companies simple steps to get started. Get the soil right, and the talent will take root and stay.

Industry observers note that to a young woman entering solar, I’d say this is a brilliant sector to work in. You’ll go home knowing you’re making a difference, helping our economy decarbonise and bringing health benefits for people and planet, now and for future generations. There are bonus opportunities too, from building things that last to recycling and encouraging nature around solar sites.

With a creaking grid and unstable global markets, we need people who are creative, flexible and quick on their feet. There’s never a dull moment, and there’s plenty of room to grow. Whatever your personality, there’s a place for you in this sector, from working on the tools to finance and everything in between.

According to recent reports, tracey Elliott is a Director at Eden Sustainable Power, where she is committed to accelerating the UK’s transition to a cleaner, more electrified future through renewable energy and private energy markets, helping consumers and generators realise the value of renewables. She combines commercial expertise with a strong focus on stakeholder engagement, skills development and industry collaboration. Tracey is Co-Chair of the Solar Energy UK Skills Working Party, helping to tackle workforce challenges and improve diversity across the sector. She speaks regularly at national energy events and has been recognised for promoting careers and inclusion in the green economy. She is Co-Founder and Trustee of The Pickwell Foundation, which works on climate change and on supporting people displaced by conflict and disaster. Tracey co-owns Pickwell Manor and Ravendere Retreats, luxury sustainable holiday accommodation and a retreat venue in North Devon.

Industry observers note that interested in joining Tracey Elliott and other women industry leaders and experts at Women in Solar+ Europe? Find out more: www.wiseu.network.

#47. Tech Report: Q&A: What is the Belém-Antalya mechanism for a ‘just transition’?

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2440 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Carbonbrief

Tech Report: Q&A: What is the Belém-Antalya mechanism for a ‘just transition’?

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2440 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Carbonbrief

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the key expected outcomes from the upcoming COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, is the launch of a “just transition mechanism”.
  • This follows years of calls from civil society to support a “just transition” as countries shift towards low-emissions energy systems and away from fossil fuels.
  • At the COP30 UN climate talks last year in the Brazilian city of Belém parties agreed to establish a “mechanism” to support this goal, called the “Belém-Antalya mechanism” (BAM).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the key expected outcomes from the upcoming COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, is the launch of a “just transition mechanism”.

This follows years of calls from civil society to support a “just transition” as countries shift towards low-emissions energy systems and away from fossil fuels.

At the COP30 UN climate talks last year in the Brazilian city of Belém parties agreed to establish a “mechanism” to support this goal, called the “Belém-Antalya mechanism” (BAM).

Groups that have championed the BAM want it to act as a central hub on just transitions, providing support for workers and communities around the world.

However, the details of exactly what the much-touted BAM will consist of remain vague, with developed and developing countries disagreeing about its functions and purpose.

Disagreements continued at the UN climate talks in Bonn in June 2026, including on the crucial question of how the BAM will be financed.

Here, Carbon Brief looks at where the idea for the BAM came from, how it could support just transitions and what to expect from COP31.

It has been revealed that A “just transition” is the idea that workers and communities should be supported in the shift to a low-carbon economy. It is a central principle behind the idea of climate justice.

Often, the term refers to those linked to the fossil-fuel industry, but it can also refer to transitions taking place in agriculture, heavy industry and various other sectors.

The concept originated in the 1980s, when US labour unions forged alliances with environmental justice groups. It has since become a key part of international climate discussions.

The preamble to the 2015 Paris Agreement includes a commitment to “tak[e] into account the imperatives of a just transition of the workforce and the creation of decent work and quality jobs in accordance with nationally defined development priorities”.

Bert De Wel, policy officer at the International Trade Union Confederation (ITUC), tells Carbon Brief:.

It has been revealed that “The labour movement is very happy with the wide audience and broad political support that the concept has received since its inception in the 1980s. The inclusion in the Paris Agreement, with the reference to the creation of decent work and quality jobs was a milestone for the movement. While other demands have been added…we continue to stress the labour dimension as being central to the concept.”.

Three years after the creation of the Paris Agreement, at COP24 in the former coal-mining city of Katowice, the Polish presidency highlighted the matter of just transitions.

The need for carbon-cutting policies to ensure “a just transition of the workforce” that creates “decent work and quality jobs” was included in the “Silesia declaration”, issued by the presidency during the first week of COP24.

While the declaration was only signed by 50 countries – roughly a quarter of the parties at the summit – it was still “noted” in the final COP text.

This helped to drive momentum behind the idea, culminating in formal agreement at COP27 in Egypt to launch a “work programme on just transition” (JTWP).

De Wel indicates the establishment of the JTWP was a “major step forward” that allowed parties to “speak about just transition in more concrete terms”.

In the years since, negotiators have worked to flesh out the JTWP, with disagreements between parties about what its purpose should be.

Broadly, developed countries would like it to focus on domestic workforces, while some nations want a more global outlook, including support for transitions in developing countries.

The JTWP has proved a challenging negotiating space, with talks at the COP29 summit in 2024 closing without an agreement, in what one observer dubbed a “betrayal”.

However, despite these frustrations, parties at COP30 in Brazil agreed to establish a new institutional mechanism on just transitions, which has become widely known as the BAM. The move was hailed as a “victory” by civil society.

In the run-up to COP30, civil society began to push for the establishment of an “institutional arrangement” that would move work under the JTWP from talk into action.

It has been revealed that (This was originally called the “Belém action mechanism” by civil society groups, who subsequently updated this to the “Belém-Antalya mechanism” following the outcome at COP30. However, in the JTWP text agreed at COP30 it is only described as a “mechanism”, sometimes also referred to as the “just transition mechanism”.).

Anabella Rosemberg, senior advisor on just transition at NGO umbrella group Climate Action Network (CAN) International, tells Carbon Brief:.

“The idea of the mechanism emerged from the collaboration of civil society, trade unions, feminist groups, youth and Indigenous peoples in the UNFCCC.

“It was clear that the kind of activities being run under the JTWP – two dialogues a year and one ministerial – would not support the delivery of just-transition strategies on the ground, so a upcoming approach was developed to get words into action.”.

Following the inception of the idea, civil society did “tonnes of stuff to boost it up the agenda”, Dr Leon Sealey-Huggins, a senior campaigner at the charity War on Want, tells Carbon Brief.

This ranged from presenting demands and proposals to different constituents, organising joint letters and writing policy papers, all the way through to designing logos, creating memes and even a song.

These efforts ultimately paid off: during the Bonn climate negotiations in June 2025, one draft text included the idea for a upcoming institutional arrangement. One of the options in the draft text was for a “toolbox, guidance framework, global platform, technical assistance network [or] mechanism”.

This inclusion was broadly welcomed as a “big win” for civil society groups, although parties acknowledged that more needed to be done to flesh out the idea.

Going into COP30, civil society groups continued to push the idea of creating a BAM, with protests, banners and badges visible around the venue.

According to recent reports, early in negotiations, the G77 and China – a large coalition of developing countries at UN climate talks – put forward their own proposal for a just transition “mechanism”. This, they suggested, could provide technical assistance, support international cooperation and help to foster partnerships in an effort to address implementation gaps.

Their proposal faced initial pushback from developed-country parties including Norway, the UK and others, who opposed it due to concerns that it would duplicate existing systems and require additional funding.

Recent findings suggest that developed countries also opposed the use of the term “mechanism”, with the EU suggesting an “action plan” as a potential alternative. Nevertheless, the creation of a “mechanism” was included in the final draft text on the JTWP.

This text was formally approved during the COP30 closing plenary to extended applause from many in the hall.

In a statement at the time, Chiara Martinelli, director at CAN Europe, welcomed the decision:.

“Delivering BAM was a major civil society win. It creates a coordinated institutional home to drive forward progress on the just transition.”.

The decision to develop the mechanism included a request for parties to work over the subsequent year – through to COP31 – on a strategy to get things started.

According to civil society, the BAM could help tackle the fractured just-transition landscape by centralising resources and helping to overcome a number of barriers.

Sources indicate that speaking to Carbon Brief, Rosemberg says the just-transition space “lacks coordination and the right kind of support and is quite disconnected from climate action imperatives”. She adds:.

“The BAM can play a role in bringing those [people] trying to make just transition happen together, identify gaps and barriers, foster cooperation and accelerate support.”.

Civil society has put forward a number of proposals likely to inform the structure of the BAM. Most consist of a mechanism with three parts, which would encompass and expand upon the work that is right now being carried out under the JTWP.

One proposal by a coalition of five NGOs suggests the mechanism is formed of a steering body, a “knowledge arm” and an “implementation arm”.

Industry observers note that the steering body would coordinate the work of the two arms of the BAM, including deciding the topics that should be discussed under the ongoing JTWP, which will continue to feature in climate negotiations. They suggest the body would recommend topics that require negotiation when “gaps that require political guidance are identified”.

Their proposal is illustrated in the infographic below, showing the steering body acting as a central hub for work within the BAM.

The final part of the BAM, the “implementation arm”, would act as a hub to enable and coordinate technical, financial and knowledge-based assistance for those pursuing a just transition.

Rosemberg says the vision of civil society is for work to go “beyond negotiators’ dialogues”. She says the BAM could enable the organisation of a “matchmaking platform” to provide support faster, as well as dedicated groups to identify and mobilise financial resources. She adds:.

Industry observers note that “Finally, through bottom-up identification of barriers, the BAM can also allow a discussion on enabling just transition that is informed by practitioners. The BAM can show that implementation does not necessarily mean taking challenges outside of the UNFCCC.”.

A separate proposal for the structure of the BAM from the Global Campaign to Demand Climate Justice (DCJ) – a separate coalition of NGOs – similarly proposes three elements. These would be: coordination and coherence; knowledge generation; and international cooperation and support.

Sealey-Huggins, who is affiliated with DCJ, notes:.

“If it works in practice, what we’ll see is a cascade of just-transition policies implemented across countries, across sectors in a unifying, transformational moment for justice-centered climate action, and that will be the key to unlocking the transition that’s been missing so far.”.

Another proposal for the BAM comes from the Grantham Institute at the London School of Economics. It suggests the three functions of the mechanism should be capacity-building, technical assistance and knowledge-sharing, but it recommends a dual-arm structure comprising a policy arm and an operational arm.

De Wel tells Carbon Brief that while there is “rather broad consensus on the functions”, parties are pushing in “very different directions” on how the BAM will be set up.

Within UN climate negotiations, some parties have raised concerns about the potential cost of the mechanism.

The push to launch the BAM comes at a time when the UNFCCC itself is facing a funding gap, following the US withdrawal. Several other parties have also delayed or reduced their contributions, in response to changes in domestic priorities.

This has led to the UNFCCC cancelling events and not filling vacated positions, as the organisation struggles to carry out its existing functions.

Sources indicate that as such, some parties have expressed hesitancy about creating another mechanism under the remit of the UNFCCC, which also requires funding. However, proponents of the BAM argue that the costs of running it would be minimal.

Rosemberg tells Carbon Brief that the BAM represents “an opportunity to streamline and make efficient use of public resources”. She adds:.

In a recent development, “The mechanism does not necessarily require the creation of a costly upcoming institution. Instead, it can leverage existing climate-finance channels and philanthropy.”.

She adds that a “similar body” to the potential mechanism, the Climate Technology Centre and Network, costs less than $10m a year. Rosemberg notes that this is “not an impossible amount to be found if there is political will to make just transition happen”.

Sources indicate that de Wel notes that the mechanism will build on existing work inside the UNFCCC and out, including the International Labour Organization’s “just transition policy gateway”. He further emphasises that “we’re clearly not asking for a new [just-transition] fund, we want all climate finance to be just-transition proof”.

Alongside highlighting the potential efficiencies of the BAM design, many have argued that the potential benefits are well worth the cost of the latest mechanism, with Sealey-Huggins telling Carbon Brief:.

“The cost to the [BAM] secretariat pales in comparison to the potential benefit of the action.”.

Despite the “victory” in Belém of agreeing to set up the fresh just-transition mechanism, climate negotiations in Bonn in June 2026 rapidly hit sticking points.

While Bonn did ultimately agree on a “skeleton” draft text to send forward for further negotiations at COP31, many details still need to be agreed in Antalya for the BAM to start functioning.

Industry observers note that de Wel cautions that a “swift approval of the agenda of COP31 allowing parties to start the negotiations” is “crucial”. He adds:.

“We can’t lose any time, there is so much work that needs to be done on [just transition]. Then we need a constructive approach by the major country blocs. If one of them starts playing tactical games, then it will be lost.”.

In a submission to the UNFCCC earlier this year, CAN called for a series of measures to get the BAM up and running. This includes calling for a decision to be made on a first face-to-face meeting of a “just-transition committee” – a core part of the mechanism in the group’s proposal – to be held in April 2027.

Ahead of COP31, negotiating groups such as the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS), the least developed countries (LDCs) and the African group expressed support for the mechanism and called for it to be focused on implementation.

The EU also supported the launch of the mechanism, but along with other parties cautioned that it should be complementary to the JTWP.

While no submissions opposed the creation of the mechanism, groups such as LDCs called for a focus on “means of implementation” – commonly understood as finance – highlighting it is likely to continue to be a key point of discussion in the upcoming summit.

Sealey-Huggins tells Carbon Brief what his “pie in the sky best-case scenario vision” for the outcome at COP31 would look like. He continues:.

Sources indicate that “G77 and China make the case again that the mechanism must be equally resourced. It must be well-designed. It must include people’s participation. It must address the barriers to implementation of just transition. It must facilitate the means of implementation. It must ensure justice at the very heart of climate action.

“And then it’s agreed and it’s implemented immediately. So this work begins straight after Antalya to start forming committees and other bodies that can undertake the implementation.”.

However, Rosemberg cautions that there is still a “question mark [remaining over] the level of ambition of the [COP31] presidencies, who need to move from simply talking about establishing any [just-transition] mechanism to engaging parties, so that we get a mechanism that is fit for purpose”.

#46. Florida Is Facing Its Worst Dengue Outbreak in Decades, With at Least 524 Locally Acquired Cases. Here's What to Know

Florida Is Facing Its Worst Dengue Outbreak in Decades, With at Least 524 Locally Acquired Cases. Here's What to Know

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this year, the Florida Department of Health has recorded a staggering 524 locally acquired cases of dengue, a mosquito-borne viral disease, as of October 31.
  • Sources indicate that most infected people either do not show symptoms or experience only mild illness.
  • Later that month, three counties in Florida declared local emergencies over the illness, and in October, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued a national emergency response to dengue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this year, the Florida Department of Health has recorded a staggering 524 locally acquired cases of dengue, a mosquito-borne viral disease, as of October 31. That’s the highest number recorded there since the disease returned to the state in 2009, according to Forbes’ John Drake. For context, only 62 locally acquired cases were documented in 2025.

Sources indicate that most infected people either do not show symptoms or experience only mild illness. But in early September, a Tampa-area woman named Gay Rabb Small died of dengue on her 80th birthday, after developing a tremor and going to the emergency room, per the Upcoming York Times’ Anemona Hartocollis.

Later that month, three counties in Florida declared local emergencies over the illness, and in October, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued a national emergency response to dengue.

Industry observers note that “It is very unusual to have transmission in the United States,” Eva Harris, an infectious diseases expert at the University of California, Berkeley, tells the Times. “This is so very much of an eye-opener.”.

Here’s what to know about dengue.

Dengue is a viral disease spread by mosquitoes, mainly the species Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, which are both present in Florida, among other places. The disease is more common in tropical and subtropical regions, where these biting insects thrive, than in temperate climates.

Around three in four infected people are asymptomatic or have mild flu-like symptoms, such as fever, headache, nausea and rash. Muscle and joint pain is another common symptom, which is why the disease is sometimes called “breakbone fever.” Symptoms usually appear within two weeks of being bitten by an infected mosquito and clear up after a week or two.

However, one in four dengue cases becomes severe. Those symptoms include extreme abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, rapid breathing and blood in vomit or stool, and anyone experiencing them should seek medical care. These signs often appear after the fever goes away, and people who have previously been infected are at a greater risk of severe dengue.

Individuals who recover from dengue can continue feeling fatigued for several weeks.

According to recent reports, although dengue vaccines exist, none are currently approved for use in the United States. They’re authorized in nations where the disease is more common, such as Argentina, Brazil, Indonesia and Thailand.

Industry observers note that vaccines are also challenging to develop, because dengue has four distinct but closely related virus types, called 1, 2, 3 and 4. When infected with one type, the body builds up pathogen-fighting antibodies against it, and immunity lasts for life, reports the Associated Press’ Mike Stobbe. But if later infected with a different type of dengue, the antibodies might fail to attack that virus and even help the pathogen enter immune cells and make copies of itself.

Recent findings suggest that experts say the best way to protect yourself is to avoid mosquito bites. Cover up with loose-fitting long sleeves and pants, apply insect repellent with DEET and control for mosquitoes in and around your home, such as by removing stagnant water—where young mosquitoes live—and treating your yard with insecticide.

Additionally, there are no specific treatments for dengue. For those with mild symptoms, physicians recommend drinking plenty of fluids and resting. Ill individuals can take acetaminophen to alleviate fever and pain, but they should avoid nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as ibuprofen and aspirin, because they can increase the risk of bleeding.

People with severe dengue might need oral or intravenous fluids or even blood transfusions.

Historically, most U.S. cases of dengue have come from travel to other countries or U.S. territories. Southern Florida has hosted many of them, because it’s a transit hub that welcomes lots of travelers from Puerto Rico and other locations where the disease is prevalent, says Dawn Wesson, an infectious diseases researcher at Tulane University, to the AP. In fact, the state has reported 382 travel-associated cases of dengue in 2026, as of October 31.

Quick fact: Previous largest statewide outbreak.

Sources indicate that before Florida’s current dengue outbreak, the largest statewide one occurred in Hawaii. Health officials there recorded 264 locally acquired cases in a six-month stretch from 2015 to 2016.

Sources indicate that however, that means locally acquired cases have outpaced travel-linked ones this year, and many infections have shown up in the central part of the state. Researchers are still trying to figure out what’s behind the trend, per the Times.

According to recent reports, rainstorms have recently flooded parking lots and playgrounds in Southern Florida, which could potentially help mosquitoes lay eggs, multiply and continue spreading dengue. Additionally, climate change is continuing to make the state a warmer and wetter place, creating an even more ideal environment for the disease-carrying creatures.

“I think the dengue outbreaks will get worse over the coming years in the U.S.,” Ira Longini, a biostatistician at the University of Florida, tells the Times.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Click to tell Google to prioritize Quanta and see more of the best coverage of science and math in your search and AI results.

According to recent reports, at its core, every cell is just a bubble of chemistry sealed inside a membrane. In modern cells, that chemistry is extraordinarily complex, orchestrating some 1 billion reactions per second. Likewise, its container, the lipid membrane, is built and maintained by elaborate biochemical mechanisms. But even the much simpler first cells would have needed a bubble too.

Industry observers note that without a physical boundary corralling molecules into a small space, whatever it was that turned into early life would have been too dispersed to assemble the complex systems that life requires, noted Bruce Damer, an astrobiologist at the University of California, Santa Cruz. “You need a container before you can get the chemistry.”.

It has been revealed that to some researchers, the cell membrane seems so essential to life’s functions that they propose it as the origin of life. In this framework, known as the “lipid first” hypothesis, Earth transitioned from a mess of primordial chemistry to something recognizably alive because of those containers.

In a recent development, but many proponents of the lipid world go even further. They argue that the bubbles did more than hold chemistry. The bubbles themselves began to evolve.

According to recent reports, evolution requires a way for parents to pass traits to offspring. Modern life accomplishes this with complex biochemicals such as DNA and RNA, which can encode and copy information in their sequences. In the 1990s, researchers imagined a different possibility: What if a chemical system, rather than a molecule, could carry heritable information and become subject to evolution?

Recent findings suggest that the idea begins with a puddle of water on the early Earth. The puddle is stocked with all kinds of small organic molecules, some homegrown and some delivered by dust and meteorites. Many of these molecules have a split personality. One end of them is drawn to water, or “hydrophilic.” The other is repelled by water in the same way that oil is. These “hydrophobic” ends will huddle together to hide from the water, while the hydrophilic ends will face outward. These behaviors cause the molecules to form a tiny sphere — a bubble.

The primordial puddle also has other molecules, simpler raw ingredients that can, under the correct circumstances, be turned into more of themselves. Here’s how that works: Imagine that a bubble contains two special molecules, molecule A and molecule B. Each of these molecules speeds up a chemical reaction that uses other ingredients in the puddle. Molecule A, in this case, speeds up chemical reactions that produce molecule B. After a while, the bubble fills up with B’s. These, in turn, may speed up the production of another kind of molecule.

Sometimes, there might be a puddle where B’s return the favor and make more A’s. The A’s make more B’s, then the B’s make more A’s. Each type keeps the other topped up in an endless loop. The bubble containing these A’s and B’s will grow, but the ratio of molecules will stay more or less steady.

In time, the bubble will split, and its molecules will be dealt out into its baby bubbles. Each of these may get some A’s and some B’s, and the symbiotic loop will keep running, building the parent’s compositional recipe more faithfully than chance alone would. Unlike with DNA, which is copied exactly, letter by letter, a proportion of molecules gets passed down to the next generation of bubbles.

In a recent development, but evolution needs more than heredity. It needs to allow for change. In our chemical soup, that possibility comes from a stray molecule C, which like a mutation tips a bubble into a different molecular loop. Faster-growing bubbles split more often and crowd out slower-growing bubbles, so the fast-moving descendants will make up a bigger and bigger share of the crowd. Slow recipes get squeezed out.

It has been revealed that in 2000, Doron Lancet, a geneticist at the Weizmann Institute of Science, and Daniel Segrè, a computational biologist at Boston University, published the results of a computer model that explored whether these dynamics could lead to lifelike behavior. They found that bubbles can pass their compositions to their daughters, which vary and compete, fulfilling the requirements for natural selection. In their computer model, at least, the lipid-world idea passed its first test.

Recent findings suggest that which molecules could build these bubbles? In the original simulation, molecules A, B, and the rest would be different kinds of lipids. The team settled on lipids, the molecules that make up modern cell membranes, in part because they mirror the model’s required half-hydrophobic, half-hydrophilic nature. When lipids are dropped into water, they can assemble into double-layered sheets. Under the right conditions, the sheets close in on themselves, forming a sphere with a pocket of water trapped inside.

According to recent reports, but in the 25 years since Lancet, Segrè, and their colleagues published the original lipid-world hypothesis, scientists have questioned whether the first compartments had to be made of lipids at all. Couldn’t other types of molecules have formed a container first? “There really isn’t a distinct lipid-world hypothesis anymore,” Damer said. Researchers have proposed that certain minerals, such as iron sulfides, could have formed the walls of a container, or that coacervates — liquidlike droplets where molecules gather and concentrate — could have acted as membrane-free vessels for early chemistry.

Damer and David Deamer, a Santa Cruz biochemist who worked with Lancet and Segrè on the original hypothesis, have stayed focused on lipids, but in a specific setting: hot-spring pools. They now study whether the repeated drying and refilling of such pools could have squeezed simple molecules between layers of lipids to develop increasingly complex systems. Damer views their more recent “hot spring hypothesis” as an extension of the lipid world.

Origins-of-life research is famously contentious, and scientists in the field debate the lipid world against other ideas about how life formed. “The idea of a lipid-only form of primitive life has never made sense to me,” said Jack Szostak, a Nobel Prize–winning biochemist at the University of Chicago. He cited the lack of experimental evidence that a lipid-based system can evolve. Plus, he said, how even simple lipids would have formed on the early Earth is “the least well-developed aspect of all of prebiotic chemistry.”.

Sources indicate that another criticism strikes at the heart of the original computer simulation. A 2010 analysis suggested that the replication of compositional information from one generation to the next would be too inaccurate for natural selection to work.

None of these objections, though, is about whether early life needed a bubble. Even Szostak, who favors an RNA-based explanation for the origin of life, agrees on the point that the lipid-first camp cares about most — that compartments are necessary to keep related molecules together. Without them, he remarked, “Darwinian evolution could not operate.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that it seems straight out of a Disney movie—wild animals from two different species becoming inseparable friends.
  • Last spring, the wildlife center received two likely orphaned turkey poults (young turkeys).
  • According to recent reports, “Since we never raise baby animals alone, we had to find a companion for the remaining poult,” the wildlife center wrote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it seems straight out of a Disney movie—wild animals from two different species becoming inseparable friends. And yet that’s what happened at the Raven Ridge Wildlife Center in southeastern Pennsylvania, between a turkey and a mourning dove.

Last spring, the wildlife center received two likely orphaned turkey poults (young turkeys). To calm them down, the team put them with a feather-duster as a stand-in mother turkey. Because turkey poults are easily stressed, they are difficult to rehabilitate, according to a Facebook post by the wildlife center. In fact, one of them didn’t make it.

According to recent reports, “Since we never raise baby animals alone, we had to find a companion for the remaining poult,” the wildlife center wrote. “We paired it with a baby mourning dove of similar size, hoping they would comfort each other while eating and exploring as they are both ground eaters.”.

Sources indicate that the pairing turned out to be a raging success. They formed an inseparable bond that Raven Ridge Wildlife Center had never seen before. Months later, the team gave the dove a soft release, meaning the bird could leave whenever it wanted. But he clearly had no intention of leaving his friend. The dove continued returning to the turkey’s cage, and the two would sit near each other on either side of the separation.

“After a few days, we put the dove back in with the turkey, and it was clear they were happiest together,” the wildlife center explained. But “we knew keeping them caged for the rest of their lives, or keeping them just because they were cute, was neither an option nor fair to these wild animals.”.

According to recent reports, as such, the team contacted a large sanctuary in Pennsylvania to request a joint release. This way, the duo could choose whether to stick together or follow their own paths. After their soft release, the dove flew into the trees and the turkey started foraging, free to stick together or join other members of their species.

“We don’t know if they’ll stay together, but our team made sure they had a safe place until they were ready to be on their own,” the wildlife center concluded.
