#41. The National Portrait Gallery Wasn't Allowed to Acquire Photographs When It Opened in 1968. Fifty Years Later, the Smithsonian Museum's Collection Has Grown to 11,000 Photos and Counting

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2611 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smithsonianmag

The National Portrait Gallery Wasn't Allowed to Acquire Photographs When It Opened in 1968. Fifty Years Later, the Smithsonian Museum's Collection Has Grown to 11,000 Photos and Counting

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2611 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, when the Smithsonian’s National Portrait Gallery opened to the public in 1968, its curators had a clear remit: to collect “painted or sculptured likenesses” of individuals who had left their mark on American history and culture.
  • This restriction wasn’t instated for aesthetic or ideological reasons.
  • “The law was on its face petty and anachronistic,” the Washington Post wrote in 1977.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when the Smithsonian’s National Portrait Gallery opened to the public in 1968, its curators had a clear remit: to collect “painted or sculptured likenesses” of individuals who had left their mark on American history and culture. Photography didn’t make the cut, despite the fact that the medium had been invented nearly a century and a half earlier.

This restriction wasn’t instated for aesthetic or ideological reasons. Instead, it came down to a turf war in the nation’s capital. Staff at the Library of Congress didn’t want to compete with the gallery when acquiring photos for their own collection, so Congress agreed to restrict the definition of portraiture in the act authorizing the museum’s creation.

“The law was on its face petty and anachronistic,” the Washington Post wrote in 1977. “It was also antidemocratic. … Only those who had the time and money or, perhaps, the vanity, to sit for painters or sculptors would have been admitted to the museum.”.

As Ann Shumard, the museum’s senior curator of photographs, notes, it quickly became “glaringly apparent that if photographs continued to be excluded, there would be countless numbers of extraordinary, significant Americans whose likenesses would never find their way to the walls of the Portrait Gallery.” But it was only in 1976 that Congress—with the Library of Congress’ blessing—expanded the museum’s mandate to include “portraits and reproductions thereof made by any means or process, whether invented or developed heretofore or hereafter.”.

In a recent development, half a century later, the Portrait Gallery’s photography collection has grown to more than 11,000 objects. To mark this milestone, the museum is staging an exhibition titled “Photographic Memory: Fifty Years of Collecting.” In addition to highlighting the breadth of the holdings, the show chronicles the history of photography itself, from mid-19th-century daguerreotypes to contemporary inkjet prints derived from digital files. Some of the works on view have never been publicly displayed before; chief among them is an 1846 daguerreotype of Dolley Madison, which is the earliest known photograph of a first lady.

Did you know? The Old Patent Office Building.

According to recent reports, “Photographic Memory” includes iconic images such as Alexander Gardner’s “cracked-plate” portrait of Abraham Lincoln, taken just a few months before the 16th president’s assassination in April 1865, as well as lesser-known works like an intimate 1898 snapshot of Native American activist Zitkála-Šá and a 1960 picture of Mahalia Jackson that captures the gospel singer mid-performance. The oldest portrait in the show is an 1843 daguerreotype of John Quincy Adams, the first president to sit for a photograph, while the most recent is a 2020 inkjet print of Spanish American chef and humanitarian José Andrés.

It has been revealed that encyclopedic in scope and ambition, the exhibition nevertheless features just a fraction of the museum’s photography collection. It “includes 129 objects,” Shumard says. “If you do the math, that’s roughly 1 percent of the total holdings.”.

Industry observers note that to narrow down the pool of potential images, the curator compiled a list of major photographers whose work is represented in the gallery, such as Annie Leibovitz and Alfred Stieglitz. “Oftentimes,” she says, “folks may be more inclined to think about the individuals depicted than the artists represented, and consequently, visitors may not be as familiar with the range of significant photographers” featured in the collection. “From there,” Shumard adds, “I then looked for images of sitters whose portraits I thought epitomized the best work of these photographers, as well as representing wide-ranging fields of individual endeavor.” She also considered the photographic processes used to create the portraits, selecting pictures that reflected the evolution of these techniques.

“There are certainly sitters and photographers who didn’t make the cut, not because I don't value both the quality of the image and the importance of the sitter,” the curator claims. Practical considerations influenced the selection, with portraits competing for limited exhibition space. “It’s really crucial when you’re laying out a show to have works that are in harmony or in conversation with one another, and sometimes something dropped away just in that process,” Shumard adds.

Other works weren’t eligible for inclusion simply because they’d been exhibited recently and are too fragile to be displayed again so soon. Ultimately, Shumard encourages visitors whose favorite figures are absent from the exhibition to conduct a search on the Portrait Gallery’s website. She states, “They might very well find that while that individual’s work is not represented in the exhibition, it’s certainly part of our permanent collection.”.

The French scientist and artist Louis-Jacques-Mandé Daguerre developed the daguerreotype, the world’s first commercially viable photographic process, in 1839. To create these one-of-a-kind portraits, photographers treated polished, silver-coated sheets of copper with iodine and bromine vapors, producing a light-sensitive surface that could be inserted into a camera to capture an image that was then developed over heated mercury.

Daguerre’s technique promptly gained traction as a relatively inexpensive, convenient alternative to traditional portraiture. “It’s not as though they’re giving these daguerreotypes away,” Shumard told Smithsonian magazine in 2019, “but it’s so much cheaper than having a painted likeness made.” Families could sit for group portraits that served as treasured mementos or visit local galleries to see daguerreotypes that were widely touted as more truthful likenesses of famous faces than paintings and sculptures.

“Photographic Memory” features both daguerreotypes and ambrotypes, the faster, cheaper process that largely replaced them in the mid-1850s. Standouts in this section include an 1856 photograph of Olive Oatman, a white woman who was taken captive by the Mohave as a teenager, and a daguerreotype of abolitionist John Brown, created by Black photographer Augustus Washington around 1846 or 1847. Whereas a posthumous oil painting of Brown demonstrates him with a frenzied, unfocused stare and an overgrown beard, the studio portrait depicts a man firmly in control of his image, with his gaze steely and his hand raised in a pledge to the antislavery cause.

The exhibition also showcases portraits of naturalist Henry David Thoreau and abolitionist Frederick Douglass. Both were acquired before the Portrait Gallery was officially authorized to collect photographs. To circumvent the ban, staff found private donors whose funds could be used to purchase the portraits for the museum’s secondary support collection.

Although this workaround enabled the acquisition of several major photographs prior to 1976, it was only in the bicentennial year that the gallery’s collecting efforts truly kicked off. That November, the Portrait Gallery hired its founding curator of photography, William F. Stapp. “He was very eager to make sure that the collection would make it possible to trace the development of photographic portraiture from its earliest days up to the present time,” indicates Shumard, who joined the staff three years later, in 1979. “It was very prescient because … since then, much of that very early photography has become increasingly rare to come by.”.

One such timely acquisition offered a glimpse at a man more often found behind the camera: Mathew Brady, the photographer best known for his unvarnished images of the Civil War. Dated to around 1851, the picture is classified as “a self-portrait, even though Brady was not actually operating the camera when the daguerreotype was made,” Shumard says. “But he is really serving as an art director in a sense. The composition is a really strong, triangular one with him at the apex,” flanked by his wife and his sister.

Brady’s work (or that of his studio, which featured Gardner, Timothy H. O’Sullivan and other photographers) is a recurring thread in the exhibition. It pops up in sections about the Civil War; westward expansion; and salted paper prints, a process used to print positive images from photographic negatives. The show highlights the Brady studio’s portraits of prominent 19th-century figures, from Confederate spy Rose O’Neal Greenhow to Union General George B. McClellan to Lincoln.

One of the Lincoln portraits on view dates to February 27, 1860, the same day that the soon-to-be president delivered a rousing antislavery speech at the Cooper Union in New York City. As historian Harold Holzer wrote in a 2006 essay, Brady sought to convey a specific image of the politician, surrounding him with “symbols of both learning and public service.” The photographer also asked Lincoln to pose while standing rather than sitting down, to “emphasize, rather than disguise, his subject’s most striking physical attribute: his height.”.

Industry observers note that after the Republican Party selected Lincoln as its presidential candidate in May 1860, Brady’s portrait of the clean-shaven, sunken-cheeked nominee circulated widely in lithograph, engraving and tintype reproductions. By introducing voters across the country to Lincoln, Brady helped the candidate win the election. Lincoln himself acknowledged the photographer’s contribution to his political success, once declaring, “Brady and the Cooper Union speech made me president.”.

In a recent development, the two Brady portraits of Lincoln exhibited in “Photographic Memory” are printed on salted paper, a medium that is “particularly vulnerable to light fading,” Shumard indicates. Although the Portrait Gallery has a sizable collection of salted paper prints, these fragile images are rarely displayed, the curator adds, as “our exhibitions typically stay on view for a longer time period, and with brighter light levels than would be advisable.”.

Sources indicate that to account for conservation concerns, the museum has placed several salted paper prints on view in a separate gallery space with motion-activated lighting. Featured sitters include religious leader Brigham Young, sculptor Harriet Goodhue Hosmer and Seminole chief Billy Bowlegs.

According to recent reports, rounding out the exhibition’s medium-specific sections is a trove of seven stereographs. Ever so slightly different, these paired prints appear three-dimensional when viewed through a stereoscope. Museum visitors can look through one such optical device to find themselves face to face with Lincoln, author Harriet Beecher Stowe and Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer, among other famous names.

Sources indicate that these portraits differ from the genre of stereographs most popular in the late 19th and early 20th centuries: visions of faraway lands. As physician and poet Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr. wrote in an 1859 essay for the Atlantic, the “infinite volumes of poems that I treasure in this small library of glass and pasteboard” transported him to Rhenish vineyards, Roman arches, Alpine glaciers and ancient Egyptian pyramids. “The first effect of looking at a good photograph through the stereoscope is a surprise such as no painting ever produced,” Holmes argued. “The mind feels its way into the very depths of the picture.”.

Sources indicate that aside from the galleries dedicated to various photographic processes, the exhibition is organized largely chronologically. “Photographic Memory” explores both the Civil War and its aftermath through images spanning the second half of the 19th century, including an evocative albumen silver print of Lincoln assassination co-conspirator Lewis Thornton Powell and a studio portrait of Ko K’un-hua, the first native Chinese speaker to teach Mandarin at an American university.

According to Shumard, Boston merchants lobbied Harvard University to hire a Chinese professor so that “students who might be interested in pursuing careers in commerce” would be able to converse with their Chinese counterparts without an intermediary. George Kendall Warren’s portrait of Ko K’un-hua, dated to between 1879 and 1882, shows “a dignified, middle-aged man in the long, high-necked, heavy garments of a scholar-official of the Qing dynasty,” Harvard magazine noted in 2008.

Although Ko K’un-hua taught just four or five students before he died of pneumonia in 1882, he “won many admirers and personal friends in America in a short time”—an achievement made all the more impressive by the pervasive anti-Chinese sentiment sweeping the nation at the time, historian Xu Guoqi writes in Chinese and Americans: A Shared History.

Jumping ahead to the 20th century, Shumard calls attention to a pair of photographs taken in 1935. One is a portrait of novelist John Steinbeck, who drapes his arms over the back of a chair while clasping a cigarette in his right hand. The other is a Dorothea Lange picture of documentary filmmaker Pare Lorentz at work in California. “Both are, of course, so focused on the Great Depression, the Dust Bowl and the migration of those who were so severely impacted by that economic and climatic disaster,” the curator indicates. The Lorentz photograph also underscores the museum’s “elastic definition of portraiture,” which extends far beyond formal studio portraits.

“There are photojournalistic images that might not have been conceived by the photographer as a portrait, but in fact, that photojournalistic image allows us to understand an individual and their role in our nation’s history better, perhaps, than a formal studio portrait,” Shumard says. She points to Gordon Parks’ 1963 print of Malcolm X handing out copies of an article headlined “Seven Unarmed Negroes Shot in Cold Blood by Los Angeles Police,” as well as a photograph of civil rights activist Ella Baker delivering a speech on the Atlantic City boardwalk in 1964. “It really captures her in action rather than in a more static pose,” Shumard explains. “Someone might say, ‘Well, is that really a portrait?’ And in my view, it is.”.

Industry observers note that other highlights from the later sections of the exhibition include Herb Ritts Jr.’s 1996 portrait of Christopher Reeve and Tseng Kwong Chi’s New York, New York. The first is a side view of the Superman actor in a motorized wheelchair, taken the year after an equestrian accident that left him paralyzed from the neck down. During Reeve’s portrait session, “you could feel his determination,” Ritts told the New York Times. “Even his chair was stoic.” Both the photographer and his subject would die less than a decade after the session: Ritts succumbed to pneumonia at age 50 in 2002, while Reeve died after falling into a coma at age 52 in 2004.

The second standout is a self-portrait from Tseng’s “East Meets West” series, which found the Hong Kong-born photographer assuming the persona of a self-declared “ambiguous ambassador.” Dressed in a Mao suit, Tseng “traveled throughout the United States as well as abroad, making self-portraits in the guise of this character at major monuments,” from the Statue of Liberty to the Golden Gate Bridge to the Lincoln Memorial, Shumard says.

It has been revealed that as Melissa Ho, a curator at the Smithsonian American Art Museum, wrote in a 2022 blog post, Tseng used his distinctive ensemble to challenge racial stereotypes about Chinese people. “His donning of the Mao suit can be understood as racial camp—a playful, self-protective maneuver that did not prevent Tseng from being misinterpreted but did allow him to take control of the manner of the misreading,” Ho argued. “Even as he presents himself to the Orientalist gaze, he is in command of the means of representation.”.

According to recent reports, overall, Shumard notes that the Portrait Gallery’s photography holdings have “really benefited from a variety of viewpoints and curatorial perspectives that allowed the collection to grow in a variety of directions” throughout the past 50 years. Stapp’s successor Mary Panzer, for example, “was particularly interested in photojournalism and civil rights photography.” Shumard, for her part, says her interest is “really from soup to nuts.” She concludes, “I’ve just enjoyed working to find good pictures across the board.”.

“Photographic Memory: Fifty Years of Collecting” is on view at the Smithsonian’s National Portrait Gallery from November 14, 2026, to November 7, 2027.

It has been revealed that meilan Solly is a senior associate digital editor at Smithsonian magazine, where she oversees the online history section and writes about everything from archaeology to the British royal family. Solly’s specialties are Tudor England, Renaissance and modern art, and World War II.

#40. Analysis: Fossil-fuel CO2 emissions set to dip in 2026 as Iran conflict hits oil use

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2589 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Carbonbrief

Analysis: Fossil-fuel CO2 emissions set to dip in 2026 as Iran conflict hits oil use

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2589 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Carbonbrief

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from fossil fuels and cement are projected to fall by around 0.4% in 2026 to 38.2bn tonnes of CO2 (GtCO2), according to upcoming figures from the Global Carbon Project.
  • The 21st edition of the annual “global carbon budget” report, published today, indicates that this small decline is largely due to a 1.9% drop in emissions from oil and the energy shock triggered by the Iran conflict and the closure of the strait of Hormuz.
  • The Global Carbon Project’s projections for fossil fuel and cement CO2 emissions in 2026 are preliminary, with a range that spans a fall of -1.5% to a rise of +0.6%.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from fossil fuels and cement are projected to fall by around 0.4% in 2026 to 38.2bn tonnes of CO2 (GtCO2), according to upcoming figures from the Global Carbon Project.

The 21st edition of the annual “global carbon budget” report, published today, indicates that this small decline is largely due to a 1.9% drop in emissions from oil and the energy shock triggered by the Iran conflict and the closure of the strait of Hormuz.

Emissions from coal continue to increase slightly.

The Global Carbon Project’s projections for fossil fuel and cement CO2 emissions in 2026 are preliminary, with a range that spans a fall of -1.5% to a rise of +0.6%.

This means a small increase in emissions can not be ruled out.

Emissions from land-use change, such as deforestation, are projected to rise in 2026.

This is primarily driven by peat fires and forest degradation in south-east Asia and is linked to the development of a strong El Niño event this year.

As a result, total CO2 emissions from fossil fuels and land use are projected to reach a record high of 43.3GtCO2 in 2026 – marginally above 42.8GtCO2 in 2025.

Research published alongside the report by the same team in Nature Climate Change finds that the growth in solar, wind and electric vehicles (EVs) now offsets around two-thirds of the emissions that would otherwise come from rising energy demand.

However, the deployment of these technologies is not yet enough to push global emissions into a sustained decline, according to the study.

The 2026 global carbon budget report also estimates that:.

(For more on previous editions of the Global Carbon Project’s annual report, see Carbon Brief’s coverage in 2025, 2024, 2023 and 2022.).

Total global CO2 emissions, which combines fossil fuels and land-use change, are projected to reach a record high of 43.3GtCO2 in 2026, up from 42.8GtCO2 in 2025.

The increase in 2026 comes entirely from a projected rise in land-use emissions, which are more challenging to estimate than fossil emissions.

(The global carbon budget groups emissions from fossil fuels and cement production as “fossil emissions”. Carbon Brief follows this convention throughout this piece.).

If land-use emissions had stayed at 2025 levels, total emissions would have fallen slightly in 2026 to around 42.6GtCO2.

In a recent development, each edition of the global carbon budget updates the historical record as fresh data and methods become available. The chart below demonstrates total emissions in this year’s budget compared with the five previous editions.

This year’s estimates of historical fossil emissions are around 0.3GtCO2 per year higher than in last year’s budget.

This is largely because the report now estimates a smaller “cement carbonation” sink in the wake of research published this year in Communications Sustainability. In other words, it estimates that cement is able to slowly reabsorb less CO2 over its lifetime than previously thought.

Estimates of land-use emissions have also been revised, including a spike in 2018 – visible in the chart above – linked to updated cropland data for Colombia.

The updated numbers show that total emissions have grown by 0.3% per year over the past decade (2016-25), compared with 1.7% per year over 2006-15.

Fossil emissions grew about 0.9% per year in the past decade, compared with 1.9% the decade before. Over the same period, land-use emissions have declined.

While the slowdown reflects real progress, a plateau in emissions is still a long way from the rapid declines needed to reach net-zero emissions and stabilise global temperatures.

Recent findings suggest that with human-caused warming reaching 1.37C above pre-industrial levels (1850-1900) in 2025, the report estimates that the remaining carbon budget  to limit warming to 1.5C, with a 50% chance, is 150GtCO2 from the start of 2027. That is less than four years of 2026 emissions.

Meanwhile, the budgets for 1.7C and 2C are 510GtCO2 and 1,035GtCO2, respectively – or around 12 and 24 years of current emissions.

Fossil emissions made up around 88% of total CO2 emissions over the past decade, with land-use change making up the remaining 12%.

This is a marked change from the first half of the 20th century, when land-use emissions were larger than those from fossil fuels.

The figure below shows global emissions, split into fossil and land-use components.

Global per-capita fossil emissions peaked in the early 2010s and have since slightly declined. At around 4.6 tonnes per person in 2026, they are about 4% below that peak.

It is worth noting that this global average hides very large differences between countries. For example, 2025 per-capita emissions in India are only 2.2 tonnes, compared with 14.5 tonnes in the US.

According to recent reports, land-use emissions come from deforestation, forest degradation, wood harvest, peatland drainage and fires. They are partly offset by forest regrowth and upcoming forests.

Net land-use emissions averaged 4.9GtCO2 per year over 2016-25, down from 6.2GtCO2 per year over 2006-15, marking a decline of around 21%. This decline holds across all three of the “bookkeeping” models used by the Global Carbon Project to track land-use emissions.

(For more on trends in global land-use emissions and how they are calculated, see Carbon Brief’s explainer.).

Land-use emissions are projected to rise to 5.1GtCO2 in 2026, up from 4.4GtCO2 in 2025.

The report attributes the increase to peat fires, almost all ignited by people, and forest degradation in south-east Asia due to drier conditions associated with El Niño.

Uncertainties in land-use emissions are much higher than for fossil emissions given the challenges in tracking them.

While 2026 highlights a nominal increase, it is only slightly above the average over the past decade.

Brazil, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Indonesia together accounted for 2.6GtCO2 of land-use emissions per year over 2015-25, or around 54% of the global total.

The figure below shows how land-use emissions for these three countries and the rest of the world have changed since 1960.

Global fossil CO2 emissions are projected to fall by around 0.4% in 2026. However, challenges associated with precisely measuring and projecting 2026 means this could end up anywhere between a 1.5% decline and a 0.6% increase.

The figure below provides a breakdown of fossil emissions over time by major country and region, including China, the US, the EU, India and the rest of the world.

The global carbon budget report sets out the following projections for 2026 in major economies:.

The figure below shows how each country or region contributed to changes in global fossil emissions in each year between 2023 and 2026.

A growing number of countries are cutting emissions while growing their economies.

The report finds that 40 countries, together accounting for 26% of global fossil emissions, significantly reduced their emissions while their economies grew over 2016-25. This compares with 22 countries in the previous decade.

Sources indicate that coal accounts for around 41% of global fossil CO2 emissions in 2026, oil 33% and gas 21%. Cement accounts for around 2%, after the carbonation sink is subtracted.

It has been revealed that oil is the main driver of the decline in global fossil emissions in 2026. Oil emissions are projected to fall by 1.9% (with a range of -2.6% to -1.2%), or 243m tonnes of CO2 (MtCO2).

The left panel of the figure below reveals that this is one of the largest annual falls in the record, with the exception of 2020 during the Covid-19 pandemic. Other large declines occurred during the global financial crisis in 2009 and in the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1992.

The chart on the right demonstrates how oil emissions are projected to fall in every major region in 2026.

The global carbon budget links most of the oil decline to higher prices and reductions in output after the Iran conflict resulted in the closure of the strait of Hormuz.

Petrol and diesel prices in the US, China and EU were 10-50% higher than in 2025, depending on the fuel and the period.

A study published in parallel by the team behind the global carbon budget reveals that growth in EVs accounted for around a fifth of the overall drop in oil emissions in 2026.

This is consistent with Carbon Brief analysis published in September that estimated that global fossil-fuel emissions were set to fall in 2026 amid the Hormuz crisis.

By contrast, coal emissions are projected to rise by 0.6% (-0.6% to +1.7%), with a strong increase in emissions in India partly offset by sharp falls in the EU and US.

Gas emissions, meanwhile, are projected to fall by 0.3% (-1.6% to +0.9%) – making them effectively flat.

The figure below reveals global emissions by fuel since 1959.

Recent findings suggest that coal emissions grew rapidly in the 2000s, at around 4% per year, but have risen only slightly since 2013. Even with continued growth, 2026 coal emissions are only around 6% above their 2013 level.

Oil emissions remain about 1% above their pre-pandemic level in 2019.

The figure below shows the contribution of each fuel to the change in global emissions between 2023 and 2026.

The annual global carbon budget report tracks both the sources of CO2, from fossil fuels and land use, as well as the “sinks” that take it up: the ocean, the land and the atmosphere.

Industry observers note that over 2016-25, the ocean took up around 27% of total emissions, or 11.1GtCO2 per year, whereas the land around 22%, or 9.2GtCO2 per year. The remaining 48% accumulated in the atmosphere.

According to recent reports, the figure below reveals the sources of emissions (above zero) and where they end up (below zero) each year. The sum of the sinks is shown as a dashed line for comparison with total emissions.

The Global Carbon Project estimates that the land sink in 2025 was the highest on record, at around 13.3GtCO2 – 50% larger than in 2024.

This reflects a strong recovery in the tropics after the 2023-24 El Niño had suppressed the land sink, along with gradual growth of the sink associated with higher atmospheric CO2 concentrations.

Recent findings suggest that the carbon budget does not always balance. In 2024, the estimated sinks exceeded the estimated sources by 6.7GtCO2, the largest “imbalance” on record. This partly offset an imbalance in the opposite direction in 2023 of 3.3GtCO2.

The report attributes much of the 2023-24 discrepancy to the timing of the atmospheric CO2 growth rate. The changes to the land carbon sink in the tropics driven by the El Niño of that year occurred late in the calendar year, so they straddle the 1 January boundary used to calculate annual growth.

In a recent development, A strong El Niño began in June 2026, but its effects on the carbon cycle are not yet visible, as changes in the carbon cycle lag several months behind changes in the climate. Consequently, the global carbon budget researchers expect the effect of the current El Niño to show up predominantly in 2027.

While natural sinks continue to absorb around half of human emissions, climate change is weakening them. The report estimates that the land and ocean sinks were 19% and 8% smaller, respectively, over 2016-25 than they would have been without the effects of climate change and natural fluctuations to the Earth’s climate.

According to recent reports, atmospheric CO2 is projected to rise by 2.2ppm in 2026, similar to the 2.1ppm rise in 2025 and well below the record 3.8ppm rise in 2024 during the last El Niño. CO2 concentrations are set to average 427.7ppm in 2026, roughly 54% above pre-industrial levels.

With global fossil emissions projected to fall in 2026, a natural follow-up question is whether they have now peaked.

The Nature Climate Change research suggests that the answer is not yet.

In the study, the researchers estimate the emissions “avoided” by solar and wind power and EVs, assuming that in their absence the same energy services would have been supplied by fossil fuels.

In a recent development, they then compare these “avoided emissions” with the emissions growth expected from rising economic activity and trends in the carbon intensity of the economy. The latter are described as “demand-driven emissions”.

Sources indicate that this is illustrated in the figure below, which shows how increasing demand-driven emissions – which overwhelmingly come from rising energy demand – would have added around 0.78GtCO2 in 2026. However, growth in solar, wind and EVs offset 0.54GtCO2 – or about 69% – of this.

The rest of the decline in global fossil fuel emissions between 2025 and 2026 is attributed by the researchers mostly to high energy prices and supply constraints.

Sources indicate that in other words, clean energy alone was not enough to cut emissions in 2026. The researchers’ central estimate suggests global emissions would have continued to rise had it not been for the energy shock from the Iran war.

The scale of avoided emissions is nonetheless large and growing swiftly. The authors estimate that solar and wind avoided around 4.1GtCO2 in 2025 and project that they could avoid 4.6GtCO2 in 2026, up from 0.28GtCO2 in 2010. China accounts for around half of this.

Most of these avoided emissions are attributable to solar and wind. EVs avoided 0.19GtCO2 in 2025. The existing vehicle stock takes time to turn over. Right now, just 10% of the global car fleet has been electrified – a figure that drops to 6% if non-plug-in hybrid cars are excluded.

Without solar, wind and EVs, the study estimates that global fossil emissions would have grown by around 1.9% per year over 2019-25 – more than double the actual rate of 0.8% per year.

It also finds that the growth in data centres, driven largely by AI, added around 0.03GtCO2 in 2025, or about 2% of the “demand-driven” increase.

Looking ahead, the researchers explore how EV, solar, and wind might affect emissions in 2028 under two scenarios.

Recent findings suggest that in the first, EV sales and solar and wind additions stay at 2026 levels. In the second, they continue to accelerate along recent trends.

As the figure below shows, rising demand for energy would add around 2.6GtCO2 between 2025 and 2028.

Clean technologies offset 63% of this in the current deployment scenario and 79% in the accelerated scenario. In both cases, overall emissions would still be higher in 2028 than in 2025.

There are important caveats to this approach. The authors note that the avoided-emissions method is a simplified counterfactual approach. It assumes that each unit of clean energy displaces fossil fuels one-for-one without incorporating potential rebound effects, such as the impact of falling clean energy costs on energy demand and fossil fuel costs.

The researchers conclude that the 2026 decline is “not a sign that emissions have peaked from the transition to cleaner energy”, but more likely a short-term response to higher oil prices.

However, the authors add that “if further acceleration of clean technology deployment can be supported through time, a sustained peak and decline in global CO2 emissions could be a few years away”.

Even then, a peak is only a first step. Limiting warming to well below 2C – let alone 1.5C, with a remaining budget of just three and a half years of current emissions – requires emissions to fall rapidly towards net-zero, not just stop rising.

Friedlingstein, P. et al. (2026) Global Carbon Budget 2026, Earth System Science Data, essd-2026-895.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Apple has built a variety of adaptations into iOS to support the iPhone Duo, so icons and menus will shift if the software detects it’s running on the inner or outer display of the foldable, rather than a standard iPhone.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It took a while, but Apple has finally launched its first foldable: the iPhone Duo is now available in Star White or Night Sky finishes, starting at $1,999 and up, depending on how much storage you want inside.

Apple has built a variety of adaptations into iOS to support the iPhone Duo, so icons and menus will shift if the software detects it’s running on the inner or outer display of the foldable, rather than a standard iPhone. In addition, iOS developers are updating their own apps to better suit the two newly introduced screen sizes introduced by the foldable.

Sources indicate that we’re also seeing several apps built or optimized specifically for the iPhone Duo, to take advantage of that foldable screen. Whether you’ve got the phone or not, they’re worth checking out as a showcase of what’s possible with the new form factor.

Toastie ($2.99) is a rather whimsical game for the iPad, iPhone, and iPhone Duo. The aim is to make the best grilled sandwich you can, and on Apple’s foldable phone you snap the handset shut and open it again to control the cooking time for your toasties.

Sources indicate that you can pick different ingredients and bread types as you go, and the ability to partially open the iPhone Duo to peek at your culinary creation is a nice touch. It’s not the most sophisticated cooking sim, but you might be surprised by how much fun it is to play.

Bring some old-school to your iPhone Duo with Tiny Computers ($3.99): With the foldable half open and propped up, the flat half turns into a virtual keyboard, and the vertical half shows a simulated display from a classic computer of your choice—with 10 to pick from.

The available computers include vintage Windows and Mac machines, plus the Commodore 64; while these aren’t full-scale emulators, you can play around with them and discover some “nostalgic secrets” as you go (including some iconic keyboard sounds).

Recent findings suggest that there are also gaming experiences specifically for the iPhone Duo to enjoy. Marbles Unhinged (freemium, $2.99 to unlock all levels) is a marble-rolling game that uses your phone’s accelerometer and gyroscope to create realistic physical tilting controls.

In a recent development, with the iPhone Duo half open, one half of the main display becomes the marble maze, and the other half becomes a ramp you use to get the marble moving to the right place at the right speed. There are 10 levels available to play for free before you have to pay.

In a recent development, simply put, Foldissimo (free, $9.99 to unlock all the songs) turns your iPhone Duo into a virtual accordion. You can adjust the airflow affecting the instrument by folding and unfolding the Apple device—faster folds pump in more air and increase the volume.

Industry observers note that there is a selection of classic song tutorials included to get you started, and you can compose your own too. You can also switch to other instruments, including panpipes and a theremin, but that’ll cost you extra. A clever idea, neatly implemented.

If you’ve got a hankering for the days when we carried camcorders around as separate gadgets—rather than just using our phones to record video—then Flipcorder ($4.99) is a perfect iPhone Duo app, complete with a retro-looking interface and workflow.

You can only record videos in 20-second bursts, up to 30 minutes a day, reflecting the limitations of camcorders of yesteryear. When you close the foldable, the outer display shows your subjects what’s being filmed, which is a smart touch. (And don’t forget to back your videos up.).

If you remember the Walkman era, then you’ll love Deck-Man ($4.99), which gives the iPhone Duo the feel of a classic cassette player. It interfaces with Apple Music and any music files you’ve got stored locally on your device to give audio playback a retro feel.

In a recent development, your albums show up as cassette tapes, and there are chunky virtual buttons for starting and stopping the audio—with the familiar fast forward, rewind, and eject buttons here too. The app even includes authentic mechanical sounds, recorded from a real cassette player.

It has been revealed that unfold Your City (free; $4.99 to unlock all the cities) utilizes the iPhone Duo’s foldable form factor to turn the handset into a virtual pop-up book that serves as your guide to the world’s most famous cities. You can even switch between day and night modes.

In a recent development, it’s a fresh twist on the usual travel guide format, and plenty of care and attention has been put into the details here (nice touches include a Tower Bridge that actually opens in London). Be warned, though: the app may have a serious impact on your travel budget.

UNSW develops three-minute lithium-ion battery health test

💡 Key Takeaways
  • UNSW researchers in Sydney have developed a prototype battery health test that they mentioned is 95.5% faster and more than 80% cheaper than existing methods, with potential to increase second-life battery use and keep battery waste out of landfill.
  • The platform is designed to work with the management systems already used by recyclers and energy storage operators, and to assess the three main lithium-ion chemistries used in electric vehicles and energy storage: lithium iron phosphate (LFP), nickel cobalt aluminum (NCA), and nickel manganese cobalt (NMC).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UNSW researchers in Sydney have developed a prototype battery health test that they mentioned is 95.5% faster and more than 80% cheaper than existing methods, with potential to increase second-life battery use and keep battery waste out of landfill.

The platform is designed to work with the management systems already used by recyclers and energy storage operators, and to assess the three main lithium-ion chemistries used in electric vehicles and energy storage: lithium iron phosphate (LFP), nickel cobalt aluminum (NCA), and nickel manganese cobalt (NMC).

It has been revealed that current testing of used batteries relies on a full charge-discharge cycle of about 10 hours, which can lead to overheating and fire if damaged batteries endure hours of high-stress cycling, according to the researchers. It costs about AUD 120 ($85) per EV battery pack.

The UNSW prototype instead sends short electrical pulses through each cell and measures how it responds. Statistical models then estimate the battery’s health in under three minutes per cell, with lab tests showing more than 90% accuracy, the researchers said. They are targeting a cost of under AUD 25.

Huadong Mo, an associate professor at UNSW’s School of Systems and Computing, noted that as more EVs reach the end of their life, Australia has a real opportunity to build a local second-life battery industry, with retired batteries supporting grid and community energy storage.

It has been revealed that “Up to 95% of a battery’s components can be recovered, some even to make new batteries. Yet only a small fraction of lithium-ion batteries in Australia are collected for recycling today,” Mo mentioned.

The researchers have partnered with Malaysia-headquartered battery recycling and lifecycle management company DY Newly introduced Energy on an AUD 1.3 million project to test the technology on more than 500 batteries in real-world conditions.

Recent findings suggest that before piloting it in recycling facilities and second-life storage systems, DY New Energy and UNSW will develop and test a machine-learning decision engine that recommends whether retired batteries should be reused or recycled. A battery management system module, called iBMS, will then feed those insights directly into battery systems for real-time monitoring and decision support.

Ziyang Lyu, research lead at UNSW’s School of Mathematics and Statistics, stated recyclers rarely receive neatly sorted batches.

According to recent reports, “One day it might be LFP cells, the next a mix of nickel-based chemistries from different manufacturers. We’ve designed our models to handle that variety, so the platform works with the batteries operators actually receive, not just ideal lab samples,” Lyu noted.

Lyu said the technology could also help manage the growing number of batteries in stationary storage. “This technology could also support the future reuse and recycling of Australia’s rapidly expanding fleet of stationary energy storage systems, contributing to a more sustainable and circular battery economy,” he said.

The project is also supported by the Trailblazer for Recycling and Clean Energy (TRaCE) Lab to Market Fund. On Nov. 13, DY New Energy stated it will partner with the Australian Research Council’s Fire Resilience Infrastructure, Assets and Safety Advancements (FRIASA) Hub to advance safe and scalable battery recycling.

#35. Industry News: How a Metabolic Spark Could Have Jump-Started Life

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1040 w)
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Quantamagazine

Industry News: How a Metabolic Spark Could Have Jump-Started Life

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1040 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Quantamagazine

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Click to tell Google to prioritize Quanta and see more of the best coverage of science and math in your search and AI results.
  • Some scientists believe that life originated from self-sustaining cycles of chemical reactions.
  • For well over 4 billion years, the fire of metabolism has powered the engines of life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Click to tell Google to prioritize Quanta and see more of the best coverage of science and math in your search and AI results.

Some scientists believe that life originated from self-sustaining cycles of chemical reactions.

For well over 4 billion years, the fire of metabolism has powered the engines of life. The ability of cells to gather, transform, and harness chemical energy from their surroundings is the central force driving the dizzyingly complex network of chemical reactions that sustains living things.

It has been revealed that metabolism is so crucial to life that some researchers believe that these reactions could have helped spark life itself. They argue that life’s first glimmers were found in self-sustaining cycles of simple molecules, before genes or cells existed. Only later did more complex molecules like RNA and DNA develop and begin storing information for the purposes of heredity.

According to recent reports, the core argument behind metabolism’s primacy is that without a self-sustaining reaction to provide energy, it’s impossible to explain how the larger and more complex molecules necessary for cellular life could have been produced at all. Energy going through the system is what life is in its many manifestations, remarked William Martin, an evolutionary biologist at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf in Germany. “It synthesizes genes that contain the information to produce the catalysts that keep this reaction going, and those catalysts have changed over time.”.

The concept that reactions driven by nonliving geochemistry could have eventually triggered living biochemistry has been decades in the making. In 1968, the American biophysicist Harold Morowitz proposed that energy that flows through a system organizes that system, and he applied this to the concept of a proto-metabolism. Essentially, Morowitz suggested that energy from external environmental sources, such as the sun or geologic processes, could nudge chemical networks into self-sustaining reactions because they were thermodynamically favored. In time, those could become biological reactions.

A very simple version of early self-sustaining reactions might be something like the acetyl-CoA pathway, a process that some modern microbes use to build complex organic molecules and generate chemical energy from hydrogen and carbon dioxide. But what conditions could have sparked these types of lifelike reactions?

According to recent reports, deep-sea submersibles first encountered hydrothermal vents in the late 1970s. These are wounds in the seafloor where geothermally heated water rich in dissolved metals pours out into the surrounding seawater. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, Günter Wächtershäuser, a patent lawyer with a doctorate in chemistry,  proposed the concept of an “iron-sulfur world.” In this possible early Earth environment, self-sustaining reactions like the acetyl-CoA pathway could have been chemically catalyzed by the iron-sulfide minerals collecting around these vents.

It has been revealed that here’s how that could have led to life. At first, a very simple pathway might have converted carbon dioxide and hydrogen into more complex carbon-containing compounds such as acetate and pyruvate, and released energy back into the environment. Hydrogen would have provided the energy; metallic catalysts kept this running in a loop. Once a primitive cycle was established, it could begin to produce increasingly complex compounds in layers, with more and more enzymatic loops, all gathering and releasing energy, building out from this original cycle. It’s possible that they could continue increasing in complexity well before any of life’s genetic mechanisms of inheritance had developed.

Industry observers note that “You start out with a simple inorganic catalyst, and then organic catalysts, and then enzymes, and the metabolic process becomes more complex,” Martin said. “But the nature of the reactions that start without enzymes has been up in the air and hotly debated.”.

Recent findings suggest that to explore possible mechanisms, Martin and his colleagues mimicked temperature and pressure conditions around hydrothermal vents in the laboratory. In 2020, the team showed that chemicals found in these vents, such as carbon dioxide and hydrogen, along with nickel and iron minerals common at these sites, could combine to create formate, acetate, and pyruvate. These compounds are essentially the “spine” of the acetyl-CoA pathway, mentioned Martina Preiner, a biochemist at the Max Planck Institute for Terrestrial Microbiology in Germany and lead author of the study. The findings “show that it’s possible to start these reactions before you have anything else,” including RNA or proteins, Preiner said.

In a recent development, however, some scientists argue that the heated and pressurized conditions around hydrothermal vents may not have been required to form these reactions. Also in 2020, Ramanarayanan Krishnamurthy, an organic chemist at Scripps Research in California, and his colleagues demonstrated that two small molecules that may have been present in an early Earth environment, pyruvate and glyoxylate, could react to form almost all the components of the reverse citric acid cycle — which is analogous to the acetyl-CoA cycle — and could do so not only at temperatures and in water conditions far removed from the more extreme environment of a vent, but also without any metal catalysts. This suggests that metabolism could have kicked off in a tepid pool rather than a deep-sea crucible.

Whatever environment provided the trigger, there is no well-formed understanding of how initial metabolic reactions could have become stable enough to develop complexity. Genetic material that can store and replicate information may have been necessary to transmit improvements to rudimentary metabolic reactions across generations.

Researchers also need to establish a connection between metabolism and genetic information, as well as determine how these proto-metabolic reactions might have coexisted without sabotaging each other once they were placed within the confines of cell membranes.

According to recent reports, “How best can we mix them together so that we don’t get a complete mess that we can’t analyze?” Krishnamurthy remarked. “That is the challenge.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Authorities in Peru say they have foiled a plot to smuggle more than 3,000 tarantulas—including species not yet described in scientific publications—out of the country.

Industry observers note that after receiving an anonymous tip, officials intercepted three travelers—two German citizens and one Polish citizen—at Jorge Chávez International Airport in Lima as they were checking in at the boarding area. When they searched the travelers’ luggage, they found thousands of eggs, hatchlings and adult spiders hidden in socks, according to a November 4 statement from the National Forest and Wildlife Service of Peru (SERFOR).

Sources indicate that “We noticed that some of them were moving,” Cora Suárez, a SERFOR forest and wildlife control technician who works at the airport, tells the Agence France-Presse. “There were small ones and large ones.”.

Recent findings suggest that workers used slender wooden sticks to gently brush the spiders into clear plastic containers. Once officials are done investigating them, the tarantulas will be taken to an authorized breeding center.

The travelers were trying to fly to Germany. Instead, they were detained by the Peruvian National Police’s environmental crimes unit and now face criminal charges.

Officials have not released the names of the individuals. However, one of the travelers was a “renowned tarantula researcher,” according to the statement, per a translation by the Latest York Times’ Amanda Holpuch.

It has been revealed that authorities suspect the individuals were smuggling the spiders for private collections, research and the exotic pet trade. Suárez tells the AFP that one tarantula can sell for roughly $560 in Europe, meaning the smugglers could have made around $1.68 million from the more than 3,000 tarantulas they had hidden in their suitcases.

The spiders originated from several different parts of Peru, including the cities of Cajamarca, Cusco and Junín, and the regions of La Libertad and Loreto. Officials are still trying to pinpoint all the species in the loot but said it included several brightly colored creatures.

In a recent development, did you know? Wildlife trafficking.

Wildlife trafficking is the world’s fourth-largest form of organized crime, with an estimated annual value of up to $20 billion.

So far, officials have identified Thrixopelma lagunas, also known as the Peruvian blue zebra or the blue birdeater. Authorities also found members of the Pamphobeteus genus, which are among the largest tarantulas in the world.

It has been revealed that one species was P. antinous, which is considered a vulnerable, legally protected threatened wildlife species in Peru. These arachnids are commonly known as Bolivian blue-leg birdeaters or steely blue legs.

Some of the spiders are species that scientists haven’t formally described, including members of the Antikuna and Avicularia genera.

“The traffickers made a meticulous selection to include different species,” Suárez says in the statement, per a translation by the Times.

#LoÚltimo. El Serfor y Aduanas incautaron en el Aeropuerto Internacional Jorge Chávez más de 3000 tarántulas que eran transportadas de manera oculta dentro de equipajes de ciudadanos extranjeros, quienes tenían previsto viajar a Alemania. Los infractores fueron detenidos por la Policía Nacional del Perú (PNP) y se les abrirá un proceso administrativo sancionador. #NoTeCompresUnDelito 🔗 Más información en: https://t.co/XhEKaixkZ1.

Industry observers note that according to Mongabay’s Spoorthy Raman, trafficking these spiders to the European Union is a relatively low-risk, high-reward pursuit. That’s because none of the species identified so far is protected under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), a global treaty intended to ensure the trade of wild plants and animals is “legal, traceable and biologically sustainable,” according to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.

Recent findings suggest that if a wild animal is legally protected by its home country but lacks an international listing like CITES or specific protection in the E.U., the E.U. does not automatically ban its import, possession or sale. Advocates are calling on the E.U. to enact legislation that closes this legal loophole.

“This is a pattern that we have observed again and again: If [the tarantulas] were not seized [in Peru], they could have been legally imported to the E.U., due to a legal gap,” Sandra Altherr, the co-founder of Pro Wildlife, a wildlife conservation nonprofit based in Germany, tells Mongabay.

#30. Analysis: Which countries have sent the most delegates to COP31?

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1241 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Carbonbrief

Analysis: Which countries have sent the most delegates to COP31?

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1241 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Carbonbrief

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • More than 92,000 people have registered to attend the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, potentially making it the largest COP in history.
  • Carbon Brief analysis of the provisional lists of delegates, published by the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), reveals that more than 14,000 delegates have been registered as “host country guests”.
  • For comparison, the final list for COP30 in Belém, Brazil, last year included only around 1,300 delegates in this category.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than 92,000 people have registered to attend the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, potentially making it the largest COP in history.

Carbon Brief analysis of the provisional lists of delegates, published by the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), reveals that more than 14,000 delegates have been registered as “host country guests”.

For comparison, the final list for COP30 in Belém, Brazil, last year included only around 1,300 delegates in this category.

As with COP30, Donald Trump’s US government has not sent a delegation. Other no-reveals include Israel and Myanmar.

It was reported ahead of the summit that Taliban officials from Afghanistan had been registered for the event as observers; however, there are no delegates from observer states in the provisional lists.

With more than 3,000 “virtual” delegates signed up to attend the summit online, the total number of people registered for the event surpasses 95,000.

With 92,934 participants registered, COP31 is provisionally the largest COP in history – topping COP28 in Dubai, which was attended by more than 80,000 people.

This total is based on the delegates that have registered to be at the summit in person. The UNFCCC releases the final figures – based on participants collecting a physical badge at the venue – after the summit has ended.

The chart below shows how the provisional figures for COP31 compare to the final totals in previous COPs – going back to COP1 in Berlin in 1995.

Industry observers note that the participant lists provided by the UNFCCC are divided between the different types of groups and organisations attending the summit. The largest group at COP31 is for delegates representing parties. These are nation-states, plus the European Union, that have ratified the convention and play a full part in negotiations.

This group adds up to 18,812 delegates – the second largest after COP28.

(In keeping with recent COPs, the UNFCCC has published spreadsheets that name every single person that has registered for the summit – excluding support staff. Previously, COPs have typically included thousands of “overflow” participants in which countries and UN agencies could nominate delegates without their names appearing on their official lists.).

For consistency with Carbon Brief’s analysis of previous COPs, the above chart includes overflow delegates as a single group. However, the participant lists do divide the overflow delegates between parties and observer groups. Including the overflow numbers takes the total for party representatives to more than 34,000.

It has been revealed that unusually, COP31 has a very large number of “host country guests”. This is a category that has only been included in the COP participant lists over the last few years. The provisional number for COP31 – 14,285 – far exceeds the final number of host guests at COP30 (1,324), COP29 (1,651) and COP28 (4,202).

The map and table below present the delegation size – split between party and overflow badges – for all the countries registered for COP31. The darker the shading, the more delegates that country has signed up.

Unsurprisingly, host nation Turkey has registered the largest delegation for COP31 – with 2,950 people.

Following behind are Brazil (1,994 people), Nigeria (1,506), China (1,021) and Indonesia (978).

The rest of the top 10 is made up of Australia (835), Uganda (627), Italy (607), Japan (588) and Kazakhstan (557).

The UK comes someway down the list with a delegation of 255.

The smallest delegation comes from North Korea (two), followed by Eritrea and Nicaragua (three) and San Marino and Trinidad and Tobago (four).

(It is worth noting that some countries – such as Brazil – allocate some of their party badges to NGOs, which can artificially inflate the size of their official delegation.).

It has been revealed that the UNFCCC’s participant lists typically provide a title – such as Mr, Ms, Sr or Sra – for each registered delegate. In the past, this has allowed Carbon Brief to work out the balance of men to women in the delegations that each country has sent to a COP.

It has been revealed that (This analysis always carries the caveat that the titles are designated by UNFCCC and not by Carbon Brief. In addition, Carbon Brief recognises that gender is not best categorised using a binary “man” or “woman” label and appreciates that the UNFCCC’s lists may not be wholly accurate.).

Overall, the COP31 provisional list suggests an average gender balance of party delegations of 59% men to 41% women.

As the chart below demonstrates, COP31 is slightly less balanced than the last two COPs, but broadly continues a trend that has seen COP delegations become a more even split between men and women.

(Note: Since COP28, the UNFCCC has also used titles that do not indicate gender – such as Dr, Prof, Ambassador and Honourable. Therefore, for this analysis, these non-gendered titles – which make up 1.3% of party delegates at COP31, for example – have not been included.).

Including overflows, there are two delegations of only men at COP31 – Eritrea (three people) and North Korea (two). There are no delegations that are only women.

The full list of COP31 party delegation sizes can be found here.

(For previous COPs, see Carbon Brief’s delegate analysis for COP21, COP23, COP24, COP25, COP26, COP27, COP28, COP29 and COP30.).

After party delegates, observers of the negotiations are typically the next biggest group at COP summits.

It has been revealed that these delegates receive their observer status through their not-for-profit organisation. This can be a UN body, a “specialised agency” – such as the World Bank or International Atomic Energy Agency, an intergovernmental organisation – such as OPEC or the Inter-American Development Bank – or an NGO.

Sources indicate that the vast majority of observers at COP31 – more than 12,000 – are representing NGOs. These can include charities, such as WWF, 350.org and Amnesty International, as well as philanthropic organisations, such as the Rockefeller Foundation and the IKEA Foundation, and lobby groups, such as the International Gas Union and the UK’s National Farmers Union.

At COP30 last year, the UNFCCC registration process introduced the option for observers to disclose the “immediate source(s) of funding” for their participation.

This option has been included again at COP31.

Recent findings suggest that of the 12,413 NGO observers registered for COP31, 14% chose not to disclose funding. The most common funders were NGOs (56%) and academic or research institutions (12%). Around 8% declared funding from “private sector or business”.

In addition, observers were “invited to declare their participation's alignment with the objective of the convention and the goals and principles of the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement”.

Overall, 13,108  delegates selected “yes” for this section, with the remaining 2,247 delegates leaving the answer blank.

Finally, there are 3,645 media representatives registered to attend COP31 in person, which is provisionally the second-largest media group in COP history – behind COP3 in Kyoto, Japan, in 1997 (3,712).

Industry observers note that the way that media organisations are described in the list is very inconsistent, which makes overall totals difficult to tally. Nonetheless, the Turkish Radio and Television Corporation (TRT) is comfortably the most-represented media group at COP31 with more than 200 delegates.

Other media outlets with at least a dozen participants include CNN, the Associated Press, Financial Times, Bloomberg, Agence France-Presse, Reuters and Sky News.

Update: This article was updated on 11/11/2026 to add further analysis on gender balance, observers and media at COP31.

#29. Can squirrels really survive any fall?

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1115 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci

Can squirrels really survive any fall?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1115 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that on any ordinary day, you might witness the breathtaking display of squirrels high in the trees, doing what seems like effortless, daredevilish parkour.
  • A large, heavy human being attempting these same maneuvers would likely fall—and would be looking at a trip to the E.R., at best.
  • Recent findings suggest that yet squirrels, it seems, tend to walk away from these situations unscathed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that on any ordinary day, you might witness the breathtaking display of squirrels high in the trees, doing what seems like effortless, daredevilish parkour. They might launch themselves off one branch, bounce off another, and somehow reorient themselves in midair like it’s nothing.

A large, heavy human being attempting these same maneuvers would likely fall—and would be looking at a trip to the E.R., at best.

Recent findings suggest that yet squirrels, it seems, tend to walk away from these situations unscathed. You’ve probably even heard that squirrels can survive a fall from any height. But according to Dr. Nathaniel Hunt of the University of Nebraska at Omaha, this comes with an important caveat: Even these brazen little gymnasts don’t stick the landing every single time.

“I would put an asterisk on the claim that squirrels can survive a fall from literally any height,” Hunt tells Popular Science. “Their size makes large falls surprisingly survivable, but they are not invulnerable.”.

According to recent reports, so, can squirrels survive, if not all, most falls? And if so, how?

It’s much more than luck that keeps squirrels landing safely; they are no more immune than we are to the laws of gravity. It’s what happens in the air—both in terms of their anatomical engineering and their instincts—that allows them to survive most falls and get right back to their nut-hiding hijinks.

According to recent reports, according to Hunt, a falling squirrel faces three challenges: the speed of the fall, its orientation midair, and the impact when it lands. A squirrel’s small body helps; at about a pound, a squirrel weighs about as much as a loaf of bread.

“Being small gives it a lot of aerodynamic area relative to its weight, so air resistance limits its speed,” Hunt says. “It also has much less kinetic energy than a larger animal.”.

So, squirrels’ light and small bodies help them hit the ground with less force, but that’s not all that’s going on. Hunt says squirrels instinctively know how to move through the air and land on the ground, which helps to optimize their already “favorable physics.” The tail is a key player in these midair maneuvers.

“The tail is more interesting than a fluffy parachute,” Hunt notes. “At low airspeeds, aerodynamic forces are small, but the squirrel can still use inertial tail movements to exchange angular momentum with the body and control orientation.” In other words, squirrels use their tail to control how and where they fall.

Research backs Hunt’s claim. A 2021 study found that squirrels experiencing unexpected falls were able to rapidly rotate their tails, a motion that caused the rest of their bodies to rotate in the opposite direction. Hunt compared the role of the tail to that of a “reaction wheel” on a spacecraft.

“Accelerating the tail in one direction helps rotate or stabilize the body in the other direction,” Hunt claims.

Industry observers note that as a squirrel’s fall picks up speed, the tail may function more like the feathers on an arrow, Hunt suggests. If the squirrel starts to veer off course, the airflow pushes against the tail just enough to redirect its body into a stable position. Even then, the tail isn’t acting like a true parachute; instead of slowing the squirrel’s descent, the tail is nudging its body in the right direction.

It has been revealed that size, anatomy, and aerial reorientation are all notable to a squirrel’s seemingly magical ability to survive most falls. However, there’s a third skill that plays an equally important part, one Hunt thinks may be “the most underappreciated part of the story.” Squirrels know how to come in for a landing.

“A recent study I co-authored found that fox squirrels managed more than 80 percent of their landing energy through their forelimbs,” Hunt says of a study looking at squirrels leaping between branches. “They also adjusted their forces depending on whether they undershot or overshot the branch.”.

According to recent reports, in other words, a landing isn’t just something that happens to a squirrel. On some level, they’re doing damage control.

Recent findings suggest that “They are not simply hitting the branch,” Hunt says. “They are actively controlling the collision.”.

So, how slowly does a squirrel have to fall to be able to walk away?

The answer lies in our furry friend’s terminal velocity, the top speed something reaches while falling once air resistance balances gravity’s pull and stops it from accelerating further. Hunt claims a squirrel’s terminal velocity can be reasonably estimated at about 20 to 40 mph, depending on its posture, limb position, and tail. For reference, Hunt estimates the terminal velocity of a cat—famous nine lives aside—at about 60 mph, while a belly-down human skydiver is likely to fall at about 120 mph.

“All of these are approximate, because posture matters enormously,” he says.

Posture explains some of the variation, but size is ultimately the main driver. A giant squirrel, therefore, would likely fare much worse in a fall, even with perfect tail control and posture.

“You could not simply build a squirrel 10 times larger and expect it to tolerate the same fall,” Hunt claims.

Likewise, a squirrel’s comparatively slow terminal velocity doesn’t mean it’s out of the proverbial woods. It might seem that once a squirrel hits its maximum speed, height wouldn’t matter much, making a fall from 10 feet and a fall from 100 feet equally survivable. Hunt cautions against assumptions like this.

“Reaching terminal velocity does not make a squirrel immune to injury,” he states. “The landing surface, body orientation, and any collisions along the way still matter.”.

This complex interplay of physics, instinct, learning, and split-second decision-making is part of what makes squirrels a fascinating study subject for Hunt.

In a recent development, “What fascinates me is that you cannot neatly separate ‘the brain’ from ‘the mechanics,'” Hunt indicates. “Squirrel agility emerges from sensing, learning, body shape, and physical dynamics working together.”.

German Renaissance Master Albrecht Altdorfer Pioneered Landscape Painting. A Work Previously Unknown to Scholars Just Emerged After 70 Years in a Private Collection

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Measuring roughly nine inches long by eight inches wide and dating from around 1520, A Thickly Wooded Landscape With a Rainbow Behind the Trees and a Distant Outcrop to the Right Beneath a Cloud-Laden Sky will head to auction at Sotheby’s in London on December 9.
  • In a recent development, “Every inch of this intimate picture is imbued with an intense mood that transcends its scale … It somehow still feels as modern and immediate as it would have appeared to those seeing it when it was first painted,” George Gordon, co-chair of Sotheby’s Old Masters department, notes in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for nearly seven decades, a small 16th-century painting of a forest hung in a private collection in Switzerland, unbeknownst to art historians. Now, the 500-year-old work has emerged into the limelight, newly attributed to Albrecht Altdorfer, a German Renaissance artist who pioneered landscape painting.

Measuring roughly nine inches long by eight inches wide and dating from around 1520, A Thickly Wooded Landscape With a Rainbow Behind the Trees and a Distant Outcrop to the Right Beneath a Cloud-Laden Sky will head to auction at Sotheby’s in London on December 9.

In a recent development, “Every inch of this intimate picture is imbued with an intense mood that transcends its scale … It somehow still feels as modern and immediate as it would have appeared to those seeing it when it was first painted,” George Gordon, co-chair of Sotheby’s Old Masters department, notes in a statement. “To add to the known body of work of one of the great masters of the Northern Renaissance is one of the most exciting discoveries imaginable in our field.”.

Recent findings suggest that the painting, which does not appear in Altdorfer’s catalogue raisonné and was only identified earlier this year, is expected to sell for up to $6.6 million. “We don’t really know what it’s worth because it’s many decades since an Altdorfer last came to the market,” Gordon tells the Art Newspaper’s Catherine Hickley. “It could fetch more than our estimate.”.

It has been revealed that until its discovery, scholars knew of just two oil landscapes by Altdorfer, both held in major European museums: Landscape With a Footbridge at London’s National Gallery and Landscape of the Danube Near Regensburg at Munich’s Alte Pinakothek. No Altdorfer painting has appeared on the market since 1980, when the National Gallery acquired Christ Taking Leave of His Mother.

Painted in oil on vellum, A Thickly Wooded Landscape is the smallest and most densely forested of Altdorfer’s surviving landscapes in any medium, including engravings, etchings and drawings. In the foreground, tangled evergreens and mossy undergrowth rise without a single human figure in sight, while a distant castle perches atop a rocky outcrop on the right. Overhead, heavy clouds part just enough to reveal a faint glow from the sun, whose light catches a delicate rainbow arching behind the trees.

In a recent development, together, Altdorfer’s three known oil landscapes form a study in shifting weather and light. While Landscape With a Footbridge unfolds in blue daylight and the Landscape of the Danube canvas glows in warm evening light, the newly surfaced work captures the hushed atmosphere immediately after a rainstorm.

“There is a sun, but the sun is really struggling to make its presence felt, and then you have a rainbow which has caught light from the sun,” Gordon tells the Guardian’s Miatta Mbriwa.

Before Altdorfer, European painters tended to treat nature as decorative scenery behind biblical or mythological narratives.

“The first independent landscapes in the history of European art were painted by Albrecht Altdorfer,” art historian Christopher S. Wood writes in Albrecht Altdorfer and the Origins of Landscape. “These pictures tell no stories. They are physically detached from any possible explanatory context … They are complete pictures, finished and framed, which nevertheless make a powerful impression of incompleteness and silence.”.

As art historian Simon Schama observes in Landscape and Memory, “it was the outstanding achievement of Albrecht Altdorfer, in particular, to make the forest itself the natural protagonist.”.

Recent findings suggest that did you know? Landscapes and beyond.

Altdorfer may have pioneered landscape painting, but his legacy extends beyond this world. In 1960, astronomers named 8121 Altdorfer, an asteroid orbiting the sun between Mars and Jupiter, in the painter’s honor.

Born around 1480 in Regensburg, Bavaria, Altdorfer spent most of his life in the city on the Danube, balancing painting, engraving and printmaking with work as an architect and local politician before his death in 1538.

Around 1511, a journey south into the Alps sparked Altdorfer’s fascination with sweeping natural vistas, while the mixed deciduous and evergreen woodlands along the Danube downstream from Regensburg inspired his dense forest scenes. He later served Emperor Maximilian I in Innsbruck and painted his most famous work, The Battle of Alexander at Issus, for Duke Wilhelm IV of Bavaria in 1529.

The current owner of A Thickly Wooded Landscape inherited the painting from his father, who purchased it in 1957 from the collection of an aristocratic Austrian family, the House of Harrach. Following public previews at Sotheby’s in Upcoming York from November 7 to 19 and in London from December 4 to 9, the work will go in front of bidders. Given its rarity, Gordon tells the Art Newspaper, “I think it’s quite likely that museums will be interested.”.

#26. The Evolving Story of How Chemistry Became Biology

The Evolving Story of How Chemistry Became Biology
