📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Click to tell Google to prioritize Quanta and see more of the best coverage of science and math in your search and AI results.
  • Scientists are homing in on the 200 million years after the conditions for life emerged on Earth but before our most ancient single-celled ancestor appeared.
  • Recent findings suggest that around 4.6 billion years ago, some 9 billion years after the birth of the universe, a cloud of gas and dust collapsed into the familiar blinding ball in our sky.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Click to tell Google to prioritize Quanta and see more of the best coverage of science and math in your search and AI results.

Scientists are homing in on the 200 million years after the conditions for life emerged on Earth but before our most ancient single-celled ancestor appeared.

Recent findings suggest that around 4.6 billion years ago, some 9 billion years after the birth of the universe, a cloud of gas and dust collapsed into the familiar blinding ball in our sky. Scraps of leftover material collided and accreted into the planets of the solar system, including our own. For the next few hundred million years, Earth was a hellish, molten landscape bombarded by meteorites. As it started to cool, water pooled into vast, acidic oceans. The days, half as long as today’s, passed under pink carbon dioxide skies. But life wasn’t around to sense any of it. Until it was.

Recent findings suggest that around 300 million years into the existence of our solar system, conditions on Earth were right for a great chemical experiment to begin. Molecules entangled themselves in self-sustaining, self-reproducing loops. Over time, these systems became more complex. At some point, they had come to life.

Life invented fresh ways to move, and to capture, store, and use energy. It began to sense, respond to, and change its environment. It communicated, ate some of its neighbors and lived inside others, and formed complex, dynamic communities. Through cycles of birth, reproduction, and death; catastrophe; and bursts of evolution, it persisted and then thrived, taking over every corner of the planet.

Then, at some point, life gained a sense of itself, a reflective intelligence with the existential curiosity to ask: Where did we come from? For tens of thousands of years, we have pondered and probed the origins of life: Monks have meditated, philosophers have argued, lovers have mused, and parents have patiently answered their kids’ questions.

“Go back in human history, go back to the Neanderthals, go back 30,000 years,” said William Schopf, a paleobiologist at the University of California, Los Angeles, “and one of the things you will see is that human beings have been wrestling with this question.”.

By the mid-20th century, it became possible to probe life’s origins through chemistry, molecular biology, and genetics. Hypotheses exploded. Scientists clashed over which type of molecule — RNA, lipids, proteins, and metabolites are prime suspects — could have started it all. The arguments have gone on for so long, without resolution or unifying insight, that some experts have considered the field to be in crisis.

Industry observers note that “There’s nothing more exciting for a scientific field than a moment of crisis,” said Betül Kaçar, an astrobiologist and evolutionary biologist at the University of Wisconsin, Madison. “That’s when I think breakthroughs happen.”.

Life’s origins are not purely a chemistry problem. “It’s not a linear reaction. … There’s no single E = mc2 and that’s origin of life’s formula,” said Betül Kaçar, an astrobiologist and evolutionary biologist. “This is biology; it doesn’t follow any rules. That’s what makes it so sophisticated and exciting.”.

A fresh wave of origins-of-life researchers, fed up with the tradition of bickering, have unshackled themselves from the idea that a single type of molecule started it all. Their open-minded approach has coincided with a change in scientific understanding. Experiments have shown that the precursors to many of life’s ingredients may have formed easily under the conditions on early Earth. What is harder to explain is how these molecular processes became a stable evolutionary system continuous with the vast diversity of life we see on the planet today. During life’s earliest days, these processes came together to store and pass on information, both consistently and imperfectly enough to allow the same living lineage to persist for billions of years on an ever-changing planet.

To study the emergence of lifelike biochemical systems, biologists are now pushing backward into the past from the living world with newly introduced genetic tricks, while chemists are pushing forward from the nonliving world with new and strange mixtures of molecules. And by combining tools from chemistry and biology, synthetic biologists are embracing informed speculation and probing novel biological systems that may not have ever existed. Scientists now engaged with the origins of life are asking not just what life is, but what it does — on an archaic world, in a lab dish, or somewhere beyond our atmosphere.

In 1952, Stanley Miller, then a graduate student at the University of Chicago, performed a bold experiment. He was inspired by a lecture⁠ given by Harold Urey, the Nobel Prize–winning chemist, on the origins of the solar system. In the 1920s, Alexander Oparin in Russia and J.B.S. Haldane in England had independently hypothesized that life gradually evolved from a “primordial soup” of molecules. Urey proposed an extension of that idea: that Earth’s primitive atmosphere was composed of gases that could, with a little help from an energy source like lightning, produce organic molecules that would rain into the ocean. From there, these molecules would accumulate, concentrate, and eventually start to link together on the way to self-replication.

A year after hearing the lecture, Miller, just 23 at the time, approached Urey with a proposal. A week later, he had scraped together what would become known as the Miller-Urey apparatus: A glass bulb filled with water simulated a primordial ocean, and a second filled with gases (methane, ammonia, water vapor, and hydrogen) approximated a primordial atmosphere. A candle heated the water, and electrodes created sparks in the gas. The “atmosphere” was then run through a condenser that cooled it into liquid “rain” that fell into the “ocean.”.

The next day, a dark brown sludge had formed at the bottom of the bulb. It contained five different types of amino acids, the small molecules that link up to form proteins, the workhorses of cells. Miller had shown that life’s building blocks could form in the conditions of early Earth, as they were understood at the time.

“It was paradigm-shifting,” noted Ramanarayanan Krishnamurthy, an organic chemist at Scripps Research. “It really changed the field and gave rise to what we call prebiotic chemistry.”.

“This is the first experiment in the field showing that these deep questions on the origins of life were not only the realm of metaphysics, philosophy, and religion,” stated Christophe Danelon, a synthetic biologist at the Toulouse Biotechnology Institute in France.

Industry observers note that in the early 1950s, Stanley Miller (top) performed a foundational experiment in the study of the origins of life. By simulating an early Earth environment inside a glass apparatus (bottom), he was able to form the precursors of amino acids.

Bettmann/Getty Images; Stanley Miller.

Sources indicate that in the early 1950s, Stanley Miller (left) performed a foundational experiment in the study of the origins of life. By simulating an early Earth environment inside a glass apparatus (right), he was able to form amino acids.

Bettmann/Getty Images; Stanley Miller.

At first, life’s origin was largely considered a chemistry problem. But biology soon played the role of muse. In 1953, just a few weeks before Miller published his famous experiment, the biologists Francis Crick and James Watson published the helical structure of DNA.

The realization that DNA was central to all life suggested that genetic molecules were probably critical to life’s origin, too. The field shifted to explaining genetics, mentioned David Baum, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Wisconsin, Madison. “We became so obsessed.”.

The molecular biology revolution further clarified the most fundamental characteristics of cells: a genome to store information, a metabolism to provide energy, and a compartment to hold it all together. The materials of life became the field’s focus; if they just found the right starting molecule, the thinking went, everything else, including self-replication and evolution, would swiftly follow.

This period also marked the beginning of the dustups that would characterize the field for decades.

“The first thing that people then chose to do was to pick one of life’s molecules and assume that was the progenitor, the kind of ‘first molecule,’ and all of the others could temporarily be ignored,” noted Matthew Powner, a chemist at University College London. “The absolute classic version of this was the RNA-world theory.”.

The RNA-world theory, the most popular and well-studied theory of life’s origin, came together following a critical discovery. RNA is a single molecular strand that copies genetic information from DNA’s double strands, which the cell then reads and translates into proteins using complex, highly evolved enzyme molecules. In the 1980s, the scientists Thomas Cech and Sidney Altman independently discovered that some RNA molecules also act as enzymes that catalyze, or activate, biochemical reactions; this research won them a Nobel Prize. RNA therefore offered a tantalizing solution to how early life could have both stored information and replicated itself without the enzymes it uses today: RNA could, in theory, do it all.

In a recent development, the RNA-first theory wasn’t the only option that emerged. In the 1970s, the discovery of hydrothermal vents in the Pacific, along with the strange creatures that call them home, roused the field once more. In 1988, Günter Wächtershäuser, a German patent lawyer with a doctorate in chemistry, proposed an “iron-sulfur” world, suggesting that iron-sulfide minerals that collect near hydrothermal vents could have kick-started primitive versions of metabolism. Around the same time, the complexity theorist Stuart Kauffman, now an emeritus professor of biochemistry at the University of Pennsylvania, popularized theories on “autocatalytic sets,” molecular chain reactions in which one molecule catalyzes the next, which catalyzes the next, and so on in a circular process. These ideas fueled the theory of a metabolism-first world, which proposes that life arose as self-sustaining networks of molecules interacting and indefinitely making more of each other. In this world, the storage of genetic information would come later.

Though the RNA world and metabolism-first world were often pitted against each other, there were other contenders. There was also a lipid world, in which the molecules that form cell membranes and contain cellular chemistry came first. There was a protein or peptide world, a virus world, a coenzyme world, a zinc world, and even a clay world. “You can find any world you ever imagined predicated on whatever your background was when you joined this field,” Powner mentioned.

Industry observers note that the scientists also debated where life started. Did it evolve in “warm little ponds,” as Darwin proposed more than a century ago, or in the oceans, in patches of ice at the poles, or at hydrothermal vents? Some molecular theories were coupled to specific environments, while others could have started in many places. Each approach had its staunch supporters.

Sources indicate that hydrothermal vents, such as these in the Mariana Trench, are seafloor openings that spurt scalding water replete with dissolved metals. The mineral- and chemical-rich environment makes vents a popular setting for hypotheses about the origins of life.

NOAA Ocean Exploration/Science Source.

“These were often presented as complete hypotheses that could explain the origin of life to the exclusion of the others,” said Aaron Goldman, an evolutionary biologist at Oberlin College.

And that meant that only one hypothesis could be right.

Throughout the early 2000s, conferences that focused on the origins of life were like arenas. Researchers argued in public, talked over one another, and even got into shouting matches. “It was unbelievable bickering,” noted Michael Travisano, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Minnesota.

“There used to be open fights,” Krishnamurthy said.

Recent findings suggest that some professors forbade their students to discuss ideas with other labs. They even dissed each other in the press. In 1992, Discover magazine reported that Miller, a prebiotic-soup proponent, didn’t want to even discuss the vent hypothesis and thought of it as “a real loser.”.

Industry observers note that “Arguments were difficult to resolve because everybody was making a good point,” stated John Sutherland, an organic chemist at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology in the United Kingdom. “Yes, you do need RNA. Yes, you do need peptides. Yes, you do need metabolites.”.

Plus, absent a time machine, there is no way to prove or falsify any hypothesis. Scientists have minimal direct evidence. “You can hold on to your theory forever, and nobody will ever really be able to say you are absolutely wrong,” stated Elisa Biondi, a biochemist and molecular biologist at the Foundation for Applied Molecular Evolution.

In a recent development, experiments were little help, as efforts to create something resembling life from a single kind of molecule were not fruitful. Researchers haven’t been able to get an RNA molecule to self-replicate, nor have they compelled an autocatalytic metabolic network to sustain itself, grow, and pass down information. The proposed locations — hydrothermal vents, shallow pools, ice caps — also couldn’t support on their own the chemistry that seemed necessary to get life going.

Sources indicate that “When people first started studying the origin of life, the perspective was we just need the really good idea that will solve [it],” Goldman remarked. “That way of pursuing the question turned out to not work.”.

According to recent reports, decades of evidence from experiments further challenged the idea that a single molecule or environment could have kick-started life on its own. Prebiotic chemistry experiments not only yielded scores of amino acids, but also created sugars, nucleobases, and fatty acids — the building blocks of proteins, RNA, DNA, and lipids — and their precursors. And detailed analysis of samples that arrived on Earth from space uncovered an array of organic materials. Meteorites such as Murchison, which fell in Australia in 1969, and Murray, which exploded over Kentucky in 1950, carried a diversity of amino acids and some nucleobases.

How life began is a “difficult question that is just on the edge of scientifically tractable,” remarked Aaron Goldman, an evolutionary biologist. “Saying we’re going to solve it is kind of like saying we’re going to solve medicine.”.

By the early 2010s, it was becoming clearer that the creation of life’s starting materials wasn’t that difficult. “It struck me,” Sutherland mentioned, “that maybe where [we’re] wrong is this assumption that you couldn’t have chemistry that makes everything.”.

This revelation shifted the field’s focus from identifying the singular molecule or process that started life to understanding how a more general prebiotic chemistry could have formed — a true primordial, biochemical soup. The individual worlds expanded to include the possibility of multiple types of molecules. However, only a subset would go on to be preserved as the building blocks of biology.

According to recent reports, the thinking used to be “How do we make anything?” noted Cole Mathis, an astrobiologist at Arizona State University. Now, it’s “How do we not make everything?”.

The process of generating many types of biomolecules in sufficient volumes could have been iterative and long, spanning perhaps hundreds of thousands or even millions of years. These materials would have had to accumulate in a contained area, whether that was a pond, a shallow sea, a vent, or all of the above, and not be washed away or otherwise degraded by time.

Scientists have proposed energetic, mineral-rich hot springs, such as the Grand Prismatic Spring in Yellowstone National Park, as environments where life may have begun.

Industry observers note that building up that initial molecular pool is “what could be really, really hard, really rare” in the universe, said Jack Szostak, a Nobel Prize–winning origins-of-life researcher at the University of Chicago. “Going from environment to environment, from reservoir to reservoir, to actually an environment where protocells can form … maybe that’s just astronomically rare.”.

Industry observers note that if an initial, diverse molecular pool was the most crucial condition, then fighting over separate worlds is a waste of breath. Many researchers today, especially early- and mid-career researchers frustrated by the infighting, are eager for new, better ideas. They’re meeting up at formal and informal workshops and meetings to build bridges between different fields pursuing the same questions instead of letting disciplinary differences calcify into battle lines. “We are now at a point where we realize, well, maybe it’s not that my world is better than your world, but they have to coexist,” Kaçar mentioned.

The general attitude among these mostly younger folks is “if you don’t do it, we’ll do it,” stated Joana Xavier, who in 2020 as a postdoc co-founded the Origin of Life Early-Career Network with Mathis. She is presently meditating on her time in the field at a Buddhist monastery in southern France.

According to recent reports, compared to their scientific predecessors, this group of researchers is “less imperialistic about our specific science,” stated Ludo Schoenmakers, a postdoc in philosophy of science at KU Leuven in Belgium. “I guess we don’t think that it automatically ranges over all of reality.”.

It has been revealed that joana Xavier sits at the Nalanda Monastery in France. When she’s not meditating, the researcher on hiatus is writing the story of the origins of life. “My glitch is, I keep navigating between extremely complex mathematical stuff and almost poetry,” she remarked.

According to recent reports, this moment in research into the origins of life is intellectually diverse and open to new possibilities. Researchers are eager to think beyond single molecules or settings and instead investigate complex networks and systems made of many molecules. They’re thinking about how evolution could have emerged from this mess. And many have stopped thinking that it had to be some singular occurrence. Hydrothermal vents or warm ponds? “Why not both?” said Joanna Masel, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Arizona. “I believe that there were multiple origins of life.”.

In a recent development, when life takes hold, a system of interacting molecules “frees itself from where it was born,” Krishnamurthy said. Origins researchers have done the same. The field is finding latest ways to ask and answer parts of the vast question by collaborating across disciplines. They are turning to bold new experiments and creative ideas that expand our understanding of what life is and what it could be.

As the biochemist Gerald Joyce, the president of the Salk Institute who led research into the RNA world, put it: “Let a thousand flowers bloom.”.

One way to approach how life started is to think like the chemists: Start with nonliving molecules and bring them to life. Another way is to think like an evolutionary biologist: Trace life backward to its most ancient root, and perhaps beyond.

If you were to take everything that’s alive today — from blooming flowers and trees to humans and dogs to single cells encrusting a hydrothermal vent — and trace every lineage back through billions of years, you’d eventually reach a single point. This cell, from which all life known to us has descended, is the root of the tree of life.

In the 1990s, this cell (or, more accurately, this population of cells) got a name: the “last universal common ancestor,” or LUCA. Biologists debated who or what LUCA was: whether it resembled a modern cell or was something simpler. LUCA left no fossils — the oldest uncontested ancient fossils date to around 3.5 billion years ago — but it has left a different material record from billions of years ago.

In a recent development, “There are only two records of past life,” noted Greg Fournier, an evolutionary biologist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. One is dead remains of ancient organisms fossilized in the rock record. The second, he said, is “the record within genomes … traces that have been passed down from the first cells to all life or almost all life alive today.”.

“We’re trying to understand meaningful, notable things about our place in the universe,” said Greg Fournier, an evolutionary biologist. “It’s equivalent to trying to find the Higgs boson, or trying to come up with a theory of quantum gravity, or trying to understand the Significant Bang.”.

By the early 2000s, the genomic era was in full swing, and over the following decades sequencing technologies got better and faster. Today, “we can sequence entire genomes containing thousands of genes in under an hour,” Fournier said. Complete genomes of species from across the tree of life started piling up. By comparing them, the biologists who build trees of life, known as phylogeneticists, could map out their evolutionary relationships.

The logic of building phylogenetic trees is straightforward: Compare the genomes of distantly related species— say, a bacterium and a human — to reveal potentially shared genes that may have evolved before those lineages split. To tell LUCA’s story, researchers identify the most ancient genes that are found in all modern living things.

It has been revealed that LUCA’s story is regularly rewritten and refined based on upcoming genetic clues as well as advances in scientific understanding. For example, bacteria often pass genes to their neighbors, or across bacterial species, in an evolutionary process known as horizontal gene transfer. Once biologists realized that these signals can wrongly suggest that certain genes have a shared evolutionary history, they had to find better ways to interpret their vast dataset. The computational techniques to do so finally arrived in the last decade. In 2024, a research group led by Phil Donoghue at the University of Bristol used some of these techniques in novel ways to paint the richest picture of LUCA yet.

In a recent development, these boulderlike stromatolites from Shark Bay, Australia, are layered structures built by microorganisms. Not far away, in Pilbara in western Australia, are fossil stromatolites dating back to 3.48 billion years ago — some of the oldest fossils known on the planet.

It has been revealed that they reported that LUCA likely operated with around 2,600 proteins encoded by a genome comparable in size to those in modern-day bacteria. Those genes and proteins suggested that LUCA had a basic metabolism, a functional cell membrane, and even a primitive immune system for fighting viruses. It had all the basic equipment for making energy, replicating DNA, and producing proteins. Altogether, the analysis painted a picture of an already complex organism.

In a recent development, “LUCA was a fully flesh, swimming, eating, reproducing, messy cell,” Kaçar noted. And wherever it lived, it likely didn’t live alone.

In a recent development, donoghue’s team found that LUCA had a metabolic pathway that is nearly identical to one found in modern microbes, known as the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway. Intriguingly, this metabolic pathway is related to another metabolic process, acetogenesis, that cannot work on its own but relies on the processes of other cells: LUCA’s neighbors. This makes it very likely that LUCA was part of a larger community or ecosystem containing multiple types of early cells.

Donoghue’s team also estimated an age for LUCA’s lineage: 4.2 billion years old. Given that the planet is thought to have cooled enough to become habitable around 4.4 billion years ago, LUCA’s community must have evolved in the blink of an evolutionary eye. “Life gets going pretty fast when the conditions are favorable,” Masel remarked.

If LUCA was already a complex population and included many types of cells, then a meaningful portion of life’s early evolutionary history must have occurred well before it lived. By then, the available molecular and cellular diversity must have gone far beyond the basic rudiments of life; it was enough for evolutionary processes to have selected for complex molecular machines and systems.

It has been revealed that this revelation has compelled some biologists, who by definition study life forms that evolved after LUCA, to shift their target to the life forms, quasi-life forms, and lifelike processes that may have existed before LUCA. They’re using new tools to push beyond the material record’s limits to predict how this cellular ecosystem might have evolved in the prebiotic soup.

“What was happening before LUCA really is the most exciting window to look at,” stated Klára Hlouchová, a synthetic biologist at Charles University in Prague. It’s also “the hardest one to pin down.” To do that, researchers are getting imaginative about the chemistries that could have emerged in this early window and rapidly led to evolutionary innovations.

Among the genes that we believe comprised LUCA are some that clearly have a more ancient origin. These genes are so old that nearly all genomes across the tree of life have not only one copy of them, but two. This points to an evolutionary event — a DNA duplication — that occurred well before LUCA evolved. Such genes can take biologists further back and closer to life’s origins.

According to recent reports, “They’re a way to look at what life was like even before the earliest organism,” Goldman said. The protein products made by these doubled genes are involved in a modern cell’s most fundamental processes, such as making proteins, transporting molecules across a membrane, and metabolizing molecules into energy.

It has been revealed that goldman is particularly interested in the latter two. Most life on Earth uses a series of molecular pumps, known as an electron transport chain, to generate energy to power cells. By tracing back the phylogenies of the molecules involved in modern electron transport chains, Goldman proposes what prebiotic, pre-LUCA versions of these molecules might have looked like.

Then Laurie Barge, an astrobiologist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, tests how these plausibly ancient molecules might have behaved in prebiotic environments. Goldman, an evolutionary biologist, met Barge in 2009 at an astrobiology conference for graduate students in Seattle. “We met and became friends there, and we’re in totally different fields,” Barge stated. “We had nothing in common … and we grew up together.” Now they collaborate to bring evolutionary biology and prebiotic chemistry together.

Laurie Barge, Jessica Weber, and Laura Rodriguez (left to right) analyze data from their prebiotic chemistry experiments at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Using test tubes, they simulate hydrothermal vent chemistries, such as this magnesium silicate chimney (bottom) that precipitates plausible minerals from early Earth and Mars.

Sources indicate that laurie Barge, Jessica Weber, and Laura Rodriguez (left to right) analyze data from their prebiotic chemistry experiments at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Using test tubes, they simulate hydrothermal vent chemistries, such as this magnesium silicate chimney (far right) that precipitates plausible minerals from early Earth and Mars.

In glass jars on their lab bench, Barge and her colleague Jessica Weber, also a NASA JPL chemist, simulate the possible mineral chemistries of hydrothermal chimneys — ones that may have been present on primordial Earth as well as those that might exist elsewhere in the universe. They synthesize minerals from their chimney experiments and mix them in vials with Goldman’s pre-LUCA molecules, and test whether and how they interact to produce chemistry reminiscent of an electron transport chain.

It has been revealed that barge and Weber are building from the bottom up to determine what is prebiotically plausible, while Goldman is going from the top down, making predictions from modern and historical clues. They may meet at a fundamental process right in the gray area between life and nonlife. “We come at the problem from two different directions,” Barge remarked. “Combining the two is powerful since then we can study prebiotic plausibility and evolutionary continuity at the same time.”.

Recent findings suggest that even if they succeed in producing aspects of a prebiotic electron transport chain, there’s no assurance that this is how this key metabolic system arose. The deeper scientists reach into pre-LUCA time, the fuzzier the picture becomes. “Still, it is important to understand the prebiotic possibilities,” Barge stated.

In a recent development, the time period before LUCA is so fuzzy that we don’t even know if life then was built using the same ingredients that life uses today. After billions of years of evolution, modern biology could have changed significantly. Evolution is not a designer; the systems that stuck were those that worked, not necessarily the optimal ones for the job. Plus, early organisms led a very different life in a very different environment more than 4 billion years ago; different materials may have been available or may have worked more effectively there.

These deep uncertainties about early evolution on Earth naturally pose questions about how life could evolve anywhere across the universe. As a child, Hlouchová would lay awake at night after watching alien movies, terrified at the question: Is there life out there? When she grew up, she started asking a different version of it: Could life emerge from other chemistries?

At her lab down the street from Prague’s medieval astronomical clock, she deconstructs the amino acid alphabet, which guides the structure and function of all life on Earth. The hundreds of millions of types of proteins found across nature are all built from the same 20 amino acids. But dozens of other types of amino acids have been found on meteorites. It’s possible to make thousands more in the lab, and scientists have speculated that there could be millions of variants across the universe. The rise of more powerful artificial intelligence systems and synthetic biology tools has equipped biologists such as Hlouchová to design molecules, produce them, and test them in the lab.

“This [the origins of life] is something we should crack as humankind,” mentioned Klára Hlouchová, a synthetic biologist. “This problem really opens up our eyes to the rest of the universe.”.

In a recent development, maybe, during life’s pre-LUCA years, proteins were built with more or fewer amino acids, or even with a totally different set. “Computationally, we think that yes — life could have used different amino acids,” Hlouchová noted. “We know that our amino acids were easily available, at least the half of them, and they would be very accessible to prebiotic synthesis on planets which would be similar to ours.” And on a different planet, with different chemistry, she said, “you could have different amino acids and … you could eventually build life using different ways.”.

According to recent reports, to test these ideas, Hlouchová is now building proteins in the lab using a reduced amino acid alphabet. Rather than focus on a specific ancient protein, as Goldman and Barge are doing, she’s looking at three specific types of folding structures found in many types of proteins — folds produced when an amino acid sequence bends and stretches into a 3D shape — that are known to be highly conserved across known life and thus very ancient in origin.

Using a combination of protein-design and structure-prediction programs, her lab removed the modern amino acid alphabet from the protein fold’s 3D structure. Then they asked the program to repopulate it using a reduced alphabet. Using a generative AI tool trained on large sets of protein folds, the programs predicted sequences that would fold up into the desired structure. Hlouchová then built the most plausible ancient proteins and imaged them.

Her team reported, in a series of recent studies, that a reduced alphabet of just 10 amino acids could support the kinds of protein structures that were likely found early in life’s development, the most robust protein folds that modern life uses. She is now working on repeating these experiments with totally different amino acids.

Using biology as a guide, and chemical possibilities as a parts list, Hlouchová is probing what life may have looked like before LUCA.

Recent findings suggest that synthetic biology “opens up a whole new world where we just don’t have to rely on life that we see today,” Hlouchová stated. “Did life have to happen this way, or could it have happened in different ways?” Answering the question could mean traveling ever farther away from what we might recognize as biology.

From the start, modern life has inspired the study of life’s origins. Miller considered his experiment’s production of amino acids, a core feature of modern life, to be irrefutable evidence that life could be produced from early Earth chemistry. And more recent researchers use today’s most widespread biomolecules and processes as proxies for features early life must have had. But researchers hold varying opinions on whether, and how much, we should allow modern life to constrain our imaginations.

“It would be foolish to ignore life as a guide,” Krishnamurthy remarked, “but it would be even more foolish to use life as the only guide.”.

Instead of focusing on the exact materials of life, some are trying to re-create its essence. The field has “been too focused on what molecules current life works with,” remarked Sijbren Otto, a systems chemist at the University of Groningen. It has “not looked enough at what life does.”.

Industry observers note that life is made up of not only molecules but functions. It can replicate, it can metabolize, and it can evolve. These functions don’t necessarily need to be performed by the same molecules that life uses today.

In a recent development, for example, could another molecular system do what DNA does? “If you generalize the definition of a gene, you say, ‘OK, it’s a molecule that stores information,’” Otto mentioned. A replication process generates copies of that information. While Hlouchová is looking at whether you can get to the same structure with different molecules, Otto is looking at whether you can get to the same function. In the early 2010s, he started testing whether nucleotides, the building blocks of DNA, are the only molecules that can store and pass on information.

Benzene rings are stable structures made of interlocking rings of carbon and hydrogen that are found in many biological molecules, including several amino acids. By chance, in 2010, Otto discovered that certain types of synthetically made benzene rings of the same size tended to stack neatly, like poker chips. When shaken or stirred, the growing stacks broke, which triggered the molecular edges to grow more benzene rings. This was a kind of self-replication.

In a recent development, the stacks of benzene rings were also, in essence, propagating information: the size of the rings. The latest stacks, which Otto found could just keep growing, always contained rings of the same size. “From that moment on, we realized we stand a chance of doing evolution with these types of systems,” he remarked.

It has been revealed that these chemical structures held the possibility of information storage and replication. The next step would be to induce metabolism, or to get the structures to facilitate other chemical reactions. They would also need a container to hold themselves together. Putting it all together was a dream, but one that’s gotten closer than ever in recent years.

It took Otto’s lab another 10 years to figure out how to get their self-replicating molecules to catalyze reactions other than their own replication, such as those that helped them make their own precursors. Then, in still unpublished work, they altered some of the molecules in a way that compelled the rings to form compartments that grew and divided. “It’s replicating, it’s metabolizing, it’s keeping itself together in a compartment,” Otto said. Eventually the “benzene cells” grew big enough to be seen under a microscope, he said.

Recent findings suggest that but does that make them alive? The only thing they’re really missing, from a functional perspective, is the ability to evolve, Otto said. That’s where his lab is headed next. “We’re trying to make something that starts to approach life,” he said. “But it will be on a life support machine for some time to come.”.

Recent findings suggest that his benzene “cells” are a far cry from life as we know it. But if you can figure out conceptually how evolution could arise, Otto argued, you can reenact that mechanism, under the simulated conditions of the early Earth and with your favorite prebiotic molecules. “I think, then, you’re closer to the origin,” Otto stated.

These scientists and others are probing the most fundamental aspects of life unhindered by the evolutionary journey that led from LUCA to today. They’re going beyond what genomics can tell us even about the pre-LUCA era to imaginatively reconstruct how the mechanisms and functions of life could have emerged. Despite their different tools, materials, and approaches, the common thread across the field is preserving the requirements and possibilities of evolution. Because no matter what molecules it’s built of, what makes life alive is the fact that it can adapt to a changing environment and invent upcoming ways to survive across deep time. Its engine of change and adaptation is evolution — and re-creating it is the shared dream of chemists and biologists alike.

It has been revealed that in summer 2026, a cell made headlines. Synthetic biologists had packed fatty sacs called liposomes with biological components: a DNA replication system and a set of 36 enzymes that read DNA and make proteins. They filled other liposomes with sugar, lipids, enzymes, nucleotides, and ribosomes — supply caches to send in as needed. Then they waited to see if their chemistry experiment would take on a life of its own.

After months of fussing around with a population of these proto-cells in the lab, the team started to see something: lifelike behaviors. The cells replicated their DNA, grew, and divided. And larger ones produced more daughter cells, resulting in a crude kind of natural selection. The researchers posted their results on the preprint server biorxiv.org in July. It was touted as a “stunning” step and a “breakthrough” for the field.

This synthetic cell is not a reflection of the origin of life; it had a 4-billion-year head start. It was built from biomolecular parts that are highly evolved and “disgustingly modern,” stated Kate Adamala, the synthetic biologist at the University of Minnesota who led the project. But it’s the first plausible demonstration of the field’s most fundamental idea: that it is possible to take a bunch of “undeniably dead” components, she said, put them together, and create something that “starts undergoing all of those functions of life.”.

Even though the cells can grow, divide, and replicate their genome, Adamala is steering clear of the word “alive.” The cell can’t feed and sustain itself; it needs constant delivery of food and ribosomes, the machinery that it needs to make proteins. But more importantly, Adamala stated, it is missing true evolution.

To produce their crude version of natural selection, Adamala’s team engineered mutations into their synthetic cells that led to different growth rates. “It’s a poor man’s evolution,” she noted. In true natural selection, cells would mutate, and the population would naturally gain genetic diversity. Her team had effectively built evolution in.

But still, the chemistry came together into something like biology. And it did not require some magic spark or special ingredient. The researchers had to figure out the molecular system — the relationships between known components — and then tweak them until the system worked better, and then better, and then better. Life is not an on-off-switch; it is more like a continuum. A chemical system becomes increasingly alive over time. And if you try to trace it back to a point at which it fully becomes alive, that point will likely be “arbitrary,” Otto stated. This is true in the lab, and it must have been true 4 billion years ago.

Fluorescent microscopy shows a synthetic cell undergoing cell division: elongating, pinching, and separating into two daughter cells.

According to recent reports, to this day, no one has convincingly re-created life — self-sustaining, self-replicating, independently evolving — in the lab. Researchers aren’t even sure whether evolutionary processes on the early Earth, in systems of molecules that may or may not have been “alive,” would look like those that drive adaptive changes in cells or organisms today.

Sources indicate that but give the scientists a little more time to work on the problem. “Our great chemists, only a handful of them, are doing this in the lab, and with only a few test tubes over a [a few] decades,” mentioned Michael Lynch, an evolutionary biologist at Arizona State University who is working with Kaçar, Travisano, and others to bring evolutionary rules to the origins-of-life field. In comparison, prebiotic chemistry on early Earth had a few hundred million years, which is “an awful long time for life to experiment.”.

Sources indicate that similar experiments could be taking place somewhere out there right now. Our galaxy alone has at least 6,000 known exoplanets and likely many, many more. A lot of them have liquid water, and some 2,000 of them could be super-Earths, even more hospitable to life than our own planet. Ancient Mars and Enceladus, a moon of Saturn, support the conditions that astrobiologists consider necessary for life. Analyses of rock samples from asteroids and the red planet continue to reveal the raw materials used by our biology.

Saturn’s small moon Enceladus hosts a salty ocean beneath an icy shell, whose jets erupting into space were observed by NASA’s Cassini spacecraft in 2005.

NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute.

Sources indicate that as researchers continue to deconstruct and reconstruct what life could have been on early Earth, they’re also exploring what could be possible elsewhere. Researchers, including Hlouchová, have used protein design tools to show that the six amino acids found on the asteroid Bennu can create many different types of protein folds.

It has been revealed that “The origin of life is very strongly connected to planetary exploration, and we should always think of this as, you know, we’re trying to understand the nature of life in the universe,” Barge stated. “We need to understand the origin of life in order to effectively look for life.”.

According to recent reports, kaçar, director of the NASA Interdisciplinary Astrobiology Research center, is leading the way in connecting the two fields. Her lab uses synthetic biology and computational methods to predict the genetic codes of ancient proteins and resurrect them inside modern bacteria. Then she monitors their activity to see what kind of patterns they might leave behind in ancient rocks. By bridging the dynamics of a molecule, its geological output, and its atmospheric impact, she’s hoping to identify biosignatures that could be used to search for life in the cosmos.

According to recent reports, NASA’s Habitable Worlds Observatory, launching in the 2040s, will be the first space telescope specifically designed to search for biosignatures in the atmospheres of planets outside our solar system. And the European Space Agency’s upcoming space telescope Plato will also be looking. Barge hopes that they will find not only clear evidence of life beyond Earth but also clues to how it began. This “is not something you can ever see on Earth because it’s all been overprinted by life,” she remarked.

According to recent reports, evidence of life elsewhere could be the key to finally dissolving the arguments and rifts that have haunted this field since its beginning. Through all these decades, scientists have theorized about the emergence of a system for which we have only one example: life on Earth. No matter how imaginative they get, scientific ideas about the origins of life remain constrained by the singular model that emerged from the prebiotic soup more than 4 billion years ago.

Scientists are now closer than ever, in the lab or deep in space, to increasing the sample size in the experiment of life. One day, there could be two.

Great Lakes irradiance surges as wet weather weighs on Southwest solar resource

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (447 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Pv-magazine

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • North American irradiance remained close to normal overall in October, but the continental average concealed sharply contrasting conditions for solar assets.
  • Across the Northeast and Great Lakes, October GHI averaged 14% above normal, with 95.5% of the region recording above-average irradiance.
  • Cleveland experienced a similarly exceptional month, with its average daily profile also setting a high for the city in the Solcast record.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

North American irradiance remained close to normal overall in October, but the continental average concealed sharply contrasting conditions for solar assets. Global Horizontal Irradiance (GHI) was 0.8% above normal across North America, while the Great Lakes and Northeast recorded substantialirradiance surpluses and the Southwest and northern Mexico experienced widespread deficits during an unusually wet month, according to analysis using the Solcast API.

Across the Northeast and Great Lakes, October GHI averaged 14% above normal, with 95.5% of the region recording above-average irradiance. The largest anomalies occurred around Upstate Latest York and parts of Michigan, where GHI was approximately 20-25% above normal. Higher atmospheric pressure, lower humidity and below-normal precipitation across much of the region reduced the frequency of cloudy periods, allowing more solar radiation to reach the surface. Buffalo recorded the strongest October GHI in its 2007-2026 series, illustrating the scale of the regional surplus.

Cleveland experienced a similarly exceptional month, with its average daily profile also setting a high for the city in the Solcast record.

These conditions were particularly relevant across the Northeast, where significant volumes of distributed solar are installed in states including Fresh York, New Jersey and Massachusetts.

In a recent development, conditions were markedly different farther southwest. A strong low-pressure trough approaching the West Coast drew Pacific moisture into the Four Corners where Arizona, Colorado, Newly introduced Mexico and Utah meet. Moisture associated with Tropical Storms Polo and Trudy, also contributed to several days of heavy rainfall throughout the month of October. The San Luis Valley received more than four times its usual October rainfall in four days, while the San Juan River at Pagosa Springs reached its second-highest crest since 1911.

Elevated atmospheric moisture extended across much of the Southwest and northern Mexico, increasing cloud cover and coinciding with a broad irradiance deficit. GHI across the region averaged 9% below the October norm. Phoenix recorded GHI approximately 10% below its 2007-2025 October average, making October 2026 the second-lowest October for GHI in the Solcast record.

The below-normal conditions covered the solar-intensive corridor from Southern California into Arizona, exposing a substantial concentration of utility-scale solar assets to the same regional irradiance deficit.

Solcast produces these figures by tracking clouds and aerosols at 1-2km resolution globally, using satellite data and proprietary AI/ML algorithms. This data is used to drive irradiance models, enabling Solcast to calculate irradiance at high resolution, with typical bias of less than 2%, and also cloud-tracking forecasts. This data is used by more than 350 companies managing over 350 GW of solar assets globally.

#24. Latest Update: Analysis: Climate-finance pledges fall 70% as countries meet at COP31

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1824 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Carbonbrief

Latest Update: Analysis: Climate-finance pledges fall 70% as countries meet at COP31

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1824 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Carbonbrief

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The amount of public funding pledged to help developing countries tackle climate change has dropped by more than 70% in 2026, according to Carbon Brief analysis.
  • Developed countries are required under UN climate treaties to provide “climate finance” and have traditionally unveiled multi-year pledges to feed into their global commitments.
  • Most of these pledges expired in 2025 and, since then, the US has withdrawn from international climate efforts and many European aid budgets have been cut.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The amount of public funding pledged to help developing countries tackle climate change has dropped by more than 70% in 2026, according to Carbon Brief analysis.

Developed countries are required under UN climate treaties to provide “climate finance” and have traditionally unveiled multi-year pledges to feed into their global commitments.

Most of these pledges expired in 2025 and, since then, the US has withdrawn from international climate efforts and many European aid budgets have been cut.

A civil-society tracker shows that only five nations have revealed latest multi-year pledges, including just one major donor – the UK.

Germany, France and Japan are among the key contributors that have so far failed to set out looks for new climate finance, while none is expected from the US.

As a result, the total amount of public climate finance pledged over the next few years amounts to just $11.7bn a year in spending, down from recent levels of around $40bn.

Experts tell Carbon Brief that global conflict, fiscal constraints and the rise of the far right are all making it harder for developed-country governments to pledge upcoming funds.

As the COP31 summit in Turkey gets underway, developing countries are stressing their urgent need for upcoming finance, after nations agreed to a new global target just two years ago.

Under the Paris Agreement, developed countries are obliged to provide climate finance to help developing countries cut their emissions and prepare for climate disasters.

This financial assistance can be channelled through multilateral development banks, UN climate funds and investments “mobilised” from the private sector.

But a large chunk is also expected to come directly from the public coffers of developed countries – primarily their foreign-aid budgets. This public spending has made up roughly a third of climate finance flowing to developing countries in recent years.

The EU, the US and others agreed just two years ago that they would “take the lead” on scaling up annual climate finance from $100bn in the early 2020s to $300bn by 2035.

Donor countries have traditionally supported such goals by announcing multi-year targets that indicate how much they strategy to spend on climate finance.

Nearly all of these pledges expired in 2025 – and hardly any major donors have confirmed new ones to replace them, covering the period out to 2030.

This lack of upcoming commitments is captured in a tracker of old and new financial commitments by climate NGOs NRDC and E3G.

Carbon Brief analysis of this data, based on an annualised breakdown of targets, demonstrates that developed countries had previously pledged around £42bn a year in public finance.

As the chart below shows, based on current pledges, this has fallen by around 71% to £11.8bn, on average, over the remainder of the 2020s.

In a recent development, not all contributors confirmed public climate-finance pledges in advance for the pre-2026 period. Some did not hit their stated targets, while others exceeded them.

While official data for 2025 is not yet available, bilateral public finance reached £43.9bn in 2024, broadly in line with the amount pledged by developed countries.

International climate finance has been consistently dominated by five nations – Japan, Germany, France, the US and the UK.

These countries – together with the EU – have provided around 90% of all the bilateral, public climate finance going to developing countries in recent years.

Of these key players, only the UK has announced a upcoming pledge, committing £6bn ($8bn) of aid between 2026-27 and 2028-29, plus £6.7bn ($8.9bn) from outside its aid budget.

This accounts for half of all the annual funds pledged from 2026 onwards – averaging $5.7bn a year.

The European Commission makes up most of the remainder, with an average annual contribution of $4.5bn promised out to 2027.

Rather than a upcoming pledge, this is due to the commission promising to spend €28bn ($31.8bn) over its 2021-2027 budget period. Its post-2027 contribution is currently being discussed as part of wider EU budget negotiations.

Industry observers note that canada has promised to spend CA$5.3bn ($4.1bn) by 2030, averaging $860m a year. The Netherlands, Switzerland and Belgium have also pledged relatively small sums.

According to recent reports, overall, despite developed countries committing to scale up climate finance, these fresh pledges are either less ambitious – or only slightly more ambitious – than previous ones. This can be seen in the chart below.

Recent findings suggest that the UK’s pledge appears more ambitious, but this is because the government has changed how it counts climate finance to include $8.9bn in “additional” public finance. When only the like-for-like aid components are compared, the latest pledge amounts to a drop in ambition. (For more details, see the methodology.).

The most significant absence is the US, which committed to reaching $11.4bn in annual support by 2024 under the Biden administration.

Recent findings suggest that since president Donald Trump took power, the US has – for the second time – withdrawn from the Paris Agreement and shrunk its aid budget. It will not provide any official climate finance in the coming years.

It has been revealed that another notable absence is Australia, which is jointly hosting the upcoming COP31 summit, alongside Turkey. Josie Lee, policy and advocacy lead at Oxfam Australia, tells Carbon Brief:.

“If Australia fails to announce a climate-finance pledge as president of negotiations, it would send a problematic message to those resisting action on climate change that might serve to embolden their agenda.”.

According to recent reports, japan is the largest overall contributor of public climate finance, but it has not traditionally confirmed targets for this type of spending. Instead, the government set out overall goals that also bundle in finance “mobilised” from the private sector.

As a result, its public-finance ambitions have not been included in this analysis.

So far, the Japanese government has not announced any latest multi-year climate-finance pledges, from either the public or the private sector.

Europe provides the majority of international climate finance, but European governments have massively cut their aid spending in recent years, citing economic strain and defence spending needs.

Germany and France, the two largest European climate-finance contributors, both pledged to reach €6bn ($6.8bn) per year by 2025. Neither has committed to anything beyond that.

Industry observers note that both nations have slashed their aid budgets in recent years, including funding for climate programmes. Germany missed its 2025 climate-finance goal due to these cuts.

Dr Anja Carolin Gebel, a senior policy advisor at Germanwatch, tells Carbon Brief that this issue has become more politically fraught since the centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) won the 2025 election and began leading a coalition government:.

“The issue of climate change – and, subsequently, climate finance – has taken a back seat in the current government coalition.”.

There has also been a political shift in France, Gaïa Febvre, international policy coordinator at Réseau Action Climat, tells Carbon Brief. She adds:.

“The upcoming presidential election and the growing influence of the far right are likely to make latest international financial commitments politically more difficult.”.

Other significant European donors are also undergoing political turmoil.

Spain’s centre-left government has triggered a snap election for the end of November, making a newly introduced climate-finance pledge during COP31 less likely.

Following a narrow election win, a centre-left bloc in Sweden is still in the process of trying to form a new coalition government.

Some nations have signalled that their climate finance will continue flowing, even though they have not officially set out specific new pledges.

According to recent reports, the Dutch government, for example, has mentioned it will provide “at least” €300m ($334m) of specific climate funding annually out to 2031. However, it has also indicated that its total public climate finance is likely to be considerably higher in both 2026 and 2027.

To highlight the lack of new pledges, developing countries are championing a “climate-finance work programme” at COP31, which could provide a space to discuss scaling up public climate finance from developed countries.

In response, the EU has stressed that its member states are the “largest providers” of public climate finance and called on developing countries to submit overdue prepares for cutting emissions. The EU and its member states provided a record €32.3bn ($40bn) in 2025.

Against this backdrop, EU climate chief Wopke Hoekstra recently told Bloomberg that “any conversation on new fresh money is dead in the water”.

Industry observers note that joe Thwaites, international climate finance director at NRDC, who runs the commitment tracker, tells Carbon Brief that “developed countries would be wise to show how they are continuing to lead on climate finance”. He claims:.

“The lack of new announcements is making the finance negotiations tougher than they need to be. The debate around the climate-finance work programme is arising because developing countries have little clarity about how much public climate finance there will be in coming years.”.

This analysis is based on the climate-finance commitments tracker, run by the NGOs NRDC and E3G, supplemented with additional research.

Recent findings suggest that only the 23 “developed” countries that are obliged to provide climate finance are considered in this analysis, plus the EU. This includes western Europe, the US, Australia, Canada and Fresh Zealand. Japan and Norway both provide substantial sums of climate finance, but have not confirmed specific public-finance pledges and therefore are not included.

Sources indicate that carbon Brief converted multi-year pledges into single years, with 2025 used as the baseline “pre-2026” year. Some countries committed to reaching a certain amount “by 2025”, in which case that value is used. Others noted they would provide a total amount over several years, in which case the average value per year is used. Belgium, Switzerland and the US only set initial targets as far as 2024, so their 2024 values were used instead of 2025.

It has been revealed that these values were compared with the average annual contribution for the remainder of the 2020s, based on the fresh pledges from the UK, Canada, Belgium, Switzerland and the Netherlands. Some climate finance has been committed by the Netherlands, but this is not expected to be its total contribution. The EU, Portugal and Greece have earlier pledges that extend into the latter half of the 2020s, although the latter two make very small contributions.

NRDC and E3G include all the UK’s newly pledged public finance in their tracker, including $8.9bn in “additional” public finance, which covers “equity, debt, guarantees, insurance and export credit” to mobilise private finance.

In previous Carbon Brief analysis comparing the UK’s new climate-finance target to its old one, this funding was not included. This is because the government did not previously count these funds towards its climate-finance goals, instead focusing exclusively on aid spending.

This analysis does not include pledges that some countries, including Germany and France, have made to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF). However, these pledges would not substantially change the main finding, shifting the overall reduction from 71% to 70%.

#22. Scientists created artificial, life-like muscles for humanoid robots

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (990 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci

Scientists created artificial, life-like muscles for humanoid robots

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (990 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For better or worse, some scientists seem dead set on infusing humanoid robots with more lifelike qualities.
  • According to recent reports, designing robot muscles that act like the real thing poses some engineering challenges right off the bat.
  • “Soft robotic muscles need to be both strong and flexible to mimic human movements, but these properties are rarely found in the same material,” study co-author and University of Pennsylvania engineer Shu Yang stated in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For better or worse, some scientists seem dead set on infusing humanoid robots with more lifelike qualities. They’ve already experimented with stretching lab-grown human skin over robot faces and with a synthetic hydrogel skin that lets robots really “feel” burns and cuts. Now, a team of engineers at the University of Pennsylvania wants to dig under the skin. In a  study published this week in Advanced Functional Materials, the team describes a highly controllable artificial robot muscle inspired by the small muscles in human eyes and fingers. They put them to the test by having a robot hand strike piano keys at varying intensities and made a set of human eye muscles able to maintain a gaze. It all feels quite uncomfortably adjacent to the 1973 sci-fi film and HBO series Westworld.

According to recent reports, designing robot muscles that act like the real thing poses some engineering challenges right off the bat. For starters, most large robots today, especially humanoid ones, rely on bulky, rigid motors and components. That’s fine for more straightforward actions like walking and lifting, but recreating the muscles that move our eyes or fingers requires far more delicate precision. In this case, the engineers needed a material that prioritized flexibility and fine control while staying strong enough to hold up after repeated use. As with many aspects of robotics, tasks that seem quite easy for humans to do are actually often the most difficult tasks for machines. While bipedal robots have been pulling off dance routines and performing acrobatics worth of a Marvel superhero for years, they still fall flat when it comes to something as simple as folding laundry or holding a gaze.

“Soft robotic muscles need to be both strong and flexible to mimic human movements, but these properties are rarely found in the same material,” study co-author and University of Pennsylvania engineer Shu Yang stated in a statement.

Recent findings suggest that for their muscle fiber, the team settled on liquid crystal elastomers (LCE) combined with graphene and an embedded ultrathin copper coil. The LCE, a rubber-like material, acts as the actual muscle, both contracting and stretching. The graphene serves as a reinforcer, making the material both a bit softer and tougher, so it holds up even when opposing muscles pull in other directions. Together, these two ingredients can produce movement, but on their own they struggle to stay put. When heated, the LCE stretches but then keeps contracting, eventually creeping back toward its original length as it rapidly cools. That’s a problem for subtle movements like holding a gaze or pressing a piano key with light, steady force, where the muscle needs to hold a precise position over a period of time.

That’s where the coil comes in. The team added the coil inside the fiber to serve as a kind of temperature gauge, and the sensors determine when the muscle is losing heat and contracting. With those readings, the team could then gradually increase temperature to ensure the muscle held its position.

“We used the resistance of the embedded copper coil as a feedback signal and adjusted the heating power in real time to keep the resistance near a target value,” added study co-author and University of Pennsylvania Ph.D. student Xuelin Wu. “Because the coil served as both a heater and a sensor, we did not need a separate sensor for feedback.”.

It has been revealed that with their artificial muscle designed, it was time to test it in real-world scenarios. First, the team fitted the muscles into a 3D-printed robot hand built to mimic finger movement. They then made the fingers press various piano keys at different levels of force and speed. Sensors placed on the bottom of the keys were able to tell how hard each note was played. The detached hand was no Mozart, but it worked.

In a recent development, next, they mounted a pair of robotic eyeballs on freely rotating ball joints inside 3D-printed shells. The muscle fibers were attached around the edges of opposing pairs, which were meant to mimic how muscles in the eyes stretch and contract. In testing, the eyes shifted their gaze on demand, with controlled, repeatable movements. The resulting video demonstration is both impressive and unsettling.

Recent findings suggest that the research joins a growing field of labs and companies racing to build artificial muscle systems. In 2025, Polish startup Clone Robotics took the idea to an extreme with a horrifying video of a faceless, human-sized robot dangling from a ceiling and writhing, its movements supposedly powered by synthetic muscles and a hydraulic system meant to mimic human muscles and blood vessels. They call  their creation the world’s first “musculoskeletal android.” Though it is likely that their video was more a shocking proof-of-concept than an actively working prototype, it nonetheless provides a glimpse into a potentially unsettling future where robots replace mechanical motors and actuators with more human-like muscle fibers.

In a recent development, protoclone, the world's first bipedal, musculoskeletal android. pic.twitter.com/oIV1yaMSyE.

The University of Pennsylvania researchers say the next step is combining more of these muscles into larger, integrated systems, where dozens of small muscles have to work together to produce more natural expressions. Down the line, they’re interested in potentially using AI computer vision to coordinate those into even more complex systems. Authenticity is the point. The long-term goal, they note, is to create robots that look and feel more and more like the real thing.

“I’m excited about the possibility of using this approach to create robots that move with the same subtlety and expressiveness we see in human faces,” concluded University of Pennsylvania engineer and paper co-author Ziyun Zhang.
