#21. GLP-1s Are Showing Promise Beyond Weight Loss. Could They Be 'Wonder Drugs' for Ailments Like Addiction, Dementia and Cancer?

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2777 w)
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Smithsonianmag

GLP-1s Are Showing Promise Beyond Weight Loss. Could They Be 'Wonder Drugs' for Ailments Like Addiction, Dementia and Cancer?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2777 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You’ve probably been bombarded with ads for GLP-1 medications under brand names like Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro.
  • But the drugs can do more than help people shed pounds.
  • These medications mimic a hormone called glucagon-like peptide-1, which is naturally generated by the gut after we eat.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You’ve probably been bombarded with ads for GLP-1 medications under brand names like Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro. Many offer a tantalizing promise of weight loss that has been plastered across New York City subway stations and broadcast during the Super Bowl.

But the drugs can do more than help people shed pounds. After all, the Food and Drug Administration approved the first GLP-1, called exenatide, for Type 2 diabetes in 2005.

These medications mimic a hormone called glucagon-like peptide-1, which is naturally generated by the gut after we eat. It tells the body to produce insulin—which is how the medications help people with diabetes manage their blood sugar—as well as slows stomach emptying and increases feelings of satiation, reducing food intake.

Beyond Type 2 diabetes and weight loss, GLP-1s have now been greenlit for a wide range of other conditions, including sleep apnea, heart problems and kidney disease. And recent evidence suggests the medications’ potential could be even broader.

Quick fact: Could GLP-1s stop the biological clock?

In a study published in September, researchers reported that semaglutide could slow aging and extend life span in older female mice.

Clinical epidemiologist Ziyad Al-Aly has been prescribing GLP-1s to patients with kidney concerns for years. One of them, a veteran in his 60s who had spent ages trying to quit smoking, told Al-Aly that after taking a GLP-1, he suddenly stopped craving cigarettes.

According to recent reports, similar stories followed, from other patients and acquaintances who no longer felt the urge to indulge their vices, such as alcohol or gambling, once they took a GLP-1. All these anecdotes mounted to a revelation in 2023.

“I was like, ‘OK, is this really happening?’” says Al-Aly, of the V.A. St. Louis Health Care System and the Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. “Something is happening more than my previous thought, that they only work on diabetes and obesity.”.

Clinical trials—the gold standard of medical research—will be required to truly put GLP-1s to the test, especially since most studies of the drugs’ potentially far-ranging benefits are in an early stage. But little by little, Al-Aly and other researchers are investigating the exciting possibility that GLP-1s may be “wonder drugs,” capable of treating or preventing all sorts of ailments, including addiction, dementia and even cancer.

Beyond the tales of people whose cravings for illicit substances quieted when they took these drugs, past research in animals and preliminary work in humans had also reported evidence of this phenomenon. But Al-Aly wanted to hunt for more data himself.

It has been revealed that using the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs’ extensive health records, he and his colleagues examined up to three years of medical information from more than 600,000 veterans. All had Type 2 diabetes; some were taking GLP-1s for it, and others were taking a different diabetes drug.

According to recent reports, their findings, published this past March in the British Medical Journal, suggest that GLP-1s can help prevent alcohol, nicotine, opioid and other substance use disorders from forming. They also might help people who already have those addictions avoid overdoses, hospital stays and death.

More specifically, when taking GLP-1s, veterans with no prior history of a substance use disorder had a 14 percent lower risk of developing any of the analyzed addictions compared with the non-GLP-1 users. Similar statistics followed for specific substances: an 18 percent lower risk of developing alcohol use disorder, a 25 percent lower risk of opioid use disorder and a 20 percent lower risk of cocaine or nicotine use disorder.

GLP-1 users with pre-existing substance use disorders also appeared to benefit, with a 31 percent lower risk of an emergency department visit, 26 percent lower risk of a hospital admission, 39 percent lower risk of an overdose and a 50 percent lower risk of death related to substance use, compared with participants taking the other diabetes drug.

“Clearly, these GLP-1 medications are working to suppress addiction,” Al-Aly notes. “And what makes it remarkable is that this was not working against smoking or alcohol or cannabis or opioids. It was working across all of them.”.

In a recent development, that’s exciting, he adds, because “there’s not a single drug in our toolbox that actually works across all substances.” Nicotine patches can address tobacco, and naltrexone takes aim at opioid and alcohol use disorders. But this work suggests GLP-1s might target the brain circuitry underlying all addictions.

GLP-1 receptors are found in brain regions involved in the reward system, which drives motivation and pleasure. Some people taking the drugs for weight loss have also reported a reduction in food cravings.

Recent findings suggest that but exactly how GLP-1s work remains an open question, claims Lorenzo Leggio, a physician-scientist and clinical director of the National Institute on Drug Abuse. “We don’t even fully understand how they work for obesity, and we don’t know if the mechanism how they work for obesity is the same as the mechanism for addiction.”.

According to recent reports, what’s more, studies looking at health records alone can’t establish whether GLP-1s directly cause people to have fewer substance use disorders—they can only find a “potential causation,” adds Leggio, also of the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism. And the findings of Al-Aly’s study might not be generalizable, since all its participants had Type 2 diabetes.

That’s where randomized clinical trials come in, where researchers arbitrarily split participants into experimental groups and tightly control parameters in prospective work. The results have been promising for alcohol use disorder, with a few published trials finding that GLP-1s have benefits. They all excluded people with diabetes, showing the effect isn’t dependent on that condition, but whether obesity plays a role is still up in the air.

Other clinical trials are in planning or underway. In fact, Leggio’s team just finished recruiting participants for another study on alcohol use disorder. But much less is known about whether GLP-1s can address other addictions, he says. Some human research hints that the drugs can at least help prevent weight gain and blood pressure changes when people quit smoking.

“The field is still in its infancy,” Leggio says.

One area where the field is a bit further along is testing whether GLP-1s can treat dementia. But here, scientists have found, the benefits are not so clear-cut.

Health record data showing reduced incidence of dementia among GLP-1 consumers led to two major clinical trials, which began in 2021 and investigated whether the drugs could slow cognitive decline in people with early Alzheimer’s disease, the most common form of dementia.

The studies, called Evoke and Evoke+ and funded by GLP-1 maker Novo Nordisk, collectively enrolled more than 3,800 participants in 40 countries. All had tested positive for a hallmark of Alzheimer’s: sticky plaques of the protein beta-amyloid in their brains. Some took the GLP-1 semaglutide—the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy—while others took a placebo.

Scientists have suspected the medication could help treat this form of dementia because past animal research has found that it can quell inflammation. Neuroinflammation, or inflammation in the brain, is becoming increasingly recognized as a driver of Alzheimer’s disease progression.

That’s because brain cells known as microglia try to remove the problematic beta-amyloid protein, but they’re unsuccessful, notes Jeffrey Cummings, a neurologist at the Kirk Kerkorian School of Medicine at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas. During that process, the activated microglia are also releasing a toxic storm of immune system messengers called cytokines, which contribute to brain inflammation.

“Anti-inflammatory drugs are among the largest class of drugs at the moment in clinical trials for Alzheimer’s disease,” notes Cummings. The hypothesis that drove the Evoke trials, for which he co-chaired the steering committee, was that reducing inflammation would curb progression of the disease’s cognitive symptoms.

In a recent development, after taking their assigned pills for two years, the trial participants completed a dementia severity assessment. They also provided blood and cerebrospinal fluid at various stages so researchers could examine biological signs of inflammation and Alzheimer’s. Compared with the control, the GLP-1 was associated with lower inflammation and a small reduction in some of those signs of Alzheimer’s disease.

However, dementia progressed at the same rate among GLP-1 users and those in the placebo group, researchers announced in November 2025, meaning the drug didn’t slow down the disease’s advance.

It has been revealed that while the Evoke trials’ negative results were a blow for the field, that doesn’t mean the pursuit is completely over. Some people wonder whether instead of altering Alzheimer’s disease progression, GLP-1s could prevent the neurodegenerative conditions from arising in the first place. The Alzheimer’s Association revealed in July the launch of a study to investigate whether GLP-1s can help reduce the risk of cognitive decline in older adults.

Recent findings suggest that cummings notes that researchers could also explore whether GLP-1s have a stronger effect on dementia in people with Type 2 diabetes—a population where observational data has shown an impact. Fewer than 14 percent of Evoke trial participants had the metabolic condition. Additionally, GLP-1s might actually be better for mitigating vascular dementia, which Type 2 diabetes also elevates the risk of, Cummings states.

Perhaps a more personalized approach would find clearer results, says Alireza Atri, an Alzheimer’s disease expert at Mass General Brigham and Harvard Medical School. He was also on the Evoke trials’ steering committee and says that looking at different subpopulations—such as those with diabetes or other metabolism-related conditions—might reveal who would find semaglutide most helpful. That could inform more targeted clinical trials in the future.

Industry observers note that what’s more, although the Evoke trials’ main analyses were performed after two years, some participants were tracked for another year. “If you actually squint and take it with a huge grain of salt, you’ll see that in almost every major outcome, there’s starting to be separation between two and three years,” says Atri. “So, it’s possible that … if the effect is mostly on certain subgroups, it may take longer to show because it’s watered down.”.

In a recent development, laboratory data also hints that GLP-1s could have an anti-cancer effect. Cancer involves some of your body’s cells growing out of control, and the drugs seem to inhibit a key molecular signaling pathway that helps the diseased cells divide and spread. Their inflammation-regulating effects could also help thwart cancer, since the disease’s development and progression are associated with inflammation.

Industry observers note that colon cancer runs in the family for hematologist-oncologist Colton Jones. Four of his aunts have died from the disease, and they all had Type 2 diabetes and were overweight or had obesity at some point. Some were taking GLP-1s.

“What I wanted to do was figure out: Could these GLP medications have any other added benefit for my family members personally?” claims Jones, of the Mays Cancer Center at the University of Texas at San Antonio Health Science Center.

So, he and his colleagues looked at health records of more than 280,000 people, half of whom took a GLP-1. The others, whose demographics mirrored those in the GLP-1 group, regularly took aspirin, which can reduce the risk of colorectal cancer. Analyses revealed that the GLP-1 users were 36 percent less likely to get colorectal cancer than aspirin users.

“I was surprised to the point where I was like, ‘This is just too good to be true.’ And so, I tested it multiple times,” looking at different participant subgroups, Jones claims. “When I saw that the signal remained consistent no matter how much I tried to tweak the data, I knew at that moment that we potentially found something.”.

In a recent development, jones presented the findings this past January at the 2026 American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) Gastrointestinal Cancers Symposium. He and his collaborators have found similar outcomes with breast cancer, pancreatic cancer, leukemia and other cancers, among high-risk individuals.

In a recent development, ariana Neely, an internal medicine physician at Jefferson Einstein Philadelphia Hospital who also worked on those studies, wanted to fill a knowledge gap related to lung cancer. It’s “one of the top causes of cancer-related mortality in the United States,” she says, but no known drug can help prevent it.

According to recent reports, neely and colleagues examined health records of more than 68,000 people at a high risk for lung cancer and found that those taking GLP-1s were 31 percent less likely to develop the disease than participants who were not on the medications. She presented the analysis in June at the 2026 ASCO Annual Meeting.

These and other observational studies have led to the planning of a massive prospective clinical trial to test whether GLP-1s can prevent breast cancer, the second most common form of cancer among women in the U.S.

It has been revealed that for the past two years, the ECOG-ACRIN Cancer Research Group has been designing a prospective study that would enroll around 10,000 participants between the ages of 45 and 79, says Elizabeth McDonald, an interventional breast imager who is helping to design the trial. That age range was chosen because postmenopausal women are at an increased risk of developing breast cancer, especially if they’re overweight. In fact, obesity is a risk factor for multiple cancers and is associated with chronic inflammation.

Some trial participants would take a GLP-1, and all would be followed for three years to see who develops breast cancer. It would be a landmark clinical trial.

“This would be the first and the definitive study, and would likely be the only study,” says McDonald, of the University of Pennsylvania Perelman School of Medicine and Penn’s Abramson Cancer Center. Robust clinical trial evidence that GLP-1s prevent breast cancer, combined with strong observational data across other cancer types, could justify its use in those forms of disease. That’s helpful because trials are extremely expensive, she notes.

That said, McDonald and colleagues are still seeking financial backing for the trial. They’re sending applications to potential funders, such as research foundations, but McDonald says they’ll probably need a substantial contribution from the federal government, which typically pays for big U.S. trials. She estimates that after procuring enough money, researchers could start the study in three months.

Sources indicate that while early data in multiple areas of medicine looks promising, that doesn’t mean GLP-1s will prove to be a panacea. The Evoke trials already failed to pan out for Alzheimer’s disease progression, and even before those results came out, researchers reported that the GLP-1 exenatide did not slow Parkinson’s disease—another neurodegenerative condition linked with dementia—in a trial in the United Kingdom.

What’s more, several drugs have shown exciting potential before—then ended up falling flat in clinical trials.

In a recent development, the Type 2 diabetes medication metformin, for example, initially seemed to have anti-cancer effects in laboratory studies, and observational data looked promising, too. So, around 15 years ago, scientists started working on clinical trials in the hopes that metformin might help prevent or treat cancer. “But when the prospective studies were done, it turned out that this was not true,” Jones notes.

Statins, commonly used to treat high cholesterol, also went through a possible wonder-drug phase. Like GLP-1s, they also have anti-inflammatory properties. Statins have been investigated for conditions including rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis and ulcerative colitis, but are currently FDA-approved primarily for problems related to the heart, blood vessels and metabolism.

“Medicine is replete with hype. When a latest medicine comes along, people get excited,” Al-Aly notes. Doctors want to see if the new tool can help their patients in multiple ways. But when put through rigorous testing, “much of that [early] evidence does not really pan out,” he adds.

Industry observers note that for now, observational evidence could help physicians and patients choose medications based on their potential secondary benefits. If a person with Type 2 diabetes wants to kick their nicotine addiction, for instance, this preliminary work suggests they should consider taking a GLP-1 instead of another diabetes drug.

In a recent development, although more research is needed, Atri thinks GLP-1s could be the real deal, since they seem to help regulate inflammation caused by the immune system—and immune responses that are too strong or too weak are seen in many illnesses. “Hence, you’re seeing this incredible effect across multiple” health conditions, he notes.

“They are probably wonder drugs in many ways.”.

McKenzie Prillaman is Smithsonian magazine’s assistant digital editor, science and innovation. She specializes in all things life sciences, with a particular penchant for neuroscience. Her work has also appeared in Nature, Scientific American and Science News, among other outlets.

#17. The mysterious golden shipwreck that led to decades of lawsuits

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1148 w)
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Popsci

The mysterious golden shipwreck that led to decades of lawsuits

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1148 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Long before the Titanic, the most famous shipwreck in the US was the SS Central America.
  • Sources indicate that 425 people died.
  • It has been revealed that that loss of life alone should be reason enough for people to remember the ship.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Long before the Titanic, the most famous shipwreck in the US was the SS Central America. The wooden steamship helped connect San Francisco with Fresh York City before the construction of a coast-to-coast rail network, and sank off the coast of South Carolina in 1857.

Sources indicate that 425 people died. Most people today haven’t heard of it.

It has been revealed that that loss of life alone should be reason enough for people to remember the ship. But the SS Central America was also hauling $1.2 million worth of gold, according to a 1992 court case about the wreck. Given the current value of gold, that’s around $236 million in today’s dollars. And that’s just what’s documented: the ship had a number of wealthy passengers, who were likely carrying their own gold, so the total could be even higher.

It has been revealed that A ship full of gold, sunk and lost for over a century. It’s odd that the ship isn’t a household name. And the story keeps getting weirder: the wreck contributed to a massive recession, and when treasure hunters found the ship in the 1980s, decades of lawsuits followed.

Recent findings suggest that say you wanted to get from San Francisco to Newly introduced York City in the 1850s. Going over land was miserable—cars were a half century away, and there weren’t many roads. There wasn’t even a rail line connecting the two coasts. Your best bet was to take a ship down to what is now Panama, a train across that narrow bit of land, and then another ship up to New York.

Recent findings suggest that the SS Central America served the Atlantic part of that journey. It left the east coast of Panama on September 3, 1857, with 592 people on board. The ship had one other stop: Havana, Cuba. By September 8, when the ship was leaving that port, the weather looked great, according to a writeup by the US Naval Institute.

It has been revealed that that changed—hurricane-force winds battered the wooden hull. By September 11, the crew was working to bail out the ship, and by noon every man joined them. It wasn’t enough: by 2pm the water reached the boilers, leaving the ship drifting. The bailing continued all night, and for a while it seemed like the weather would clear up long enough for a full evacuation. It wasn’t to be—the storm resumed by mid-morning. The captain signaled a nearby ship, the Marine, for help. Only 100 people—including the 59 women and children—boarded the Marine.

Industry observers note that the captain went down with the ship around 8pm local time, along with most of the remaining men, who were pulled in by the undertow of the sinking ship. The few men who survived did so by grabbing doors, chairs, and anything else still floating, until another ship—the Ellen—could find them. In total, 425 people lost their lives.

Recent findings suggest that the human cost was high, but there was also a huge economic fallout. A 1992 paper by Lawrence D. Stone, the researcher whose work led to the rediscovery of the wreck, states that the gold on board was intended to shore up several banks already on the brink of collapse. Within a month, almost all banks in the US stopped offering gold in exchange for paper money.

Sources indicate that naturally, a ship this famous—with this much gold on board—became a bit of a legend. Countless people attempted to find the wreck, but no one succeeded until the Columbus-America Discovery Group of Ohio found the wreck in the 1980s. The crew was led by treasure hunter Tommy Gregory Thompson.

The discovery happened thanks to advanced technology—sonar and state-of-the-art remote-controlled submarines. But also because of math.

Industry observers note that stone, whose work I mentioned earlier, explained his method in a 1992 paper. He employed Bayesian search theory. This method begins with finding hypotheses about where the wreck may be, judging how likely each theory is, and ultimately making a map outlining the probability of the ship being in various areas. A route for the search is designed to start with the highest probability areas, continuing from there to lower probabilities.

According to recent reports, the survey took 40 days, covering 1,400 square miles of ocean off the Carolina coast. The wreck ended up being in a relatively low probability area, though one included in the route. In 1988, a remotely operated vehicle provided a view of the wreck.

According to recent reports, “The storybook result would have been for the Central America to have been found in a high probability area near the beginning of the search,” wrote Stone. “Given the actual result, what can we say about the value of the procedures for developing the search initiative? The most obvious thing to say is that they worked.”.

According to recent reports, that’s the thing about probability: the most likely thing isn’t always what’s true. That doesn’t mean it’s not worth calculating—it can still lead to good results.

It has been revealed that but what about the gold? Over the next few years the team brought up most of the commercial gold shipment. A federal judge put its bullion value at about $21 million in 1993, but coins and ingots from a famous shipwreck are worth far more to collectors. In 2000, the bulk of it sold for about $50 million. Today most of the gold is in the hands of private collectors.

This would normally be where the story ends: the treasure is found, the treasure hunters get paid, and everyone is happy. That’s not what happened this time.

By 1989, the insurance companies that covered the SS Central America back in the 1850s argued that the gold belonged to them. Their logic: We paid damages to clients who lost the gold, therefore it’s ours. The insurance companies lost that lawsuit, but it was only the beginning.

Sources indicate that thompson took $12.5 million from investors to fund the treasure hunt. Those investors sued in 2005, alleging they never got any proceeds from the treasure, even after the 2000 sale of the gold. Several members of Thompson’s crew sued in 2006. Thompson went into hiding in 2012, only to be arrested in 2015. He wasn’t released until March of 2026. Some 500 gold coins remain unaccounted for.

According to recent reports, it’s an odd footnote to a fascinating story of history, math, and science. And who knows? Maybe this story will still be going a hundred years in the future.

And there may be more to the story of the SS Central America. A 2018 expedition recovered more gold from a safe on the ship, in a passenger compartment. There could be more down there.

#16. This Four-Person NASA Crew Spent Over a Year on 'Mars.' Here's What They Did for 378 Days in a Simulated Martian Habitat

This Four-Person NASA Crew Spent Over a Year on 'Mars.' Here's What They Did for 378 Days in a Simulated Martian Habitat

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (826 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On October 31, four NASA crewmembers returned from “Mars.” Not the actual Red Planet, of course, but a 3D-printed Mars habitat in Houston where the three men and one woman lived for 378 days.
  • Now, the Mars analog astronauts—Ross Elder, Ellen Ellis, James Spicer and Matthew Montgomery—have started telling the world what took place after they disappeared into NASA’s Mars Dune Alpha habitat at the Johnson Space Center on October 19, 2025, for the agency’s second Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) mission.
  • The mission aimed to test the kinds of physical and mental conditions that a team of Mars explorers would endure on the Red Planet, including long-term isolation, disrupted communication with people on Earth and food cultivation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On October 31, four NASA crewmembers returned from “Mars.” Not the actual Red Planet, of course, but a 3D-printed Mars habitat in Houston where the three men and one woman lived for 378 days.

Now, the Mars analog astronauts—Ross Elder, Ellen Ellis, James Spicer and Matthew Montgomery—have started telling the world what took place after they disappeared into NASA’s Mars Dune Alpha habitat at the Johnson Space Center on October 19, 2025, for the agency’s second Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) mission.

The mission aimed to test the kinds of physical and mental conditions that a team of Mars explorers would endure on the Red Planet, including long-term isolation, disrupted communication with people on Earth and food cultivation. The habitat includes both a base and a mock outdoor environment, so the crew could practice Marswalks.

It has been revealed that “For more than a year, they have lived in an isolated environment, conducting critical research and helping us better understand what it will take to send humans to Mars,” Vanessa Wyche, director of NASA’s Johnson Space Center, said during a livestream, just before the crew emerged. “Inside just 1,700 square feet, they managed to live with limited resources. They maintained their habitat. They grew crops, and they carried out simulated Mars operations.”.

After the speech, NASA astronaut Jack Hathaway, who had just completed a mission at the International Space Station, knocked on the door to the Mars habitat, called out “trick or treat” and opened it to reveal the crew’s smiling faces. Since then, the analog astronauts have been participating in post-mission evaluations and debriefs that, along with the data collected during their year in the simulated environment, will help inform future missions to Mars and those closer to home, per a NASA statement.

So, what did they do for all that time?

“Most days, we had things that were scheduled, from maintenance and science and engineering activities and some operational activities. So, we often do extravehicular activities, also known as EVAs or spacewalks,” Elder, who was the mission’s commander and test pilot, tells CNN News Central. “We would do drone and rover operations where we control certain equipment outside of the habitat, and we would practice additional data collection for both human health and behavioral sciences.”.

Recent findings suggest that each team member brought unique expertise to the mission. Elder was an experimental test pilot at the U.S. Air Force. Ellis, the mission’s medical officer and tactical thinker, is a U.S. Space Force officer. Spicer was the flight engineer and systems specialist, and he has experience in satellite communications and spacecraft development. Montgomery’s diverse background in hardware engineering, robotics, technology startups and independent films made him the “Swiss Army knife of crewmates;” he served as the mission’s science officer and versatile engineer.

Quick fact: When was the first CHAPEA mission?

The first mission of this kind also lasted 378 days, during which crewmembers Kelly Haston, Ross Brockwell, Nathan Jones and Anca Selariu entered the Mars Dune Alpha habitat on June 25, 2023, and emerged on July 6, 2024.

It has been revealed that elder tells Fox News that combining their skills created “magic.” But that didn’t happen by accident; the selection process lasted about a year and a half and included personality evaluations by NASA psychologists, Montgomery tells the outlet. What’s more, they got to practice before entering the habitat.

“The crew spent a lot of time together prior to the mission, so we got to work on our teamwork and build relationships,” Montgomery tells Nature’s Kaia Glickman, including during a winter camping expedition that overlapped with a blizzard. “These high-pressure scenarios set a nice foundation for pre-training, where we spent five weeks together before going into isolation. Through all of those tools that we built, we had a really good dynamic as a team inside of the habitat, and conflict was very minimal.”.

Montgomery and his crewmates could still speak with mission control, but the communication system intentionally mimicked delays that would occur on a real Mars mission. That meant messages could take up to 22 minutes to deliver, and the team even had to deal with a planned two-week communication blackout. Future travelers to Mars will experience this communications barrier when Earth and the Red Planet are temporarily on opposite sides of the sun, blocking radio signals from traveling between the planets, according to Nature.

“Over the next several years,” Spicer tells Fox News, “the NASA researchers will be going through the data from our mission, as well as the previous CHAPEA mission, to figure out how well we did and what they still need to work on in the coming years to get real people to Mars.”.

Tech Report: COP31: How Ed Miliband answered Carbon Brief readers’ questions

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • UK foreign secretary and COP veteran Ed Miliband spoke with Carbon Brief earlier today at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, to answer readers’ questions.
  • Carbon Brief readers submitted questions via CB Connect on topics including the UK’s “climate leadership”, the COP31 electrification target, as well as the roadmaps on deforestation and fossil fuels.
  • Despite recent criticism over the approval of the Jackdaw gas field, Miliband argued that the UK is still seen as a climate leader, due to its “ambitious targets on net-zero”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UK foreign secretary and COP veteran Ed Miliband spoke with Carbon Brief earlier today at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, to answer readers’ questions.

Carbon Brief readers submitted questions via CB Connect on topics including the UK’s “climate leadership”, the COP31 electrification target, as well as the roadmaps on deforestation and fossil fuels.

Despite recent criticism over the approval of the Jackdaw gas field, Miliband argued that the UK is still seen as a climate leader, due to its “ambitious targets on net-zero”.

Pushing back on a question about COP reform, Miliband explained how he is “quite pro the institution of the COP”, given its role in bringing countries together for climate action.

He emphasised the importance of action on methane and the UK’s “support” for the “35×35” electrification pledge.

First attempt to address screen printing-induced degradation in copper-plated heterojunction solar cells

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The mechanical pressure and thermal treatments involved in screen printing can damage the sensitive passivating contact structures of HJT solar cells, increasing recombination losses and reducing conversion efficiency.
  • Researchers in China have investigated the mechanisms behind screen printing-induced degradation in copper-plated HJT solar cells and developed a method to mitigate the effects, potentially improving their suitability for large-scale manufacturing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, screen printing is widely used in solar cell metallization, but the process can cause degradation that adversely affects device performance. The glitch is particularly relevant for copper-plated silicon heterojunction (HJT) solar cells, which offer a promising route to reducing metallization costs and reliance on expensive silver.

The mechanical pressure and thermal treatments involved in screen printing can damage the sensitive passivating contact structures of HJT solar cells, increasing recombination losses and reducing conversion efficiency. Understanding the underlying degradation mechanisms is therefore essential to optimizing metallization processes without compromising cell performance.

Researchers in China have investigated the mechanisms behind screen printing-induced degradation in copper-plated HJT solar cells and developed a method to mitigate the effects, potentially improving their suitability for large-scale manufacturing.

It has been revealed that “The screen-printing process for photoresist application in HJT cells differs fundamentally from conventional screen printing of silver paste,” corresponding author Lang Zhou told pv magazine. “In silver paste printing, the screen openings account for only 2–5% of the total area, while the remaining surface is covered by an emulsion layer that prevents direct contact between the mesh and the wafer. In contrast, full-area photoresist coating typically uses a screen without emulsion coverage to ensure uniform resist deposition across the entire wafer surface. As a result, the mesh comes into direct and extensive contact with the wafer during each printing cycle.”.

Sources indicate that the researchers said previous investigations had revealed a gradual decline in conversion efficiency from 26.2% to 25.7% over 15,000 consecutive printing cycles in commercial solar cell production. The losses were mainly attributed to reductions in open-circuit voltage and fill factor, while short-circuit current density and electrical resistance remained largely unchanged. Further measurements indicated that minority carrier lifetime degradation increased from 0.61% with a new screen to 11.0% after 15,000 printing cycles.

The scientists used three-dimensional confocal microscopy to identify progressive wear of the screen mesh knuckles as the main cause of the degradation. As the knuckles wore down, their contact area with the wafer increased, placing greater mechanical stress on the underlying passivation layers. Although scanning electron microscopy revealed no visible surface scratches, photoluminescence measurements confirmed increased recombination losses, suggesting damage to the sensitive amorphous silicon/crystalline silicon interface.

Industry observers note that to address the glitch, the researchers developed an emulsion buffer layer to prevent direct contact between the screen mesh and the wafer surface. They evaluated six different patterns, with emulsion coverage ratios ranging from 2.9% to 16.6%.

The results showed a trade-off between mechanical protection and photoresist coating uniformity, as higher emulsion coverage reduced damage but impaired ink distribution. An emulsion coverage ratio of 4.7% provided the best balance, limiting minority carrier lifetime degradation to 0.41% after 10,000 printing cycles while maintaining relatively good coating uniformity.

The researchers attributed the improvement to the emulsion layer preventing direct contact between the screen mesh and the wafer surface, thereby reducing cumulative mechanical damage to the sensitive passivation layers.

“The findings demonstrate that a relatively simple modification to screen design can substantially mitigate printing-induced degradation, offering a practical approach to improving the manufacturing reliability of copper-plated HJT solar cells,” Zhou remarked.

The researchers presented their findings in “Screen-printing photoresist induced efficiency degradation and mitigation in Cu-plated SHJ solar cells,” published in Solar Energy.

Sources indicate that the development comes amid growing interest in copper metallization as an alternative to silver-based contacts in HJT solar cells. In April 2026, researchers at China’s Nankai University developed a silver-free HJT solar cell with 25.2% efficiency using plasma-induced interface engineering and copper electroplating. The approach addressed adhesion, contact resistance and stability challenges at the ITO interface, highlighting the potential of copper-based metallization for high-efficiency devices. pv magazine Global.

Recent findings suggest that in a separate development, scientists at Germany’s Forschungszentrum Jülich achieved 23.08% efficiency in a fully copper-metallized HJT solar cell. The silver-free device exhibited a relatively small efficiency penalty compared with its silver-metallized counterpart, while cells combining silver-copper paste on the front side with silver contacts on the rear reached 23.95% efficiency. The findings underline the potential of copper to reduce silver consumption, although further improvements in processing and electrical performance remain necessary. pv magazine Global.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Between 2016 and 2022, archaeologists conducting excavations along a planned stretch of England’s A14 highway unearthed an array of astonishing discoveries, including a Roman amulet carved to resemble the mythical Gorgon Medusa, the earliest physical evidence of beer production in Britain and an Iron Age comb crafted from a human skull.

Comprising more than 280,000 artifacts, the finds—uncovered between modern-day Cambridge and Huntingdon—shed light on life in the region over roughly 12,000 years. But some discoveries raised more questions than answers: Why, for example, did a single ditch at the Bar Hill site in rural Cambridgeshire contain some 8,000 amphibian bones?

Industry observers note that as Vicki Ewens, a senior zooarchaeologist at the Museum of London Archaeology (MOLA), told the Observer’s Dalya Alberge in 2022, “In my experience, mainly working on sites from London, we don’t get that many frogs. To have so many bones coming from one ditch is extraordinary.”.

Ewens and her colleagues outlined several possible explanations for the unusual cache. Perhaps the amphibians fell into the ditch (also described as a gully) and found themselves trapped. Or maybe they succumbed to extreme cold during their wintertime hibernation. Alternatively, they could have served as the centerpiece of a meal—or several—enjoyed by Iron Age humans, although the absence of cut marks on the bones rendered this scenario unlikely.

Four years after MOLA first announced the find, experts have finally solved the mystery of the ancient animal cemetery. Based on a groundbreaking analysis of amphibian arm bones, researchers led by Ewens and Paul Clarkson, an archaeologist at England’s Bournemouth University, concluded that most of the frogs whose remains were found in the ditch died young, eaten by birds of prey such as short-eared owls and hen harriers in the second or third century C.E., during Britain’s Roman era.

Sources indicate that A combination of environmental factors and human activity produced ideal conditions for this avian feast to unfold over a relatively short timeframe. As the authors write in the journal Environmental Archaeology, water levels in the Fens—the marshy wetland that houses the gully—retreated during the Roman period, enabling frogs in drying-out ponds to reproduce at a faster rate. When birds in search of their next meal arrived, they had no trouble spotting their prey: Locals had felled the trees in the area to make way for grazing livestock, leaving the amphibians with limited woodland protection from aerial predators.

“We don’t often get an owl’s eye view of what it was like in the past from archaeological sites,” Clarkson states in a statement. “These bones not only tell us about life for people living near the Roman Fens, but they also give insights into the natural world—what wild animals were getting up to in the past, and what life was like for them.”.

The majority of the bones belonged to frogs and toads (specifically common frogs), but shrews, voles and mice were also present in the assemblage. The remains represented no fewer than 469 individual animals.

It has been revealed that to estimate the frogs’ ages at their time of death, the researchers measured the amphibians’ distal humeri, or arm bones—a method previously described by Clarkson and several co-authors in a 2025 paper. According to the study, the team determined that a large number of the frogs died in either their first or second year of life, during a “short, intensive predation event” spanning autumn to the following spring, “probably along migration routes to and from hibernation sites.” An abundance of frogs likely attracted “local and migrant predators to the area to feed on them and also, coincidentally, on other locally available prey, such as voles, insectivores, birds and fish.”.

It has been revealed that based on breakage patterns and physical traces of digestion seen on the bones, the paper’s authors ruled out several species that typically prey on amphibians, including otters, gray herons and grass snakes. Instead, they suggest that the “lightly digested and relatively unbroken bones” are more consistent with medium-sized birds such as short-eared owls.

Initially, the archaeologists identified the gully as a roundhouse in an enclosure dating to Britain’s Iron Age, which began around 750 B.C.E. and ended with the Roman invasion in 43 C.E. But radiocarbon dating of the bones shifted this timeline forward by several hundred years.

Sources indicate that how did humans fit into this puzzle? Although the researchers considered the possibility that ancient people intentionally deposited the bones in the ditch, the only evidence for this scenario was the presence of a Roman-era brooch among the animal remains. In all likelihood, the authors argue in the paper, the mass predation event only took place because humans weren’t in the area at the time: Short-eared owls “only choose quiet roosting sites, so people must have rarely visited this area, particularly with dogs.”.

Why locals steered clear of this specific spot in the autumn and winter remains unclear, but the scientists posit that “the most probable explanation is seasonal movement of livestock.” Avoidance tied to social or ritual reasons is also possible.

“I had so many theories as to why such [a] large collection of frog bones were recovered from this small feature,” Ewens notes in the statement. “This research reveals how even the smallest animal recovered on a site can help us to understand not only past environmental conditions but human activity within a wider landscape.”.

Industry observers note that meilan Solly is a senior associate digital editor at Smithsonian magazine, where she oversees the online history section and writes about everything from archaeology to the British royal family. Solly’s specialties are Tudor England, Renaissance and modern art, and World War II.

Its flexible silicone adds to its durability, and a name window helps quickly identify luggage without revealing too much to prying eyes. Nine total colors add personality and help a suitcase stand out. It comes in a pack of two—no bag left untagged!

If you’re shopping for someone who loves something super personalized, beyond just color, the $19 Grommet Bag Tag from Visitag is for them. You can customize the front and back, or just the front: choose from 12 tag colors, six emoji locations (for an extra $2.50 per emoji), 12 characters of embroidered front-and-back text, and 17 thread colors for the embroidery on either side of the tag. The ID card is located inside the bag tag, giving just enough privacy. Durable and fun, and a way to make your suitcase stand out from every other spinner on the carousel … what more could someone want in a travel gift!?!

It has been revealed that the $29 Apple AirTag is a savior to anyone who has ever lost a device or bag. Its precise tracking makes it even easier than before to find bags; a louder speaker and redesigned chime help with the hunt. Consider upgrading to a four-pack to cover all your bags. The Chipolo Loop Rechargeable Bluetooth Tracker is a great Bluetooth tracker for Android phones, or any phone really, thanks to its universal compatibility with Apple Find My or Google’s Find Hub.

I’ve used this $38 BAGGU 3D Zip Set to store extra cords, emergency must-haves like Band-Aids and hand sanitizer, and to keep shoes separate from clothes. My favorite use for these utilitarian pouches is stowing all my goops and other toiletries. The large pouch expands to 10 inches by 7 inches; the medium one expands to 8.5 inches by 5 inches; and the smallest expands to 7 inches by 3 inches. Recycled ripstop nylon means I don’t have to be so gentle with these durable pouches, and they’re machine washable, a must for cleaning up rogue spills.

According to recent reports, these $40 Matador FlatPak Toiletry Bottles hold 90 milliliters of volume at half the bulk, so you’ll have enough shampoo, body wash, conditioner, and lotion for the entire trip. Flip the cap to dispense, and unscrew it to access the large fill opening. These space-saving travel bottles are five times lighter and almost four times more compact compared to their silicone counterparts. We also love the firm’s Waterproof Canister to protect vitamins, pills, 1ml/2ml travel scents, and other small bits.

According to recent reports, this $40, 16-ounce bottle from Zojirushi is just as high-quality and reliable as the company’s rice cookers (another gift we love to give). It features an electropolished SlickSteel interior that resists stains and prevents corrosion, plus a safety lock that prevents spills from accidental lid openings. An air vent on the mouthpiece lets water flow down the sip spout without gushing or overflowing, lessening the risk of spills. And one has kept our hot and cold beverages at a pleasant temperature for entire transcontinental flights. Looking for a bit more capacity? This bottle is also available in a 20-ounce size.

The $129 LARQ PureVis 2 significantly improves on its original PureVis bottle, which we reviewed in 2023. It now comes with USB-C charging, water intake tracking, and a filter straw that reduces chlorine, VOCs, and PFAS (PFOA/PFOS). It still includes powerful UV-C LED purification that runs every two hours and eliminates 99% of biocontaminants like E. Coli from your water and bottle. The Advanced filter tackles everything from the essential filter, along with haloacetic acids (HAAs, a disinfection byproduct), lead, and flame retardants, with an increased filter life of 40 gallons. Double-wall insulation keeps drinks cold for 24 hours, making it excellent for long travels. Choose from 23 or 34 ounces.

Recent findings suggest that the $38 VIM & VIGR 15-20 mmHg Merino Wool Graduated Compression Socks help improve blood flow and reduce leg achiness after hours in a pressurized cabin. Plus, the merino wool naturally regulates temperature, wicks moisture, and resists odor, making these a double-whammy for comfort. These compression socks are also ideal for hiking and make a great gift for anyone who spends a lot of time on their feet. VIM & VIGR creates compression socks with fun designs, because life is too short for boring socks.

Recent findings suggest that the Trtl Men’s Travel Hoodie is a $140 sweatshirt designed for long flights in chilly cabins or cross-country car trips in the cooler months. It may look like a regular hoodie with a kangaroo pocket, but a closer look reveals travel-focused features. It comes with a large zippered pocket and two smaller pockets that secure keys, headphones, phones, and a passport while keeping them within reach. Other travel-friendly features include a triple-layer hood that softens sounds in loud environments (e.g., Baby on Plane, Man with Undiagnosed Sleep Apnea Snoring, Bachelorette Fallout, etc.), lower armholes for easy removal in tight spaces, and no neck tags for comfort. And yes, it has thumbholes! Pair this travel hoodie with our favorite neck pillow and/or some noise-canceling headphones (keep scrolling for suggestions) for a perfect nap in transit.

According to recent reports, between cabin pressure and whatever passes for a meal in economy, a man’s guts may be going through things before you reach the gate (as a vegetarian often fed chickpeas and/or lentils, I’m speaking from experience). Well, these $109 pants were made for that, and other things. The four-way stretch fabric, with 11% elastane, plus a laser-perforated panel across the back let out the heat while you’re stuck in your seat. And a hidden elastic waist and drawstring keep the pants up without having to worry about a belt that might slow things down going through security (though Roark did add belt loops in case you have to rush to a more upscale dinner when you land). But wait, there’s more! Zip pockets can secure a passport, and a stash pocket in the back is deep enough for a phone when you’re fumbling with luggage. We’ve worn a pair from DC to Kona, as well as Atlanta to Tokyo, and would highly recommend them over sweatpants if you’re looking for long-haul comfort (particularly to warmer destinations) that lets you look more put together. And, while Roark doesn’t make these specific pants in a women’s style, they do have other options.

In a recent development, TSA may have loosened its shoes-off security rules, so you may not have to loosen your laces. But like everything when flying, that’s subject to change (especially if you get pulled aside for an extra screening). Plus, even if you can keep them on in the airport, you might want to take them off somewhere over the ocean. And if you’ve ever tried to tie your shoes again in a cramped economy row, you know it requires some contortionist skills. Not with Kizik shoes. The laces are just for looks. The shoes are designed so the heel compresses as you slip your foot in, then springs back into place (up to 30,000 times a pair). Some have a disguised mechanism, while others (like the $129 Athens 2 above, available in many colorways) show the compression cage. And they’re comfortable from Day One, thanks to the breathable stretch-knit upper (or soft leather on the Vegas 2), insole, and rocker sole/high-rebound midsole, which helps as you rush through a connection or explore a city. So go ahead, kick those shoes off when the seatbelt sign goes off.

It has been revealed that the $149 Purple Harmony Anywhere Pillow is for those who are picky about where they rest their head while counting Z’s, whether it’s in a hotel, on a friend’s couch, or while roughing it outdoors. The pillow packs luxury in a compact size: the Honeycomb GelFlex Grid and Talalay latex core keep the pillow firm and cool, while giving plenty of neck support. A moisture-wicking mesh cover keeps things airy, because a hot pillow makes for unhappy travels. Need something more targeted for those long hours in 32C? The Purple Back Pillow is great for portable lumbar support, and has made multiple overnight flights more bearable for us.

Plane cabins and train cars can get chilly; the $90 Rumpl Travel Puffy Blanket balances warmth and comfort with packability. In fact, it’s almost as large as a throw blanket and packs down to the size of a 32-ounce water bottle (shown above for perspective, but not included). Even better, it easily clips onto a backpack. Choose from sunset-inspired shades or your favorite solid color to show off your style while keeping cozy.

It has been revealed that these $359 Bose QuietComfort Headphones make an excellent, practical gift and are essential for travel: Planes and trains can be noisy, and playing your media sans headphones is a party foul on every mode of transportation. Bose makes some of the best noise-canceling headphones for airplane travel, from over-ear models to true wireless earbuds. This updated model comes with pill-shaped earcups, a 24-hour battery life, Immersive Audio, QuietControl noise cancellation that mutes practically all outside sound, and updated ActiveSense Tech to smooth sound spikes in Aware Mode.

Industry observers note that not everyone likes massive over-ear headphones (like the Bose above), or the feeling and more limited battery life of true wireless earbuds. Well, Marshall has a solution: The $229 on-ear Milton A.N.C. Bluetooth 6.0 headphones, which bring active noise cancellation to a less typical form factor. Six microphones feed the adaptive noise canceling, which is surprisingly effective despite not having the benefit of a complete seal around the ear. Plus, a charge lasts 50 hours with ANC on, and 15 minutes plugged in can get you 9.5 hours more, so Newly introduced York to Singapore and back ain’t a thang. And adaptive loudness/EQ/spatial audio settings help give those days in the air even more vibes. There’s a USB-C-to-3.5mm cable for wired listening (just remember your seatback entertainment system adapter, and to have the headphones charged because they don’t run passively). They fold up and only weigh 200 grams, so they’re perfect in an already-stuffed personal item, maybe even a jacket pocket. And they’ve got that classic Marshall cool, all textured, leather-like vinyl with brass logo/control knobs. You’ll be rockin’ even when you’re not walkin’ ….

In a recent development, we haven’t met wireless earbuds that haven’t announced “battery low” at some point before a flight ended, which isn’t optimal, especially if an attempt at getting some sleep is involved. But these $99 Bose wired earbuds will never give you up, never let you down, never get run down and desert you. Run off the USB-C port of any smartphone, tablet, or laptop, these bring back a newtro style Bose hasn’t made in a decade. And they are unlikely to discontinue it again anytime soon, considering the overwhelming positive response. Using the proprietary QuietControl algorithms that make other Sound By Bose products so good, they cut most perceived noise while providing a convenient three-button in-line remote that switches between Quiet, Aware, and off modes, plus offers playback controls. Plus, multiple eartip-and-stability band size combinations ensure a secure fit. And even if one comes loose on the way in/out of the included case, the 4.2-foot cable means you won’t have that moment of terror that an earbud rolled three rows back.

This $80 Anker Universal Charger combines compatibility with outlets from more than 200 countries into one power block charger. It detects local voltage in one second and is Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratory (NRTL)-certified for safe, stable charging. Unlike other international outlet adapters, this one is 25% smaller and designed to stay securely plugged in. And its USB-C/USB-A ports can charge four devices at once, including tech that requires higher voltage, like laptops and tablets.

No outlet is guaranteed in this world, but Anker’s $135 Laptop Power Bank keeps your devices charged when a place to plug in is nowhere to be found. Although it’s branded as a laptop power bank, it can also charge headphones, phones, handheld gaming devices, and more. It can charge an iPhone to full battery at least three times before running empty. The power hub can charge four devices at once. Two built-in USB-C cables mean you won’t have to root around for a charging cable when you need to recharge your tech. It also has a USB-A and USB-C port if you have a proprietary charger for a specific device.

Physical books can be clunky while traveling, especially as a voracious reader. The $160 Rakuten Kobo Clara is a black-and-white eReader that comes ad-free from the jump. I personally prefer it to the Amazon Kindle (which will cost you $170 to go ad-free) for this reason. The Rakuten Kobo Clara BW has 16 GB of storage and can carry up to 12,000 eBooks or 75 audiobooks. An optional Dark Mode makes for better nighttime or dark cabin reading, while ComfortLight PRO adjusts brightness, color temperature, and blue light to help you sleep easier while traveling.

This $80 JBL Clip 5 portable speaker packs pro sound into a pint-sized package. I always bring a small speaker like this one when I’m traveling so I can bump my getting-ready playlist from something that’s more powerful than my phone speakers. Pack it into a personal item or carry-on, or attach it to your person with an improved carabiner clip that sports a wider opening. The JBL Clip 5 has 12 hours of playtime on a single charge, is waterproof and dustproof, and can connect to other JBL Auracast-enabled speakers to get the party started when the plane lands.

Capture travels, adventures, and precious moments in high fidelity with the $700 Insta360 X6 8K Camera. Dual custom-built Sony 1/1.1″ square sensors, a 4-nanometer AI chip that can make edits of your day’s adventures while you sleep, and two imaging chips create quality images and video that feel just like the IRL moment, and 140 minutes of battery runtime keeps the camera rolling for every moment on the itinerary. Built-in stabilization, windproof microphones, and waterproofing up to 65 feet help you capture all the action, wherever it is. This travel gift is excellent for the travel vlogger and adventure enthusiast who records trips for friends, family, and followers to enjoy.

#5. Can Network Science Transform Health and Nutrition?

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 46m • 📚 Deep Dive (9250 w)

Can Network Science Transform Health and Nutrition?

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 46 min read (9250 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Quantamagazine

⏱️ ~46 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Almost every part of our lives exists in a network.
  • In this episode, two of the pioneers of network science – Albert-László Barabási and co-host Steven Strogatz – discuss how the field took shape, the ideas that underpin it, and why this is more than graph theory under a different name.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Click to tell Google to prioritize Quanta and see more of the best coverage of science and math in your search and AI results.

Chanelle Nibbelink for Quanta Magazine.

Nothing really exists in isolation. Almost every part of our lives exists in a network. Consciousness arises from what neurons do together, life from what genes and proteins do together, society from what we do together. When researchers began mapping real-world networks in the 1990s – from the World Wide Web to Hollywood actors linked by films – they found that wildly different systems shared architectural features that their components alone could not explain. This suggested common organizing principles for how networks form and develop.

In this episode, two of the pioneers of network science – Albert-László Barabási and co-host Steven Strogatz – discuss how the field took shape, the ideas that underpin it, and why this is more than graph theory under a different name. The conversation then turns to health and nutrition. Disease-related genes cluster in “network neighborhoods”, Barabási explains, which may help identify better drug targets and predict which patients will respond to which drugs. That work led him to his Foodome project, which catalogs the molecules found in the food we eat and asks what they do inside our cells. By his count, around 135,000 compounds lie outside conventional nutrition, which concerns itself mainly with energy, building blocks, and vitamins. These compounds, which he calls the “dark matter of nutrition,” and their effects on the body are only beginning to be understood.

Listen on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, TuneIn or your favorite podcasting app, or you can stream it from Quanta.

STEVE STROGATZ: Hello, I’m Steve Strogatz.

JANNA LEVIN: And I’m Janna Levin.

STROGATZ: And this is The Joy of Why.

Sources indicate that LEVIN: A podcast… where… you can’t make me laugh, okay. A podcast from Quanta Magazine where we explore some of the biggest unanswered questions in math and science today.

Recent findings suggest that STROGATZ: Well, hey, Janna, I’m gonna take you back in a time warp to the 1990s. Do you wanna go there with me?

STROGATZ: There was a trend back then, where people would play a game that they called Six Degrees of Separation.

LEVIN: Yeah, it was like the Kevin Bacon game.

Recent findings suggest that STROGATZ: Right. So if people don’t remember, Kevin Bacon, he was in a lot of movies and a game developed around him where you would name an actor, whoever, Marlon Brando or James Dean, and then you have to figure out a path of co-stars. You know, Marlon Brando was in such and such movie with somebody who was in a movie with Kevin Bacon. In that case, we would say Marlon Brando was two steps away. He had a Bacon number of two.

Industry observers note that LEVIN: [Laughs] Right. Now, this though has some actual mathematical underpinnings. And as I remember, you did substantial work on some of this, how we’re all connected and how the world is smaller than we think, how that happens. You know, how do you… Do you know the guy Joe from Chicago? And you’re like, “Of course I know Joe.” Right?

In a recent development, STROGATZ: Well, it is true. My student Duncan Watts and I got very interested in the math of Six Degrees of Separation, like what would a network have to be like to have that property? And around that time, when we published our paper, soon after we heard from Malcolm Gladwell before he was really famous as Malcolm Gladwell, and he wanted to talk about this idea, and he ended up writing an article that was called Six Degrees of Lois Weisberg.

STROGATZ: Yeah, that’s the point. Everybody knows Lois. Lois knew everyone in Chicago and all over the place.

And so, we all know that there are these connectors in our networks, and that’s actually what we’re gonna be hearing about to some extent in this upcoming interview with László Barabási.

So, he is a network scientist at Northeastern University. He’s also got an appointment with Harvard Medical School and with the Central European University in Budapest, Hungary. And he has been looking at the role of what he calls hubs. You know, these outsized Lois Weisberg-like nodes in a network that seem to have a tremendous number of connections and the effect that they have on the behavior of the network as a result.

LEVIN: This probably has application for other complex systems than just human social systems?

STROGATZ: Oh, it certainly does. Understanding networks, not just from the perspective of human social life, has had all kinds of consequences for our understanding of how diseases spread through populations, but also how brains are wired together. The way genes are connected in gene regulation networks, or even the power plants that provide energy to all our homes and businesses.

Recent findings suggest that so, yeah, very significant implications way beyond human society. So, for that, let’s turn to one of the experts. Here we go with László Barabási.

STROGATZ: Welcome to The Joy of Why, László.

ALBERT-LÁSZLÓ BARABÁSI: Oh, Steve, this is so much fun. I am a major listener of podcast, and Joy of Why is actually on my active list, so it’s so much fun to kind of see the sauce being made.

Recent findings suggest that STROGATZ: [Laughs] Well, it’s great to have you here. So just for full disclosure to our listeners, we have known each other a long time. It must be close to 30 years by now. I’d like to begin by going down memory lane with you to the early days of network theory. You spent a lot of your career looking at the world through the lens of networks. Why don’t you start by telling us what we mean by networks, and also what looking at the world this way offers us?

BARABÁSI: Well, you forgot to disclose the fact that we were responsible, you and I, for the field of network science, right? So we were once competitors, too. But let’s talk about why I think both of us cared about the networks at that time. Because fundamentally, nothing exists in isolation, right? A gene, a neuron, a human doesn’t make sense at all to kind of think about them in isolation. They all start making sense when they connect to other things. So consciousness is really about what the neurons do together. Life is what our genes and molecules do together. Society is what we do together.

And if we tend to focus, as much of science did historically, on the pieces, we are actually missing the why. Why do we have intelligence? Why do we have life? Why do we have societies?

STROGATZ: A-ha. So it’s this relational perspective. You’re pushing back against the usual straw man of reductionism, it sounds like.

It has been revealed that BARABÁSI: Don’t we all, right? Because, I mean, listen. Reductionism is a key tool in science, right? Without that, we cannot do networks. We need to know the pieces.

According to recent reports, but we as scientists got so busy looking at the parts that we have forgotten the whole thing. And then network science is really one of the disciplines whose starting point you gotta map out how things are connected and why that matters.

It has been revealed that STROGATZ: It’s interesting you talk about mapping things out, because back in the 1990s, especially towards the second half of the 1990s, each of us with our students wrote papers that made a major splash. That’s what you’re referring to when you speak of us starting the subject.

Sources indicate that but what do you think was known at the time we were starting and what was not known? What was it we collectively were trying to figure out?

BARABÁSI: Yeah. So I think none of us discovered networks, right? Networks were there for a long, long time, and many disciplines were aware of that, right? And I think in my mind, two things have changed.

Recent findings suggest that one of them is the availability of data, right? Our ability to take advantage of the revolution that was really brought to us by the internet to really start putting the pieces together and create the maps of how metabolites in the cell are connected to each other, how actors in Hollywood — your work, right — are connected to each other through common movies and so on.

And so one really opportunity that we all took advantage is the availability of the data. But then that by itself, in my mind, would have not been sufficient, right? Because if data becomes available, we could still have a theory of biological networks and a theory of social networks and difference.

In a recent development, the key discovery that we and others had made at that time is once we look from the network perspective of these systems, there are many more similarities in the architecture of real systems than differences. And I think that was surprising to all of us because I don’t have to convince anybody that a metabolic network within the cell should be different from a social network or should be different from the wiring of the brain. They have totally different purpose, totally different scale, totally different units who are being connected in different ways of interactions.

So what really shocked many of us physicists, mathematicians, biologists, is that many of these networks have common architectural features that could not be simply explained by the nature of the nodes and the links or the nature of the components, but it was hinting to some deeper organizing principles that governs connectedness.

STROGATZ: That’s very well expressed. That’s nice. This is a field, as you remember, and I certainly do, there’s a question of turf. You know, there are people, for instance, in pure math, who will say, “Don’t tell me networks are fresh. We’ve been doing graph theory since the Königsberg bridge problem with Leonhard Euler sometime in the 1700s.”.

But so, what are some of the differences in philosophy and content between, say, this subject and the older subjects, let’s just to pick two, graph theory and social networks?

It has been revealed that BARABÁSI: Of course. We are very grateful to many of our colleagues, the Erdős and Rényi and the László Lovász of mathematics and the Milgrams and the Manfred Kochens of social networks and so on, because they really been using graph theory to look at various problems related to connectedness.

I think the fundamental difference was that on one end, graph theorists never really bothered or were interested to look at real networks. Social network theorists, however, were limited to very, very small networks. And once the data became available on other networks, from biological to very large social networks, we started features that simply could not be observed at those smaller samples.

And most important — and I think this was the key — we and everybody realized that the models that the field has built up, for instance, the 1950s to pretty much the end of 1990s, were not sufficient to describe the reality of these systems. So there was a need for a very, very different way of thinking about that.

In a recent development, what was missing is that graph theory and social networks were using graphs as kind of cartographers to map out what’s out there, but they were not thinking so much about how things came into being. Why are networks the way they are? That is, networks are not static objects. They are dynamical entities that evolve in time. The large networks we see are the result of massive growth processes and how this temporal evolution, how these dynamics defines the way they look, their architecture, and their ability to do things, which is being alive, to think, to function as a system.

Sources indicate that STROGATZ: That’s a really nice point that there is this temporal aspect which was not particularly the concern of traditional graph theory. You know, now we all just talk about the internet, but to us in the ’90s, the World Wide Web was a shocking thing.

This is before social media. There was no Facebook. This was just web pages on the internet. There was a browser called Mozilla that came on around 1994, if I remember right, and you could start to do the thing that we called web surfing. So you started to have this visceral sensation of hopping from page to page through this vast, mysterious, hard-to-picture structure and you did some of the first work pioneering what it was like to navigate and explore this amazing, weird virtual world that didn’t exist until the ’90s. As you say, it’s like cartography, exploring a whole newly introduced world.

BARABÁSI: I’m glad you mentioned that because this unlocked network science for us. As a historical note, I wrote my first network paper in 1995 that never got published. It’s still there on the archive. And ’95 and ’96, I spent trying to convince computer scientists to help me map out the World Wide Web, and no one bothered to respond.

According to recent reports, I have sent countless emails to people who were building, like, robots at that time. We didn’t call them search engine. We called them robots and crawlers, and just asking for their data, and no one bothered to respond. It wasn’t ’til 1998 when How Hong Jon, my postdoc, who had a very strong programming skill came along, that we could actually finally embark on that project and map it out.

According to recent reports, and let me give you a little historical anecdote even for the listeners to indicate what kind of world was that. So right after we mapped the World Wide Web and our paper came out in ’99, I was immediately invited to the Internet Archives in San Francisco to give a talk, and there were about 10 of us speakers there, right?

Sources indicate that and there was a guy who came along, and he put a massive box on the table and remarked, “You know, I just funded a manufacturer, and why don’t you just take my T-shirt?” And the T-shirt said Google on it. It was Larry Page handing out, as a graduate student, his first T-shirts actually.

In a recent development, BARABÁSI: So, the fundamental difference between what we did and Larry Page did is that we just mapped out the network and not the content, and he, of course, cared about the content. And of course, that difference turned out to be a couple of trillion dollars in the long run. BARABÁSI: Oh, we have to geek out a little bit to do that, right? So I’m Hungarian and why I started thinking about networks back in late 1994 and ’95 is that I read pretty much the Hungarian graph theory literature, which is these two mathematicians, Paul Erdős and Alfred Rényi, as well as there was a book by Béla Bollobás.

Sources indicate that and they had a very simple and very powerful concept. They said, “Well, there are very complicated networks out there, and they look random, so why don’t we assume that they’re purely random? Let’s assume that the nodes are just randomly connected.” The dice decide who is your friend and nothing else but the dice.”.

Recent findings suggest that and based on that, they made a set of predictions, and one of the key predictions was that in a random universe we are very similar in how many friends we have. Remarkably similar.

So for us, the biggest shock when it came to the World Wide Web, that the number of links per node did not follow a Gaussian, the proverbial bell curve, but rather there were many, many web pages with a very few links and a few major hubs. And that was a purely empirical observation. Technically, we said the degree distribution follows a power law. What it meant is that there were major hubs holding together many small nodes, and that required an explanation, and that’s where growth comes in. Because what we realized back then is that the fundamental limitation of the random networks is that they assume that the way networks form is that we have a bunch of nodes that need to be somehow connected.

But in reality, networks form by one node at a time growing. Nodes join the system. Whether it’s a social network and people come in and join the club, whether it’s a biological networks where upcoming molecules are being synthesized and joining the network, and so on. Every network that is out there, without exception, is the result of some kind of long-lasting growth process. Sometimes four billion years, sometimes a few years, but it’s always growth.

And there was another feature what was also important is that when a new node comes in the system, it doesn’t just randomly pick any node, but it’s always biased towards the more connected nodes.

In a recent development, popular people are easier to be introduced to. Highly connected proteins are easier to actually connect to for biological reasons. But fundamentally, new nodes tend to connect to the more connected nodes. This is what we call preferential attachment.

Recent findings suggest that and this growth and preferential attachment, we were able to show is responsible for the emergence of the hubs. That is, if a network is growing and the choices are not random, hubs will naturally emerge. And this was such a simple explanation, such a simple deviation from what has happened in modeling that existed before, and suddenly was able to explain lots of systems, not only the World Wide Web, but even the Hollywood actor network but also like computer chips and citations and so on.
