Industry observers note that STROGATZ: Welcome back to The Joy of Why. We’re speaking with network scientist, László Barabási.

According to recent reports, you’ve, in more recent years, after this substantial boom in the late ‘90s, continued to do all kinds of pioneering work in applying networks to many different domains, let’s say medicine. Network medicine has become a thing.

STROGATZ: So, for people who haven’t heard of network medicine, what is that thing?

BARABÁSI: Well, network medicine really built on the back of genomics. Genomics provide us the list of the components in the cell. If you sequence your genome, you get precisely what genes you have, hence what proteins you have, what RNA you have in your body, and so on. So that gave us a complete inventory of the components. But they didn’t tell us how the pieces interact, who is interacting, who is binding to whom, and so on.

However, many diseases are rooted not in the fact that a component is broken. What does a mutation do that may cause a disease? Typically, it deforms a protein. What’s the consequence of deforming the protein? That the protein cannot link to other proteins or other metabolites. Either cannot bind to other proteins and cannot form bigger machineries, or cannot bind to another molecule and cannot catalyze a chemical reaction.

So really, the essence of life or how the cell works is through the connections that the components have to each other. The machineries in the cell, from mitochondria to hemoglobin, are the result of many proteins assembling tiny networks and creating little machineries that do things in the cell, like carry oxygen.

And the rest of the proteins are busy catalyzing the many chemical reactions that we talked about it, because one of the features of life is that virtually none of the chemical reactions that we have in our body take place by themselves. They always need a protein catalyzer for that.

Network medicine, on one end, tries to map out these interactions and then use that knowledge — the map — to really kind of understand what happens when a component is broken and downstream, where the effects are within the network, and eventually what disease you get as a result. And equally notable is like how do you intervene into this network to cure that disease, to fix the consequences of that broken component?

STROGATZ: Since I mentioned turf wars earlier, like in the case of network science, it would seem to me that any biomedically savvy person listening to this would think, “Is network medicine really something new?” Say, a biochemical pathway or a signal transduction pathway that the people working in cell biology like to talk about, are those just network medicine by another name, or, or were they missing some part of the picture?

BARABÁSI: They were always focused on the local effects. So, a pathway is really a set of reactions that always occur together. And yes, of course, as I mentioned earlier, there was a 150-year history in biology to systematically map each of these reactions out. But the tendency was that you became an expert on this reaction and the neighborhood, and there was no way to interrogate the full system, right?

And why does that matter? The simplest way to think about why it matters to have all of this bigger picture is because we don’t know how to treat molecular defects. Medicine does not yet know how to fix a mutation, right? There are dreams that we will get there, but by and large, none of the drugs that we have out there is really fixing the cause of the problem.

According to recent reports, what do we do? We go downstream from the problem, and we intervene down there to fix the consequences. So, if a protein is not working and is not catalyzing a particular chemical reaction, then you start giving them the molecule that is missing to the patient, right? So, for you to know where to intervene, you need to have the Google Map. You need to know how things are connected and what’s the right point where you enter.

In a recent development, so one study we did actually once I returned to Boston, to Harvard in particular, was that we looked at all the drugs out there. And the hypothesis always is that what a drug does is that it binds to a disease protein, right, a protein that is broken in the case of the disease. And shorter of a better term, it fixes the problem, right?

Recent findings suggest that but in reality, 85% of the drugs do not bind to anything related to the disease, that they don’t bind to what we call disease proteins or disease genes. They always act downstream. Because you don’t wanna mess with the disease genes. The disease genes are often very important genes that are involved in multiple processes. You wanna kind of correct the problem by going where the effect is that the gene is not doing or the protein is not doing what it’s doing.

It has been revealed that so if you wanna discover fresh drugs — discover what we call drug targets — we know all the disease genes from genomic screening, but that’s not enough. You have to go downstream from them, and network medicine gives you the pathways to say where should you look.

And this is exactly one of our big discovery, back around 2015, in the network medicine space, that every disease has what we call a disease module, which means that the genes involved in the disease are not randomly distributed in the network, but they tend to agglomerate in a certain network neighborhood, right?

Let’s take Upcoming York City, right? If the map of New York City would be the map of a cell, then you would find that you know the disease genes would not be randomly distributed around it. But all mental diseases are all around Times Square. And metabolic diseases may be around Wall Street, and maybe asthma would be all around Washington Square, right?

Sources indicate that so in the cell, there are these well-defined network neighborhoods where the disease resides. You need to map that out because that’s where you need to perturb in that neighborhood to fix the problem.

Recent findings suggest that and really, the last kind of twenty, thirty years was marked by a massive experimental effort to map these interactions out. These are a hundred to two hundred proteins who form a sub-network, and the kind of changes in that sub-network are typically associated with the emergence of RA.

According to recent reports, and precisely because this module is so large, when you take a drug like Humira, that is perturbing one part of the network. However, if your defect or your changes are in a different part of the network, it will not impact you.

It has been revealed that and what network medicine adds to this picture is that it maps out the relationships between them. In this case, we find about sixteen genes whose activity systematically changes, and so these are what we call biomarkers. So, it’s really was an interesting story of a combination of network medicine mapping out the neighborhood where the disease resides, and then using AI to build what we call a classifier to tell you whether for you or will the drug will work or not.

And this matters because in the case of Humira, this is a $90,000 treatment per year, and it takes about six months or longer to know whether the drug has an effect for you, whether it works for you or not.

Sources indicate that and so we noted, “Okay, food is molecules, so why don’t we just map out somehow what does food do to our cells?” And the canonical picture is what food does is gives us energy, and nutrition is dealing with that, right? #4. Tech Report: Thawing Permafrost May Have Created a Newly introduced Type of Landslide, Which Could Become More Common as the World Warms

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (696 w)
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Smithsonianmag

Tech Report: Thawing Permafrost May Have Created a Newly introduced Type of Landslide, Which Could Become More Common as the World Warms

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (696 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in 2017 and 2018, a pair of strange landslides moved huge masses of rock and dirt in Canada’s Northwest Territories.
  • The two natural disasters are part of a newly introduced class of landslides scientists are calling “permafrost detachment slides” in a study published in the journal Geophysical Research Letters in September.
  • Industry observers note that “It’s a very dramatic manifestation of the changing climate,” says study co-author Joseph Young, a geoscientist who conducted the work at the University of Alberta in Canada, to Matt Simon at Grist.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in 2017 and 2018, a pair of strange landslides moved huge masses of rock and dirt in Canada’s Northwest Territories. The events occurred in the central Mackenzie Valley, and one of them even dammed a river and created a lake.

The two natural disasters are part of a newly introduced class of landslides scientists are calling “permafrost detachment slides” in a study published in the journal Geophysical Research Letters in September. They may have been partially triggered by severe wildfires that occurred in 1995, which destabilized the ground and allowed the base of the permafrost to thaw. What’s more, these events may become more common as the planet continues to warm.

Industry observers note that “It’s a very dramatic manifestation of the changing climate,” says study co-author Joseph Young, a geoscientist who conducted the work at the University of Alberta in Canada, to Matt Simon at Grist. “They’ve only started happening in the last 10, 15 years, and it’s a very drastic and abrupt change in the landscape.”.

Young and his colleagues began the study after seeing something strange in the Northwest Territories in 2019. While conducting field research, they spotted large landslide scars in valleys that they knew were stable permafrost, or permanently frozen earth, reports Stephanie Pappas for Live Science.

To better understand what happened, the team homed in on two major events: the Johnson River slide in August 2017 that moved about 4.5 million cubic meters of dirt and rock, and the Redstone River slide in August 2018 that sent roughly 18 million cubic meters of debris tumbling down. Satellite imagery captured between 1980 and 2020 and field studies revealed some odd characteristics, the team found.

Recent findings suggest that “Typically with permafrost, everything just thaws and melts in a slurry and moves like a mud downslope,” Young tells Live Science. “But with these large landslides, we found blocks of frozen material in the debris.”.

Sources indicate that the team monitored the temperature near the 1995 burn area near the slides and, for comparison, undisturbed forest from September 2020 to August 2022. Their data went into computer simulations, which allowed the researchers to investigate how the wildfires decades earlier may have affected the region.

The Northern Hemisphere’s permafrost regions cover an area equal to nearly 2.5 times that of the contiguous United States.

Their resulting hypothesis? The fires that swept through the landscape burned off the vegetation that usually keeps the permafrost cool on sunny days. “After about 20 years or so, that thermal signature from the burned forest can reach the base of permafrost,” Young tells Grist. “It’s slight, but it’s there.”.

It has been revealed that as the frozen ground warmed, it weakened and formed cracks, allowing water to seep in. That allowed the permafrost to thaw even more, destabilizing its bottom layers. Eventually, that caused the ground to detach and created the two landslides at the center of the study. They’re among more than 150 permafrost landslides in the area that happened around two decades after the severe wildfires, meaning the newly proposed mechanism could have contributed to many of these catastrophic events.

Recent findings suggest that the findings suggest scientists need to better study what’s happening below the surface of permafrost regions, indicates Dmitry Nicolsky, a geophysicist at the University of Alaska Fairbanks who wasn’t involved in the work, to Nikk Ogasa at Science News. “We don’t know how [the ground] will move—it might go slowly or it might go catastrophically.”.

Thankfully, Young notes experts can look out for signs of an impending permafrost detachment slide and predict when it’s going to happen.

“That’s kind of the silver lining,” he tells Julia Parrish at the CBC. “It doesn’t just happen overnight; it kind of happens in a more progressive manner over the course of about 20 years after a fire, where you get a slow downslope movement of these slopes.”.

#2. Latest Update: Two Centuries After This Bronze Leg Emerged From a Scottish Bog, Archaeologists Believe It May Have Belonged to a Towering Statue of a Roman Emperor on Horseback

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (940 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smithsonianmag

Latest Update: Two Centuries After This Bronze Leg Emerged From a Scottish Bog, Archaeologists Believe It May Have Belonged to a Towering Statue of a Roman Emperor on Horseback

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (940 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 1820, a larger-than-life gilded bronze lower leg was pulled out of a bog in the Scottish Borders region.
  • But ahead of “Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire,” an exhibition at the National Museum of Scotland (NMS), researchers have determined that the so-called “Milsington leg” was not stolen from the south, nor was it violently severed.
  • “This really turns on its head our understanding of Rome’s second attempt at conquering Scotland,” Fraser Hunter, principal curator of prehistoric and Roman archaeology at NMS, says in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 1820, a larger-than-life gilded bronze lower leg was pulled out of a bog in the Scottish Borders region. For more than two centuries, historians discredited the idea that the Roman-era artifact came from Scotland, instead assuming that it was hacked off a monument in England and hauled north by marauding tribes.

But ahead of “Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire,” an exhibition at the National Museum of Scotland (NMS), researchers have determined that the so-called “Milsington leg” was not stolen from the south, nor was it violently severed. Instead, they posit that it formed part of a colossal equestrian statue of the Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius that once stood in southern Scotland in the second century C.E., before it was dismantled by retreating Roman troops.

“This really turns on its head our understanding of Rome’s second attempt at conquering Scotland,” Fraser Hunter, principal curator of prehistoric and Roman archaeology at NMS, says in a statement.

Roman campaigns into modern-day Scotland began in the 70s C.E., several decades after the conquest of Britain. Emperor Hadrian, who ruled from 117 C.E. to 138 C.E., consolidated the Romans’ northernmost limit in northern England, where Hadrian’s Wall still stands.

Recent findings suggest that hadrian’s successor, Antoninus Pius, pushed his armies north again, and in the early 140s C.E. fortified a position about 100 miles north of Hadrian’s Wall, known as the Antonine Wall. A few years after Antoninus Pius died in 161 C.E., the Roman armies retreated south, back to Hadrian’s Wall.

The timeline of the second century C.E. Roman invasion of southern Scotland—and eventual withdrawal—provides the context for the bronze limb.

Close inspection reveals that rather than bearing jagged axe or saw marks, the upper edge remains intact, just as Roman metalworkers originally cast it in the 140s C.E. An absence of gilding around the knee indicates that the leg was covered by a tunic or cloak, part of a larger statue, perhaps similar to the equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius in Rome.

“When you look, you see it hasn’t been hacked off, it’s a complete leg,” Hunter explains to the Telegraph’s Ruby Cline. “So rather than loot, it looks as if the statue has been carefully decommissioned at the end of its life.”.

When Roman forces abandoned southern Scotland, they routinely dismantled and buried prized monuments, including stone altars and inscriptions from the Antonine Wall, rather than leave them behind, per the statement.

Installing a large, visually impressive statue in a border region was purposeful for Antoninus Pius, for whom victory in Scotland was “something which was worth celebrating,” Hunter explains in the statement.

Politically, too, “it makes sense, the Romans producing propaganda right in those contested areas,” Hunter tells the Telegraph. To Scottish Iron Age communities with virtually no tradition of naturalistic human portraiture, a gleaming gilded emperor on horseback would have appeared “really, really alien,” Hunter tells the Guardian’s Severin Carrell.

Following its excavation in 1820 near Hawick, Scotland, the Milsington leg spent a century tucked away in the Dalkeith Palace, near Edinburgh.

Upon hearing of the discovery, Scottish writer Sir Walter Scott noted in a February 1820 letter to Lord Montagu that finding such a large Roman artifact “in so wild a place, has something very irritating to the curiosity,” adding that he hoped to examine the piece and possibly dig for the remaining fragments himself.

A post shared by @nationalmuseumsscotland.

Industry observers note that in the exhibition, the Milsington leg is mounted onto a full-scale silhouette reconstruction of horse and rider. The exhibition also features a digital facial reconstruction of a decapitated man buried near the Roman fort of Inveresk, alongside an intricate, tin-coated enamel brooch from Pathhead that may have been a diplomatic gift from Roman forces to a local leader. Other artifacts on view are a unique animal-relief earthenware bowl, the skeleton of a carefully buried cavalry horse and two altars from a temple dedicated to Mithras, a deity of the sun.

Recent findings suggest that beyond imperial grandeur, the exhibition illuminates how Rome’s presence reshaped indigenous society in the northern reaches of the province of Britannia. Hunter estimates that roughly 10,000 Roman soldiers—including auxiliaries from North Africa and modern-day Romania—alongside another 10,000 camp followers, wives and enslaved people lived across southern and eastern Scotland during the Antonine occupation, per the Guardian.

Hunter suspects that undiscovered Roman forts once stood near where the limb was deposited and hopes that future surveys or metal detectorists might finally turn up the emperor’s torso or his bronze steed, more than 200 years after the leg emerged from the bogs.

Industry observers note that “It offers us a tantalizing glimpse into the kind of grand monuments which once stood in southern Scotland and reveals the importance Pius placed on his victories in Scotland,” Hunter says in the statement. “But it begs the question ... where is the rest of the statue?”.

“Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire” is on view at the National Museum of Scotland in Edinburgh from November 14, 2026, through April 18, 2027.
